h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Intention] We profess that God is the Lord and Father of all things, the beginning and end of everything; that His Son, Our Lord Jesus Christ, was made flesh, died, and rose from the dead to save all men; and that the Holy Spirit is the Lord and giver of life. For the glory of the Holy Trinity, for a greater manifestation of the Incarnate Word, and for the honor of the Church founded by Christ which “subsists in the Catholic Church which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the bishops in communion with him,” we want to give “testimony that the world can neither be transfigured nor offered to God without the spirit of the beatitudes.” We ask the Blessed Virgin Mary to grant us the grace to persevere in this purpose until death.
f: LG 8. LG 31.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: We want to live in a state that “constitutes a closer imitation and an abiding re-enactment in the Church of the way of life embraced by God’s Son when he came into the world...” by the practice of the evangelical counsels, thus contributing to the revelation of “the variegated nature and the multiple dynamism of the Incarnate Word of God.”
f: LG 44. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to members of the Council of the Union of Superiors General, November 26, 1979.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Name] We want our Religious Family to be known as and called “the Incarnate Word” as we approach the 2,000th anniversary of the Incarnation, an unsurpassable event greater than the creation of the world.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Universal Purpose] Our objective is twofold. First, we seek the glory of God and the salvation of our own souls, and those of our brethren. We do this especially by practicing those virtues that allow us to share more fully in Christ’s emptying of Himself.
f: Cf. Phil 2:7-8; PC 5.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Specific Purpose] Secondly, we specifically pledge all our strength to inculturate the Gospel, that is, to extend the Incarnation “to all men, in the whole man, and in all of the manifestations of man,” in accordance with the teachings of the Magisterium of the Church. In this respect, His Holiness Blessed John Paul II teaches: “The term ‘acculturation,’ or ‘inculturization’ may well be a neologism, but it expresses very well one of the elements of the great mystery of the Incarnation.”
f: Cf. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Meeting with men and women of culture and entrepreneurs in the Seminary of San Toribio in Lima, n. 5 (5/15/1988) (a todo el hombre y a todas las manifestaciones del hombre) (Translation is ours). Especially: GS 53-62, EN 20, CT 53, etc. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the Pontifical Biblical Commission on Biblical Science and Magisterium of the Church, April 26, 1979. OR (04/24/1979) Spanish Edition.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Consecration by Means of Vows] In order to achieve greater perfection in our service to God and His people, we take three vows: chastity, for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven (Mt 19:12); poverty, sell what you have (Mk 10:21); and obedience, which is better than sacrifice (1 Sm 15:22). We do this in order to more closely imitate the chastity, poverty, and obedience of the Incarnate Word.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Foundation] We want to always be rooted in Jesus Christ, and only in Christ, who has come in the flesh (1 Jn 4:2) and lives forever. We want the fullness of Christ in everything and everybody, for no one can lay any other foundation (1 Cor 3:11) than Christ, the Rock. We want to love and serve Jesus Christ – His Body and His Spirit – and to help others love and serve Him. We want to love and serve the physical Body of Christ, the Eucharist, as well as His Mystical Body, the Church. His Church consists of us – who must become “other Christs” through the holiness of our lives – and of all men in whom we see Christ himself, especially the poor, the sinners, and enemies. We want to be “like another humanity of Christ.” We want to be chalices full of Christ, chalices that allow the superabundance of His grace to overflow upon others. We want to show by our lives that Christ is alive, and that His Spirit is the soul of the Church, because anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Rom 8:9).
f: Cf. 1 Cor 10:4. BLESSED ELIZABETH OF THE TRINITY, Elevation 34.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Spirituality] In this respect, we believe that our spirituality must be profoundly marked by all aspects of the mystery of the Incarnation, namely: a) the origin of the Incarnation; b) Christ’s two Natures (Human and Divine); c) the union of these Natures; d) the purpose of the Incarnation.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: a) The Origin of the Incarnation. We must have a deep and firmly-rooted devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, the active principle of the Incarnation, and to the Persons of the Most Holy Trinity to Whom the work of the Incarnation is appropriated, that is, to the Father, insofar as He is the Principle of the Son – For I proceeded and came forth from God (Jn 8:42), and to the Holy Spirit, insofar as He is the personal Love from Whom all divine works proceed – “by the Holy Spirit [He] was incarnate…”. The primacy of the spiritual derived from this devotion must permeate our thoughts, feelings, and actions since it is God at work in us, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:13). The teaching of the Incarnate Word in this respect is clear: seek firsthis kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things shall be yours as well (Mt 6:33). Our devotion to the Most Holy Trinity must also produce a total abandonment to God’s “will of good pleasure” for us, following the example of the Virgin Mary who said: I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word (Lk 1:38).
f: Apostle’s Creed.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: b) The Two Natures of Christ: Human and Divine. We want to fervently practice the transcendent virtues of faith, hope and charity, in order to be the salt... and the light (Mt 5:13ff) and thus not to be of the world. To do this, we must pray without ceasing (1 Thes 5:17), and we must go through the active and passive purification of the senses and of the spirit for unless you repent you will all likewise perish (Lk 13:3).

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: We want to fervently practice the virtues of self-denial: humility, justice, sacrifice, poverty, suffering, obedience, and merciful love…; more succinctly, we simply want to take up our cross. We must be in the world and, in Christ, assume all that is human, since “what is not assumed is not redeemed,” but rather “becomes a new idol replete with all the old malicious cunning.” As priests, working as spiritual directors, we must enlighten the temporal order and form lay people so that they can “direct temporal matters according to the plan of God.” We must not take on “matter” that is not worthy to be assumed, such as sin, error, lies, evil: abstain from every form of evil (1 Thes 5:22).
f: Cf. Mt 16:24. Cf. Jn 17:11. SAINT IRENAEUS, quoted in DP 400. DP 400, 469. LG 31.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: c) The Union of the Natures. The center of our life must be Jesus Christ, true God and true man, who unites both natures in one, unique, divine Person. We profess that truly the Word became flesh (Jn 1:14), and He is the one mediator between God and men (1 Tm 2:5); He is the only one who has the words of eternal life. Among the Persons of the Most Blessed Trinity, He is the Person who proceeds as the term of the Incarnation. In a particular way, our devotion to Jesus Christ must be made manifest in the imitation of: His emptying of Himself, namely, in the mystery of the Incarnation; His second emptying of Himself in the mystery of the Passion – the supreme priestly action – that, by way of contrast, makes us admire the kenosis of the Incarnation even more deeply; The mystery of His Second Coming which constitutes the fullness of His First. Intimately united to the mystery of our religion, [that] He was manifested in the flesh (1 Tm 3:16), and therefore also united to our love, are the “three white things of the Church”: the Eucharist, which perpetuates the Incarnation under the species of bread and wine by the action of the Catholic priesthood; the Most Holy Virgin Mary, who gave her yes so that from her flesh and blood the Word was made flesh; the Pope, in whom the Truth, the Will, and the Sanctity of Christ become flesh.
f: Cf. Jn 6:68. Cf. Phil 2:7. Cf. Jn 1:14.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: We must embrace the practice of those virtues which are seemingly opposed, and we do so against all false dialectics; we must respect the essence of the virtues without confusing them. We must avoid all false duality by practicing truthfulness, fidelity, coherence and authenticity of life, against all falsehood, infidelity, pretense and hypocrisy; we must restore entirely all things in Christ, for he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor 15:25), and thus take possession of the entire universe for Christ, by uniting all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth (Eph 1:10).

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: d) The Purpose of the Incarnation. In Christ we want to seek the glory of God and the overall well-being of man. By introducing His firstborn Son into the world, the Father manifested His glory: we have beheld his glory (Jn 1:14); it follows that we want always to have the right intention: whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).
f: Cf. Heb 1:6.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: Since “every individual human being is the way for the Church,” and since “it is only in the mystery of the Incarnate Word that the mystery of man truly becomes clear,” we want to work for man’s overall well-being by showing him his nature, dignity, vocation, inalienable rights, freedom, and eternal destiny and thus achieve the goal of faith, which is the salvation of souls. We will earnestly focus our attention and apostolic activity on all things until we see Christ being formed in all men.
f: DM 1; cf. RH 13. GS 22. Cf. 1 Pt 1:9. Cf. Gal 4:19.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Apostolate] In a special way, we will be devoted to preaching the Word of God, sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12), in all its forms by: studying and teaching Sacred Scripture, theology, the Church Fathers, liturgy, catechesis, ecumenism, etc.; conducting outreach missions and preaching the Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius of Loyola; focusing on the education and Christian formation of children and young people; preaching through works of charity especially in the service of the most needy (abandoned children, the handicapped, the sick, the elderly); searching for and forming suitable ministers of the Word through the publication of journals, treatises, books, etc. We want to spread the Word through verbal and written communication.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Marian Slavery] We want to manifest our love and gratitude to the Blessed Virgin by making a fourth vow of slavery to Mary according to the spirituality of Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort. This will secure her indispensable help in perpetuating the Incarnation in all things. We do not want our Religious Family to be guided by any spirit other than the Holy Spirit. If our Religious Family is led by another spirit at any time or in any place, we beg our Lord to eliminate it from the face of the Church.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: [Fidelity to the Holy Spirit] Only with absolute fidelity to the Holy Spirit can we skillfully use the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph 6:17). Our feeble breath is only fertile and irresistible when it communes with the Wind of Pentecost.

h: Our Religious Family: General Principles or Our “Way” (cf. Acts 9:2)
t: In order to achieve the best total and unrestricted docility to the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of Christ, we need the Holy Virgin Mary to be the form, mold, and guide of all our actions. In this way, we can say with our entire soul and heart, now and forever, “Totus tuus, Maria!”
f: Cf. Rom 8:9. SAINT BONAVENTURE, (inter opera) Psalt Maius, Canticum ad Instar illius, Is 12 (Opera Omnia – Vives, Paris 1868) Vol. 14, 221 a.b.; SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNON DE MONFORT, TD 216; Episcopal motto of Blessed John Paul II.

t: In the name of Christ, we desire to be a Religious Family: whose members are willing to radically live the demands of the Incarnation, the Cross, the Sermon on the Mount, and the Last Supper; wherein the humiliations of Nazareth and Calvary can be imitated; wherein one can enter the secrets of Tabor and Gethsemane; wherein it is possible to experience the Father’s paternity, the brotherhood of the Son, and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, so that we can love each other as sons of the same Father, brothers of the same Son, and temples of the same Holy Spirit, forming one heart and soul (Acts 4:32).

We desire to consecrate ourselves to God by the public profession of the evangelical counsels, forming a religious institute. We will live a fraternal life in common, separated from the world in a way befitting religious, so that all our members may tend to perfection in accord with their consecrated state. Harmoniously integrated into our Religious Family, we also include religious who may not be priests, and associations of the faithful who want to live in a genuine spirit of family according to their lay vocation.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 598, §2. Cf. CIC, c. 677.

t: Imitating “Christ proclaiming the Kingdom of God,” we want to dedicate ourselves to apostolic work under the direction of clerics, thus assuming the exercise of Sacred Orders. Some members of our Institute have an exclusively contemplative life, either monastic or eremitic. Likewise, it is possible that some members of the apostolic branch could live a more contemplative type of life for a predetermined time, since “a pause for true worship has a greater value and spiritual fruit than the most intense activity, were it apostolic activity itself.”
f: Cf. CIC, c. 577. Cf. CIC, c. 588, §2. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the Superiors Generals of Orders and Religious Congregations, n. 4, (09/24/1978). OR (12/3/1978) Spanish Edition.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: Like all institutes of consecrated life, religious as well as secular, we have a universal and common end – often called vocation – by which we want to follow Christ more closely under the action of the Holy Spirit. We want to dedicate ourselves totally to God as our supreme Love, so that, dedicated by a new and special title to his glory, for the edification of the Church and for the salvation of the world, we may achieve the perfection of charity. Through this charity, to which we are led by the profession of the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience, we want to be united in a special way to the Church and her mystery.
f: Cf. CIC, Norms Common to All Institutes of Consecrated Life, cc. 573- 606. Cf. CIC, c. 573.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: Likewise, we tend to the proper end of all institutes of religious life, which is the total consecration of our person, manifesting the admirable betrothal established by God in the Church, the sign of heavenly life. In this way we will accomplish the full offering of ourselves as a sacrifice acceptable to God by which our entire existence becomes continuous worship to Him in charity.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: This consecration is manifested by forming a Religious Family, professing vows publicly, and living a fraternal life in common. The public testimony we must give includes detachment from the world. To live according to the Holy Spirit, we must separate ourselves from the spirit of the world: … the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him (Jn 14:17).
f: Cf. CIC, c. 607-709. Cf. CIC, c. 607.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: Finally, as our specific and singular end, we want to dedicate ourselves to evangelization of the culture – to work, “through the power of the Gospel, to transform:

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: - mankind’s criteria of judgment, - determining values, - points of interest, - lines of thought, - sources of inspiration, - models of life.”
f: EN 19.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: We want to do this so that the “very power of the Gospel should permeate:

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: - thought patterns, - standards of judgment, - and norms of behavior.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Sapientia Christiana, 1. OR (6/3/1979), 7, Spanish Edition.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: We cannot forget what the Second Vatican Council pointed out: “One of the gravest errors of our time is the dichotomy between the faith which many profess, and the practice of their daily lives.” In large part, this is because the world “in recent times has come to the point of separating and detaching itself from the Christian foundations of its culture,” leading to the de- Christianization of the culture.
f: GS 43. ES 14.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: To permeate cultures with the Gospel, we regard the following elements as fundamental: the teachings of the Second Vatican Council’s Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World (Gaudium et Spes), the Apostolic Exhortations Evangelii Nuntiandi and Catechesi Tradendae, Blessed John Paul II’s speech to UNESCO and others on the same subject, the Puebla Document, the Encyclical Letter Slavorum Apostoli, the Encyclical letter Redemptoris Missio, the Post-Synodal Apostolic Exhortation Pastores Dabo Vobis, n. 55, c, and any forthcoming directives, orientations and teachings of the Magisterium of the Church that may be issued regarding the specific purpose of our small Religious Family.
f: Second part, chapter 2,53-62. Cf. EN 20. Cf. CT 53. Discourse to the U.N.O. for Education, Science, and Culture, (June 2, 1980); OR (06/15/1980) Spanish Edition. Cf. Speech to the Bishops of Zaire in Kinshasa (May 3, 1980) 4-6; OR (5/11/1980) Spanish Edition; Discourse at the Episcopal Conference in Kenya, Nairobi (May 7, 1980), 6; OR (5/18/1980), Spanish Edition; Speech to the Bishops at the cathedral in Delhi, India (February 1, 1986), 5; OR (2/9/1986) Spanish Edition; Speech to the congregation at the celebration of the Word Chambacu, Cartagena, Colombia (July 6, 1986), 7-8; OR (7/20/1986) Spanish Edition. Cf. 385-443.

h: Article 2: Common, Proper, and Specific End
t: We wish to form the most filial and fraternal bond with the Pontifical Council for Culture to achieve a more widespread and better accomplishment of the Institute’s aim.

We believe that one of the most important ways to attain the Institute’s purpose is through work focused on key areas of culture, namely: families, education (especially in seminaries, universities, and colleges), mass media, and thinkers or intellectuals. Regarding the latter, we will work in the calling, development, discernment, formation, consolidation, accompaniment, and further exercise of a vocation to the intellectual apostolate.

The specific charism of our Institute requires all its members to work in supreme docility to the Holy Spirit and according to the example of the Virgin Mary, so that Jesus Christ will be the Lord of all that is truly human, even in the most difficult situations and under the most adverse conditions.

This charism is the grace to know how to work concretely so as to extend the presence of Christ in families, education, the mass media, the scholarly, and in all other legitimate manifestations of human life. It is the gift of making each person “like a new Incarnation of the Word,” thus fulfilling our essential call to be missionaries and Marian.
f: BLESSED ELIZABETH OF THE TRINITY, Elevation 33.

t: The mission, received from the founder and submitted to the Church for approval, is to bring to fullness the effects of the Incarnation of the Word, “the epitome and root of all good”; this is to be done especially in the vast world of culture, i.e., the “manifestation of man as an individual, as a community, as a people, as a nation.”
f: SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, Homilies on St. Matthew, 2,3. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the Men of the Culture on the Occasion of the Jubilee of Redemption, December 12, 1983. OR (12/25/1983) Spanish Edition.

t: The spirit which has animated our Institute from its beginning, and which must determine its own identity within the Church, is the spirit of faith and love. All members must live the mystery of the Incarnate Word and its relationship with every creature in this spirit: “The Word is expressive not only of the Father, but of all creatures... (and as regards to creatures) He is both expressive and operative.”
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST I, 34, 3.

t: This spirit is to live and to make others live under the action of the Holy Spirit, without coercion of any kind; this must be done by scrupulously respecting each individual’s conscience, promoting healthy pluralism, bringing others to fully live the freedom of God’s children, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Cor 3:17). At the same time, we must operate while never forgetting that the kingdom of God is… righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17).
f: Cf. Rom 8:21.

t: There is no point in extending ourselves to many countries or having numerous members if we lose our spirit. Infallibility and indefectibility are only promised to the Catholic Church, in the person of Peter and his successors. We will not lose our spirit as long as we are faithful to the Church and observe the will and intentions of the founder in everything related to the patrimony of the Institute.
f: Cf. CIC, c 578.

t: [Introduction] We seek to be anchored in the sacrosanct mystery of the Incarnation – the mystery of the Word made flesh in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary. We can say that our spirituality is derived from the Person of the Word and His Mother, so that, in the Holy Spirit, we may become united to the Father. All the principles of our Institute’s spiritual life, as stated in the Directory of Spirituality, stem from the elucidation of the mystery of the Incarnate Word.

[The Primacy of Jesus Christ] “[T]he name, the teaching, the life, the promises, the kingdom and the mystery of Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God” must take priority in our lives and actions, so that we do not put anything before His love.
f: EN 22.

t: [Pre-existence of the Person of the Word] In confessing the eternity, distinction and divinity of the Second Person of the Holy Trinity, we wish to nurture our desire to abandon ourselves completely to God’s “will of good pleasure,” to our love for the Trinity, and to the people created by God in His image and likeness.
f: Cf. Gen 1:26.

t: [The Mystery of the Incarnate Word]

His First Coming, accomplished by the Holy Spirit in Mary’s womb, must lead us to a total docility to the same Spirit and to a deep love for Mary, Jesus’ mother and ours. Based on the mystery of the Incarnation, the work of the Spirit in the Virgin Mary, we should always sing the mercies of God since “the immortality of blessedness becomes credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.” We must understand clearly that without Jesus Christ we can do nothing, and that we must always tend to grow in virtue with all our strength.
f: Cf. Ps 89:1. SAINT AUGUSTINE, On the Holy Trinity, 13,9. Cf. Jn 15:5.

t: Jesus is the “Way” to the Father, and nobody goes to the Father except through Him. He has the only name by which we are to be saved (Acts 4:12). He is the One who makes the Church a “sacrament, that is, a sign and instrument of communion with God and of unity among all men.” He is the One who sustains all Church dogmas since He is “the truth that contains all others.” He is the One who shows us the primacy and weight of eternity over all temporal reality. To know that Jesus is true God must move us to practice the transcendental virtues: faith, hope and charity. It must move us to give an irreplaceable importance to a life of prayer, and to the need for active and passive purifications of the senses and the spirit. Becoming man is “the first and fundamental mystery of Jesus,” and “God had never been so close to man – and man had never been so close to God – as in that precise moment: in the instant of the mystery of the Incarnation!” To know that Jesus is true man must make us realize that nothing authentically human is foreign to us provided we know how to assume it; it must make us love, in Him, every human being in his or her totality, and to practice the mortifying virtues of self-denial. To know that both natures become indissoluble in Him must move us to recognize the double reality of grace and nature, without creating an erroneous fusion; we must be moved to practice seemingly opposing virtues, without falling into false dualisms. Thus, the superior must assume the inferior, always seeking God’s greater glory and the salvation of humankind, which is the goal of the Incarnation.
f: Cf. Jn 14:6. LG 1. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Speech to professors and students at Antonianum Pontifical Athenaeum in Rome (January 16, 1982), 5; OR (1/31/1982) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message (September 6, 1981), 1; OR (9/13/1981) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message (August 2, 1981), 2; OR (8/9/1981) Spanish Edition. “What has not been taken has not been redeemed”; cf. AG 3, footnote 15.

t: His Earthly Life. From the instant of the Incarnation, He gives us an example of a priestly surrender to the Father which we must imitate. In Mary’s womb, we are already present through the principle of koinonia, which teaches us to depend completely on His mother. In His hidden life, He teaches us to grow, to work, to be silent, to be subjected and to live with festive joy. All of His words and actions nurture our spirituality.
f: Cf. Lk 2:51. Cf. Lk 2:42.

t: His Departure from This World. In a special way, our Lord’s Paschal mystery is an inexhaustible source of spirituality. His Passion, Death, descent into hell and Resurrection must always illuminate our lives. We must be experts in the wisdom of the cross, in the love of the cross, and in the joy of the cross.

His Glorious Life. The splendid fact that Christ rose from the dead should lead us to live as a resurrected people, to live the freedom of God’s children, the characteristic of a New Man, in accordance with the New Law – the Holy Spirit. We should do so with immense joy, especially on Sunday, by knowing how to celebrate and by carefully dedicating ourselves to our mission.

His Mystical Life. It is the wonder of the Church, Christ’s Body, nurtured by God’s Word, One, Holy, Catholic (missionary and ecumenical) and Apostolic, enriched and founded on the “three white things.”

His Second Coming. We are certain that the Lord is coming and that we are walking toward Him. One day He will return in power and majesty; He will raise the dead and preside over the final judgment and the renewal of the universe.

All other parts of the Constitutions are inspired by the Directory of Spirituality and must be understood in light of it. We have sought to give absolute precedence to the section on spirituality because we understand that this is the requirement of our charism. As such, the Directory of Spirituality must be regarded as a doctrinal text that serves as the foundation for the constitutional articles, as a point of reference for possible modifications that the future might require, and for the application of the Constitutions to new circumstances.
We can synthesize our spirituality as follows:

Not Jesus or Mary; not Mary or Jesus. Neither Jesus without Mary; nor Mary without Jesus. Neither only Jesus, but also Mary; not only Mary, but also Jesus. Always Jesus and Mary; always Mary and Jesus.
To Mary through Jesus: Behold, your mother! (Jn 19:27).
To Jesus through Mary: Do whatever he tells you (Jn 2:5). First Jesus, the God man; then Mary, the Mother of God. He, the Head; She, the Neck; we, the Body.
Everything through Jesus and through Mary; with Jesus and with Mary; in Jesus and in Mary; for Jesus and for Mary.
In short, simply: Jesus and Mary; Mary and Jesus.
And through Christ, to the Father, in the Holy Spirit.

Religious life, through which we surrender ourselves totally to the service of God, the source of perfection, consists mainly of fulfilling three vows: chastity, poverty and obedience, spurred by charity.
The profession of vows has the following nature:

- First, it fulfills our baptismal grace most effectively. It re-moves the obstacles that may separate us from the fervor of charity and the perfection of divine worship, and consecrates us more intimately to the service of God. Consecration by the three vows is rooted in baptismal consecration and is its most perfect expression. The person who consecrates his life to God in this way fulfills Baptism’s call to perfection: We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death (Rom 6:4).
f: Cf. LG 44.

t: - Second, it resembles martyrdom since the religious possesses the same will as a martyr. Both accept their death to this world in order to unite themselves totally to Christ and partake of His kingdom: “Even when persecution is lacking, peace has its martyrdom; although we do not submit our flesh to iron, we destroy in the soul the passions of our flesh with the spiritual sword.”
f: SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, Homilies on the Gospels, 1,3.

t: - Third, the religious profession constitutes a true holocaust of oneself, since in light of the vows, the religious offers himself and his possessions wholly and without reserve to God. Through the vow of chastity, he offers the good of his body; through the vow of poverty, he offers the good of external things. Through the vow of obedience, he offers the good of his soul.
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST II-II, 186, 7.

t: - Finally, the religious profession is a true consecration through which the religious becomes something sacred, destined for divine worship; the religious becomes the property of God.

With the profession of vows, we strive to uproot the threefold concupiscence from within us; this concupiscence, which is incompatible with the Father’s charity, includes: the lust of the flesh (disorder in eating, drinking, and goods of the senses); the lust of the eyes (eagerness to see everything, to possess it all); the pride of life (disorder in honors, ostentation, boastfulness, self-sufficiency). These correspond precisely to the temptations with which the devil tried to seduce our Lord: Gluttony: If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread (Mt 4:3). Vainglory: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down (Mt 4:6). Pride: All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Mt 4:9). “The matter of all sins” is found in these three temptations “because the causes of temptations are the same as those of greed: the delight of the flesh, the hope for glory and the ambition for power.” This is the ruse the father of lies used with Adam and Eve when he tempted them to taste the forbidden fruit, as it was good for food, and… it was a delight to the eyes, and… was to be desired to make one wise (Gen 3:6).
f: Cf. 1 Jn 2:16. SAINT AMBROSE, Exposition of the Gospel of Saint Luke, 4, 35.

t: For this reason, Christ provides three weapons against these snares, summarized in the three vows of the religious. Poverty corresponds to the command of giving alms, which includes everything done out of love for one’s neighbor, and the rejection of wealth and ambition. Chastity corresponds to fasting, which includes everything that the religious does to restrain concupiscence. Obedience corresponds to prayer, through which “man shows reverence to God… insofar as he subjects himself to Him, and by praying and confessing that he needs Him as the author of his goods.” Herein lies everything that the religious does to give proper worship to God; therefore, the vow of obedience, stemming from this worship of God, constitutes the essence of the religious life.
f: Cf. Mt 6:1-4. Cf. Mt 6:16-18. Cf. Mt 6:5-13. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST II-II, 83, 3.

t: By the vow of chastity and in imitation of Jesus Christ …having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (Jn 13:1), we want to offer God a holocaust of our body and our natural affections, living “the obligation of perfect continence observed in celibacy.” This vow implies a preferential choice of an exclusive love for God since we have freely chosen to be like eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Mt 19:12).
f: Cf. CIC, c. 599.

t: Virginity, which is primarily of the heart, flows from, and is oriented to, charity so as to fulfill the supreme commandment to its maximum perfection: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind (Mt 22:37). Thus, the vow of chastity enables the religious to be completely free to tend to God, since he is anxious about the affairs of the Lord, how to please the Lord (1 Cor 7:32), offering his body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God (Rom 12:1). The vow of chastity, fully lived, constitutes triumphant purity which tends with all its strength toward God. The religious joyfully sacrifices his carnal affections, surrendering himself to Jesus Christ and directing all his love to Him. The fruit of this consecration is dominion over everything, together with a free will that is quick to please God alone.

This vow gives great spiritual fruitfulness to the religious, since it is God who makes fertile and vivifies the heart of the one who, through virginity, resembles the angels and the resurrected who neither marry nor are given in marriage… being sons of the resurrection (Lk 20:35-36).

“Only the love of God calls in a decisive way to religious chastity. Moreover, this love makes so uncompromising a demand for fraternal charity that the religious will live more profoundly with his contemporaries in the heart of Christ. Chastity witnesses to preferential love for the Lord and symbolizes in the most eminent and absolute way the mystery of the union of the Mystical Body with its Head, the union of the Bride with her eternal Bridegroom. Finally, it reaches, transforms and imbues man’s being in its most hidden depths with a mysterious likeness to Christ.”
f: ET 13.

t: We should always desire a triumphantly victorious chastity. This victory can be attained in various degrees: substantial, eliminating grave sins; perfect, eliminating even minor sins; triumphant, the most perfect, which not only obtains the elimination of the most subtle of sins perceived by a delicate conscience, but also goes beyond the mere avoidance of sin. This can be done through promptness (eliminating every discussion or any cooperation with temptation, which leads to an immediate and radical victory) or in regards to totality (immolation of the heart and negation of the passion, even in indirect aspects – vain beauty, natural love, etc. – that are related to the senses and to sex but that are not strictly sinful by themselves). This superior path of refinement, promptness, and above all, of total self-denial in the sexual sphere is characteristic of the religious form of chastity in relation to the natural tendency (a tendency whose existence is acknowledged, but that is not given expression in a merely natural way). This surrender of the will can be classified in two ways: negative: painfully endured mortification, positive: joyful and desired sacrifice to obtain union with God, characterized, according to Saint Paul, by a spiritual and virginal matrimony. This matrimony is proper to religious life. The heart is not suffocated but offered and made sacred. This attitude alone is worthy of the religious state. The loving surrender it implies must be joyful, in order to immerse oneself in the spiritual realm of divine love, which is the ultimate purpose of virginity.
f: Cf. 1 Cor 7.

t: Our Lord is the Way we must follow and the example we must imitate: Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). In His preaching, Christ teaches us: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Mt 5:3), and He invites whoever wishes to attain perfection: if you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me (Mt 19:21).

Evangelical poverty consists of the voluntary surrender of material riches and the external goods of this world with the aim to seek only God. In Saint Jerome’s words, it means “to follow the naked Christ being ourselves naked.”
f: SAINT JEROME, Letter to Rusticus, 125. ML 22,1085.

t: The perfection of evangelical poverty does not consist of the mere lack of riches or material goods (effective poverty), but in the detachment and voluntary renunciation of them (affective poverty): Indeed I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as refuse, in order that I may gain Christ (Phil 3:8).

The evangelical counsel of poverty implies a life poor both in act and in spirit, following the example of Christ. Such a life is eagerly restrained and detached from earthly riches, and as such, it implies dependency and a limitation on the use and disposal of goods, according to the Constitutions. Thanks to this renunciation of temporal goods, the vow of poverty becomes endless worship of Divine Providence since the religious is certain that “bodily danger does not threaten those who with the intention of following Christ, abandon all their possessions and entrust themselves to Divine Providence.” The Father, full of goodness, who takes care of the birds and the flowers of the field, will not abandon those who confidently surrender their lives to Him.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 600. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST II-II, 186, 3, ad 2. Cf. Mt 6:25-34.

t: Practicing this vow is the utmost sign of humility: “In one who, like Christ, is poor willingly, poverty itself is a sign of maximum humility.”
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST III, 40, 3, ad 3.

t: Poverty assumed for the sake of Christ increases the freedom of the noble spirit which the religious must possess because of his consecration: “Poverty is good and contains within itself all the good things in the world. It is a great dominion – I mean that he who cares nothing for the good things of the world has dominion over them all.”
f: SAINT TERESA OF AVILA, The Way of Perfection, 2, 5.

t: Therefore, the religious, in his desire to always live poverty, must not regard anything as his own, or attach his heart to anything; he must not dispose of anything himself without the Superior’s permission. Thus, he will better imitate Jesus Christ who was “poor in his birth, even poorer in his life, and utterly poor on the Cross.”
f: SAINT BERNARD, The Mystical Vine, 2, 3.

t: Our Lord Jesus teaches: Sell your possessions…provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail… for where your treasure is, there will be your heart also (Lk 12:33-34). On one particular day, these words resounded in our heart, and we decided by the grace of the Holy Spirit to follow Christ, who Himself was poor on earth, through the vow of poverty. Religious poverty can be exercised with greater or lesser perfection. There are four main degrees:

1. To abstain from possessing something as one’s own or from accomplishing an act of ownership without the Superior’s permission. This is the obligatory matter of the vow. Its non-fulfillment, even in small matters, is always a sin that is either grave or venial, depending on the case.

2. To deprive oneself of the superfluous (and even of the appearance of riches and luxury), being content with simply what is necessary, and with the heart detached from it. Its non-fulfillment will not break the vow, but rather the virtue of poverty.

3. To prefer for one’s own use, and to choose whenever possible, that of least value, that which is least pleasant or least comfortable. In actions, it means to gladly accept, and even to ask for, the lowest offices, the most difficult assignments, anything that makes us most like the poor. The perfection of poverty begins here.

4. To accept with joy, for the love of God, privations of necessary things for the sake of holy poverty. It means to boast as Saint Paul through hunger and thirst, through frequent fasting, through cold and exposure (2 Cor 11:27). It was said of Saint Francis of Assisi that “no one was as ambitious for gold as was he zealous for poverty.” This degree constitutes the perfection of poverty.
f: TOMÁS DE CELANO, Vida de San Francisco, Vida Segunda, Ed. BAC, Madrid 1975, 375. (Translation is ours).

t: We can practice the fourth degree of poverty even more intensely and so gain total detachment not only from material goods (which is the proper object of the virtue of poverty), but also from everything that is not God Himself. This will result in the perfection of charity and a complete, consummated holiness. As Saint John of the Cross expressed, “To love is to labor to divest and deprive oneself for God of all that is not God.” The soul will not concern itself with:
f: SAINT JOHN OF THE CROSS, Ascent of Mount Carmel, 2, 5, 7.

t: - the esteem and good opinion of men, - health and corporal strength, - the charges and offices that will be given to or taken from him, - the events of prosperity or adversity that may happen, - dying young or old.

“Live as though only God and yourself were in this world, so that your heart is not controlled by anything human.” And: “Nothing, nothing until only the skin remains, and the rest for Christ”; “…when with self love I did not want it, it was all given to me, not going after it… after I have come to nothing, I have found that I lack nothing.” Conclusively, we have to love everything that God wants us to love, without being slaves to our affections for creatures. This means to love without being chained, to possess without remaining imprisoned, to use without selfish pleasure, to keep absolute independence and to look for God’s glory in everything and for everything.
f: SAINT JOHN OF THE CROSS, Sayings of Light and Love, 144. SAINT JOHN OF THE CROSS, Maxims and Spiritual Sentences, 68, 4. SAINT JOHN OF THE CROSS, Mount of Perfection, 74.

t: We take to heart the instruction given by Friar Francisco de los Ángeles to the twelve apostles of Mexico, when he warns them that they will go “to the vineyard not hired for pay, as some others, but as true sons of so great a Father, seeking not your own things, but those of Jesus Christ…who wished to be made the last and the least of men and who desired that you, his true children, will be the last as well, trampling underfoot the glory of the world, dejected through disgrace, possessing a very deep poverty, and being such that the world will scorn you and will judge your life as foolishness and your end as without honor. Thus, by being made foolish to the world you may convert that same world with the foolishness of your preaching. And do not be troubled, for you are not hired for a price but sent without promise of pay.”
f: FRAY JERÓNIMO DE MENDIETA, Historia Eclesiástica Indiana, Mexico 1945, 3, 9.

t: Regarding personal goods, the following is established:
f: Cf. CIC, c. 668.

t: - Those with temporal vows retain the capacity to possess patrimonial goods, but not to administer them. Therefore, before making the first profession, they must relinquish the administration of the same and freely dispose of their use and usufruct.
- Everything that a religious earns by his own work or by means of the Institute, as well as what he receives by way of pension, subsidy, or insurance, he acquires for the Institute.
- Before the perpetual profession, every religious of the Institute will make a last will and testament according to civil law.

- The religious of the Institute must aspire to live poverty to the maximum and absolute degree to more perfectly and more radically imitate Christ in His poverty. Therefore, every religious, immediately before or after perpetual profession, can voluntarily renounce his present and future goods. If possible, this total re-nunciation is made so as to be valid in civil law as well. The professed who has renounced all his goods loses his capacity to acquire and possess, and so his actions contrary to the vow of poverty are null. Whatever he acquires after the renunciation belongs to the Institute.
The Institute must provide its members with all necessary means according to the Constitutions, in order to reach the goal of their vocation.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 670.

t: Following the example of the Incarnate Word, members of the Institute surrender themselves totally to God and give up their will by their vow of obedience.

He learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8). “Sacred Scripture says, ‘He learned obedience,’ that is, how serious it is to obey, because He himself obeyed in the most difficult and serious things, until death on the cross. He thus shows how difficult obedience is. Because those who are not expert in obedience and have not learned it in the most difficult things think that obedience is very easy. But for you to know what obedience is, it is necessary that you learn to obey in the most difficult things. Those who do not learn through obedience to be subject, will never know how to command well when they should command.” Therefore, let the subjects obey, and the one who commands will be good.
f: Cf. Phil 2:8. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Commentary on Hebrews, 5, 8; 2, 259.

t: With the vow of obedience, the religious obligates himself to submit his will to his legitimate superiors, who act on behalf of God when they command according to the Constitutions. The religious pledges to obey his superiors in everything that relates to religious and apostolic life, imitating Jesus Christ, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil 2:8). In this way, the religious becomes docile to the Holy Spirit, and his soul is constantly ready for whatever God determines: We beseech you, brethren, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work (1 Thes 5: 12-13).
f: Cf. CIC, c. 601.

t: The religious must see in his superior someone who acts as Christ, as Scripture teaches us: Obey your leaders and defer to them, for they keep watch over you and will have to give an account, that they may fulfill their task with joy and not with sorrow, for that would be of no advantage to you (Heb 13:17). Such obedience is the essential element of religious life since the religious state is a learning and training process to reach perfection. This learning process requires submission to the direction of another. This vow offers the most excellent of all goods to God, namely, one’s own will. It contains the other two vows that are made through obedience, and it properly refers to the acts that pertain more to the end of religious life, since nobody is a religious without this vow (even if one makes the other vows).
f: Cf. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST II-II, 186, 8.

t: Some, unfortunately, do not obey, because they are moved by their own spirit, the spirit of the flesh or the spirit of the world. “Many live in obedience more from necessity than from love. Such [people] become discontented and dejected at the slightest excuse; they will never attain peace of mind unless they subject themselves wholeheartedly to the love of God.” When one withdraws himself from obedience, one also is withdrawn from grace: “He who attempts to escape obeying withdraws himself from grace. Likewise, he who seeks private benefits for himself loses those which are common to all. He who does not submit himself freely and willingly to his superior, shows that his flesh is not yet perfectly obedient, but that it often rebels and murmurs against him. Learn quickly, then, to submit yourself to your superior if you wish to conquer your own flesh.” We must never forget that “obedience is the aroma of sacrifice… nevertheless, if your superiors were unable to perform their duties, if they were somehow defective, I say this in order for you to understand me: even if they were repulsive, you would acquire greater merit by obeying them, you would be more certain of obeying God. The defects of superiors make obedience infinitely more meritorious and pleasing to God. In order to obey, you must not take into account the superior’s human qualities; you must not consider whether the order [given] is reasonable or not, but rather, you should consider that obedience is reasonable. If we obey only because of the reasonableness of what has been ordered, obedience itself will be destroyed. We, being worthless and useless, must deny ourselves at the feet of the Church and our superiors, and obey for love of Christ and be considered as a scouring pad … so that no one might surpass us in faithful obedience, obsequiousness, and love of the Holy Father and the Bishops, to whom the Holy Spirit has given the governance of the Church of God.” Saint John of the Cross teaches the same: “Always look upon the superior as though [looking] upon God, no matter who he happens to be, for he takes God’s place. And note that the devil, humility’s enemy, is a great and crafty meddler in this area. Much profit and gain come from considering the superior in this light, but serious loss and harm lie in not doing so. Watch, therefore, with singular care that you do not dwell on your superior’s character, behavior, ability, or any other courses of action, for you will harm yourself so much so as to change your obedience from divine to human, as it will be motivated only by the visible traits of the superior and not by the invisible God whom you serve through him… If you fail to strive for indifference regarding the superiority of one over the other, with respect to your personal feelings, you will by no means be a spiritual person, nor will you keep your vows well.”
f: THOMAS A KEMPIS, Imitation of Christ, I, 9. THOMAS A KEMPIS, Imitation of Christ, III, 13. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of the Epiphany of 1935. SAINT JOHN OF THE CROSS, Precautions, Second Precaution against the Devil.

t: Saint John Bosco’s words would become a reality if we were truly obedient religious: “If you will obey according to what is indicated, I can assure you in the name of the Lord that you will have a peaceful and happy life in the congregation. But, at the same time, I must advise you that from the day you put obedience aside, doing only your will, you will start feeling religious life as a burden. If in religious communities you find unhappiness, and even some people to whom community life is heavy, observe with attention, and you will see that this is caused by a lack of obedience.” We must engrave in our hearts Saint Francis de Sales’ words: “In obedience all is secure; out of it, all is to be suspected.”
f: SAINT JOHN BOSCO, Rules or Constitutions of the Society of Saint Francis de Sales, 8. SAINT FRANCIS DE SALES, Treaty of the Love of God, 6, 13.

t: Religious obedience has three degrees:
- First degree: obedience of execution consists of carrying out an order even without inner submission.
- Second degree: obedience of will includes inner submission, that is, easily adapting our will to that of the superior with love and courage.
- Third degree: obedience of judgment, when we submit both our inner judgment and our intelligence to the superior, unless what he commands is clearly contrary to reason.

Religious obedience is totally opposed to both judgmental obedience, that is, obeying with murmuring and complaining, and the spirit of antagonism, namely, forming groups that oppose everything ordered by the superior. Religious obedience is also opposed to subservience and pharisaic obedience, that is, a cowardly and hypocritical obedience that shows a defeated will, but not a surrendered will, and that even tries to move the superior in its own direction.

In addition to our baptismal dependence and submission to the Roman Pontiff, by the vow of obedience we further obligate ourselves to obey Him as our Highest Superior, following Can. 590, §2: “The individual members are bound to obey the Supreme Pontiff as their highest Superior, by reason also of their sacred bond of obedience.” Members are also subject to the authority of the Bishops. Members will follow the Bishops with pious subjection and respect in whatever relates to the care of souls, the public exercise of divine worship, and all other works of the apostolate. In the exercise of the external apostolate, religious are also subject to the authority of their own superiors and must re-main faithful to the discipline of the Institute.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 678.

t: To command under obedience, valid only when the legitimate superior does so in writing in the presence of two witnesses, will always be the exception. The superior commands under obedience when he uses a formula “by virtue of holy obedience,” “under formal precept,” or the like, or when the manner of commanding, or other circumstances, clearly manifests that such is his desire.

In addition to the vows of chastity, poverty and obedience, we make a fourth vow – consecration to Mary. This consecration is a total surrender to Mary so as to better serve Jesus Christ, and has two aspects:

This consecration to Mary is done as a “filial slavery of love” according to Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort’s commendable method. He refers to such slavery as “willing” or “loving,” because, as we are moved only by love, we freely and willingly offer ourselves and all our goods to Mary and to Jesus Christ through her. This offering is a fuller and more conscious renewal of the promises made in our baptism, when we were clothed in Christ, and in our religious profession. Moreover, Mary’s dominion and maternal providence over all things, especially over the souls of the faithful, becomes manifest through this loving slavery. According to Saint Bonaventure, “Any faithful soul, and even the universal Church, is a slave of Mary the Queen.” Blessed John Paul II says, “Surrender to Mary, in the spirit of St. Louis Grignion de Montfort, has seemed to me the best means of participating fruitfully and effectively in this reality, in order to draw from it and share with others its inexpressible riches… I think we are confronted here with the sort of paradox often to be noted in the Gospels, the words ‘holy slavery’ signifying that we could not more fully exploit our freedom… For freedom is measured by the love of which we are capable.”
f: SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNION DE MONFORT, TD, 70-72. Cf. Gal 3:27. SAINT BONAVENTURE, Speculum Beata Mariae Virginis, 3, 5. Quoted by ANDRÉ FROSSARD, Be Not Afraid!, New York 1984.

t: By this slavery of love, we offer Christ through Mary not only our bodies, souls, and goods, but also our good works (past, present and future), together with their satisfactory and meritorious value. Thus, she may dispose of everything according to the will of her Son and for His greater glory. We are certain that we must go to the Incarnate Word through Mary, His Mother, and that she will form “great saints.”
f: SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNON DE MONFORT, TD 121-125. SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNON DE MONFORT, TD 47.

t: “Marianizing” life is the fruit and natural consequence of the consecration to the Blessed Virgin Mary. To “marianize” life, one must first do everything through Mary. The phrase “through Mary” indicates the way, that is, the fusion of intentions. The Mother of God keeps nothing for herself, but she teaches and tells us in all things, just as she did to the servants at Cana, “Do whatever he tells you” (Jn 2:5).

Second, we must do everything with Mary. She is our companion and model, the masterpiece of God, who must guide “all our intentions, actions and operations.” The Apostle Paul said, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1); with greater reason we can say the same of the Virgin Mary – in whom the Almighty, whose name is Holy, has done great things. “While in the most holy Virgin the Church has already reached that perfection whereby she is without spot or wrinkle, the followers of Christ… turn their eyes to Mary who shines forth to the whole community of the elect as the model of virtues.”
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA, Spiritual Exercises, 46. Cf. Lk 1:49. LG 65.

t: Third, one must act in Mary, in intimate union with her, which means that an abiding unity should exist between the consecrated soul and the Mother of God. He who loves abides in the beloved; this is ardent love, tending toward a mutual union, becoming more profound and more solid with each positive act. In this way one imitates the Incarnate Word who came into the world and dwelled in Mary’s womb for nine months; and Jesus’ last command and gift becomes effective: ‘Behold your mother!’ And from that hour that disciple took her to his own home (Jn 19:27).

Finally, one must do everything for Mary. The Blessed Virgin, who always submitted to Christ according to the Father’s eternal design, must be the end that guides all our actions, the object that attracts the heart of each consecrated person, and the motive at the beginning of each task. Mary is the “proximate end, our mysterious intermediary, and the easiest way of reaching Him.”
f: SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNON DE MONFORT, TD 265.

t: Therefore, every faithful slave of Jesus in Mary must invoke her, salute her, think of her, talk about her, honor her, glorify her, entrust himself to her, rejoice and suffer with her, work, pray and rest with her. In brief, one must seek to live always, through Jesus and Mary, with Jesus and Mary, in Jesus and Mary, and for Jesus and Mary.

Truly community life is the greatest penance. However, unlike mathematics, in which one-plus-one equals two, in community life, one-man-plus-one-man equals two thousand. One man along with another grows in courage and strength; his fear disappears, and he escapes from any trap.
f: Cf. F. CERVÓS, Vida del angélico joven San Juan Berchmans, Madrid 1920, 150: “Mea máxima poenitentia vita communis.” (Translation is ours).

t: The beauty and riches of fraternal life in common are much greater than the difficulties that it entails: How good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity! (Ps 133:1).

Fraternal life truly shows that we are united in Christ: You are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28), as a distinct Religious Family. Fraternal life must exist so as to become a mutual help in fulfilling each member’s personal vocation. Through fraternal communion, rooted and based in charity, members need to be examples of universal reconciliation in Christ. They must be a “domestic church.”

In our communities we must try to live out the essence of the Kingdom that Jesus Christ came to inaugurate on earth: The kingdom of God is… righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). Our communities will be authentic to the degree that we live in justice, peace, and joy, which are identified with holiness. When holiness is non-existent, there is no law or superior that can prevent disintegration. As Saint Pius X said, “Where sanctity is lacking, there corruption will inevitably find its way.”
f: SAINT PIUS X, Haerent Animo, 5.

t: We want justice to shine in our communities, that justice which gives everyone his due: latria to God, veneration and obedience to superiors, respect to equals, service to inferiors, and to everyone, in its measure, charity. Justice is so beautiful that neither the morning nor the evening star can compare to it. Blessed John Paul II said that for St. Gregory VII, justice is “the order of God in the world, justice orders all human things, from the smallest to the greatest, according to the will and the law of God, so that man should not be deformed by sin, but molded into God’s image.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Homily at the Mass celebrated in Concordia Square (May 26, 1985), 1; OR (7/7/1985) Spanish Edition.

t: Joy, the fruit of the Holy Spirit and the effect of charity, requires us to make use of any and all means so that “nobody may be disturbed or grieved in the house of God.” We must live fraternal charity: that is, outdo one another in showing honor (Rom 12:10); bear their weaknesses, both physical and spiritual, with unlimited patience; be eager to obey one another; seek not one’s own good as much as one’s neighbor’s; practice true fraternal love; live always in the fear and love of God. Love your Abbot (superior) with true and humble charity; do not let anything come before Christ who will take all of us together to Eternal life.”
f: SAINT BENEDICT, Holy Rule, 31. SAINT BENEDICT, Holy Rule, 72, 1-12.

t: Fraternal charity should be lived so that in observing our life, one could say, “Look how they love each other and are willing to die for each other,” or, like it was said of the first Christians, “They love one another almost before they know one another.” Do not believe that charity is [merely] utopian, since we have heard expressions like these before. We should always be determined to preserve charity even though there might be false friends, who interfere to spy on our freedom in Jesus Christ (Gal 2:14), who pretend to be with us but do not belong to us. Love is eternal! (1 Cor 13:8). Each one of us should be able to write our biographies by replacing the word “love” with our own name in Saint Paul’s hymn to the Corinthians. Therein, he describes fraternal love with two general characteristics and thirteen features, eight negative and five positive: Love is patient and kind; love is not jealous or boastful; it is not arrogant or rude. Love does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrong, but rejoices in the right. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Cor 13:4-7). “Formally love is the life of the soul, just as the soul is the life of the body.”
f: TERTULIAN, Apologeticum, ML 1,534. MARCUS MINUTIUS FELIX, Octavias, ML 3,289. Cf. 2 Cor 11:26. Cf. 1 Jn 2:19. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST II-II, 23, 2, ad 2.

t: Peace is also a fruit of the Holy Spirit and an effect of charity. By charity we direct all our affections to God, and this order brings about peace. Dissipated souls do not let the Holy Spirit guide them, and therefore, they do not live in Christ’s peace. This peace is one of the many benefits our Lord brought to the world and is an effect of His redeeming passion: [The Father wanted] through him to reconcile all things for him, making peace by the blood of his cross, whether those on earth or those in heaven (Col 1:19-20).

Man reaches this interior peace when he eliminates the battle within himself that sometimes arises because of the struggle between the flesh and the spirit, or because of a conflict in his will between two opposing loves.

Peace can be false. This occurs when it is shrouded within an apparent good, or when it is achieved at any cost by doing one’s own will. True peace will be perfect only in the Heavenly Homeland; on this earth it is imperfect, but we can always preserve it, even amid the greatest contradictions, tribulations, and tragedies, as the Apostle Paul admonishes: Have no anxiety… And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will keep your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Phil 4:6-7). We achieve this peace by making love the weight of our souls; by it our heart is carried to what it loves: “My weight is my love.” If that love is placed in Christ, peace will be found there, since He is the foundation of all: For through Him all things were created… and in Him all things hold together (Col 1:16-17). Peace should be sought internally, not externally. It should not be sought by filling our hearts with useless worries and resentments against everything around us, because our soul’s peace does not depend on the removal of external obstacles, but rather on the elimination of the affection for sin: What causes wars, and what causes fighting among you? Is it not your passions that are at war in your members? (Jas 4:1). Peace should be sought internally because God is inside us: “You were more inward to me than the most inward part of me.”
f: SAINT AUGUSTINE, Confessions, 13, 9, 10. SAINT AUGUSTINE, Confessions, 13, 6, 11.

t: Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed (Jas 5:16). The Chapter of Faults is a great help in this regard, and is generally held every week. The purpose of this exercise is to humiliate the spirit and to mortify the flesh which once more realizes its own weaknesses.

Members should accuse themselves only of exterior faults they have committed before others, and never of purely interior faults. The accusation must be simple, brief, sincere, and without omissions, humble and without justifications, and charitable and without accusing anyone or revealing another’s defects.

Despite the fact that his faults may be humiliating, others should think more highly of, and have a greater esteem for, the member accusing himself. For though they have to judge the member as guilty, now, thanks to his confession, they realize that he is humble and loves humiliation, and by that humiliation, he has already erased his fault.
Outside the Chapter of Faults, we must never speak of what occurred in it.

Fraternal correction holds an important place in building up our communities according to the example of the only Church of Christ. One of the spiritual works of mercy is to correct those in error. It is a warning, by words or gestures, to the guilty neighbor, especially in the case of ignorance or negligence. It is made privately and solely out of charity, from brother to brother, in order to remove him from sin, either by taking him out of it or by preventing it from being committed. It is neither the correction of the superior as a judge (judicial correction), nor of the superior as a father (paternal correction). “Brothers, ministers and servants, as well as all the rest, always avoid getting angry or irritated by the sin or the defect of others, for the devil takes advantage of one person’s guilt to mislead many. Instead, as best as you can, spiritually assist those who have committed sin, because the healthy do not need a doctor, but the sick do.”
f: SAINT FRANCIS OF ASSISI, Writings.

t: The duty is grave. Not only should we help our neighbor in his material needs but also in his spiritual needs, according to God’s command: If your brother sins against you, go to him and show him his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother (Mt 18:15). This duty refers to mortal sins already committed, and to venial sins which, due to their frequency or consequences, may lead to mortal sins. Material sins, committed in invincible ignorance, should be corrected if they are the cause of scandal, if there is a danger of falling into bad habits, or if they affect the common good. Correction should be carried out by anyone, whether superior or subject, with charity and righteous, rational judgment, even though he himself is a sinner. It is normally directed toward equals or the inferior, though sometimes toward the superior, but in doing so, their authority as superiors should not be disregarded.

In order to be appropriate and necessary, the correction must pertain to a true matter and must be presented clearly and spontaneously. It must be: necessary, seeing that our neighbor will not correct himself without it; effective, that is, not counterproductive or liable to fail; feasible, that is, that it could be carried out without serious discomfort or detriment for the party making the correction, unless he should do so out of the duties of his office or piety; opportune, taking into account the time, place and manner.
In manner, the correction should be:

- charitable: seeking the good of the one corrected with the utmost sweetness and gentleness: If a man is overtaken in any trespass…you who are spiritual must restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Gal 6:1);
- patient: though positive results may not be immediately obtained, you should persevere until it is God’s time, as the drop of water which, slowly and with perseverance, erodes the stone;
- humble: consider the way Christ would do it, without presumption or boastfulness. It must show respect if directed at a superior;
f: Cf. 1 Tim 5:1.

t: - prudent: choose the moment and the occasion, deferring it if the offender is disturbed or not alone. Correction should be entrusted to someone else if better suited, avoiding humiliation, if possible;
- discreet: do not correct every fault, nor do it all the time. We should not be antagonists of other people’s lives, and we should avoid indiscreet jealousy;

- ordered: avoid publicizing, if possible, following the order of the Gospel. First in private, then in front of one or two witnesses, and finally, tell it to the superior who will start paternal correction and will resort to judicial correction when there is no other solution. This order can and should be the reverse if its effectiveness is in doubt, or the sin affects the common good.

In summary, “Let us therefore implore forgiveness for all those transgressions which we have committed through any suggestion of the adversary. And these who have been the leaders of sedition and disagreement ought to have respect for the common hope. For those who live in fear and love would rather that they themselves, and not their neighbor, be involved in suffering. And they prefer to bear the blame themselves, rather than that the harmony which has been well and piously handed down to us should suffer… Who then among you is noble-minded? Who compassionate? Who full of love? Let him declare, ‘If on my account sedition and disagreement and schisms have arisen, I will depart, I will go away wherever ye desire, and I will do whatever the majority commands; only let the flock of Christ live on terms of peace with the presbyters set over it…’”
f: SAINT CLEMENT OF ROME, Letter to Corinthians, 51, 1-2; 54, 1-2.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE SUPERIORS Article 1: One Governs Many
t: The principle of community life and unity was discovered many centuries ago: “The multitude is governed better by one than by many.” This principle of unity is the superior in whom justice and mercy should shine. Saint Thomas teaches, “Justice without mercy is cruelty; mercy without justice is the mother of dissolution.”
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST I, 103, 3. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Super Evangelium S. Mattheum lectura, n. 429.

t: We believe that Saint Ignatius of Loyola gives the best description of a Superior General. Analogously, this description is suitable for any other superior:
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA, Constitutions of the Society of Jesus, 8, 3.

t: - He should be closely united with God in prayer and in all his actions because God blesses the other members through him. He should implore God for all graces on behalf of the community.

- He should set an example for others, and shine in the practice of virtues, especially charity and humility. He should have his passions under control so that they may not hinder him from seeing and considering everything clearly, and utilizing proper judgment. In his conduct and words, he should never cease to edify the members of the Institute as well as others: “Woe to the superiors who destroy with their example what they preach with their words!”
f: SAINT JOSEPH OF CALASANZ, Life, 31, sentence 46.

t: Also shining in him should be an unyielding rectitude of intention, seeking only to please God, together with kindness and meekness, so that even those who are corrected or punished would realize that he is moved by charity. He should also possess generosity of spirit and fortitude to begin great works in the service of God, and to persevere until their completion. He should suffer the weaknesses of many, without faltering because of compliments or threats; he should rise above the vicissitudes of fortune and failure, and be willing to give up his life, if necessary, for the good of the Institute in the service of Jesus Christ.

He should be gifted with great understanding and judgment both in speculative and practical matters. Above all, he must possess prudence and discernment of spirits in order to realize and meet all spiritual and material needs. He should also be capable of giving advice and remedying situations.
He should be vigilant and careful to begin works, and re-sponsible to continue and finish them, without negligently leaving them half-finished.

He should be healthy and mature enough to carry out the responsibilities required by this role for the Glory of God, as well as possess the necessary experience. He should be neither too old nor too young, because the former lacks strength and the latter experience.

He should have those external qualities that would facilitate and help him in edifying his neighbor and serving God in his position, especially credibility and a good reputation before the members of the Institute as well as others outside it.

For all these reasons, the superiors who are elected should be the most virtuous and meritorious in our Religious Family. If the superior should lack any of the above characteristics, he must not lack true kindness and love for the Institute, nor sufficient prudence and knowledge. All the rest can be compensated for with the help of God.

Above all, the priest should be a father, because he fathers children through the cross, by prayer, apostolic zeal and preaching. Christ was the first in this ministry. That is why He is called the everlasting Father (Is 9:6). The other priests are fathers by participation in His fatherhood; they are fathers “through Him, with Him and in Him.”
To accomplish this, the priest must:
- Have a vivid consciousness of the Divine Fatherhood and His majesty, to whom everything belongs;
- Not usurp the glory of God: the bonds of spiritual fatherhood are stronger than the bonds of the flesh, but they must not snatch from God what belongs to Him: “Let God’s glory be for God.”
- Ask for the spirit of fatherhood, having the Spirit of His Son and pure love toward God: “Ask Him for the spirit of fatherhood toward His children whom we father.”
- In this way, the priest becomes a visible image of God the Father, whom we cannot see: No one has ever seen God (Jn 1:18).

However, this “sweet thing of fathering children” necessarily implies the cross: “The children we are to father by the word should not be children of voice as much as children of tears… those who become fathers should learn to weep.” The true father must die to himself in everything so that his child may live. “Will he not consider remaining silent when necessary, so as to help his children even when they complain about every small thing? Will he not be careful to avoid arousing envy by loving one more than another, or of seeming to love one more than the other? He takes care to feed his children even when it means he must take the morsel from his mouth, or has to leave the presence of angelic choirs to lower himself and give his child food. He must always be temperate to avoid making the child feel he loves him less. And even though sometimes the father’s heart might be tormented with a thousand concerns, so that he needs, for his own tranquility, to give free rein to his sadness, and empty himself with tears, when his child comes, he still must play and laugh with him, as if the child was his sole focus. For, who can count all together the temptations, dryness, dangers, deceits, scruples, and other thousands of fantasies that come from everywhere? How the father needs to be vigilant so that his son will not follow them! How much wisdom he needs to bring the child back once he has fallen for these! Patience, so he does not get tired of hearing the same questions over and over again which he has heard and responded to a thousand times, and so that he can explain again what he has already said before! What constant and courageous praying he must do to God, begging that his child not die! For, if he dies, believe me, father, no pain can equal this; neither do I believe that God has allowed another sort of martyrdom in this world as painful as that of the true father whose son dies. Therefore, he who desires to be a father is greatly helped by having a gentle heart, a heart of flesh, so as to be compassionate toward his sons (which is a martyrdom in itself), and another heart of iron, in order to suffer the blows that their death will bring, so that the father will not stumble nor be driven to leave his office, nor faint, nor spend days just crying.” Herein lies the ideal of the shepherd! From here also, “Those who escape this work of fatherhood, therefore, did not take any part in engendering spiritual children.” This is the antithesis of a true father, the negation of the priesthood, as paternity is its fullness.
f: SAINT JOHN OF AVILA, Letter to Friar Luis de Granada, op. cit., Vol V, 20- 21. SAINT JOHN OF AVILA, Second Memorial to the council of Trent, Vol. VI, 92.

t: We must realize that the community is built day by day, moment by moment. It has always been subject to insidious treatment, i.e. the case of Brother Ruffino with Saint Francis of Assisi, for example! Today the same thing happens, and perhaps even more so. The community has tribulations and temptations: some in general to all the members and some in particular to the superiors or to the subjects.
f: BROTHER UGOLINO, Little Flowers of Saint Francis of Assisi, 1, 29.
