The Master of Novices must encourage the novices to live human and Christian virtues, and bring them along a path of greater perfection through prayer and self-denial; he must instruct them in the contemplation of the mystery of salvation and in the reading and meditation of Sacred Scriptures. He must prepare them for the celebration of God’s worship in the Sacred Liturgy, form them to live a consecrated life to God and to all men in Christ through the evangelical counsels, and instruct them in the character, spirit, purpose, discipline, history, and life of the Institute; he will strive to infuse in them love for the Church and her holy shepherds.
f: Cf. CIC, cc. 646, 652; CONGREGATION FOR INSTITUTES OF CONSECRAT- ED LIFE AND SOCIETIES OF APOSTOLIC LIFE, Directives on Formation in Religious Institutes, 45-53.

t: After an assessment period, the novices will receive the religious habit.
In order to be valid, temporary profession requires:
1. that the person making it is at least eighteen years of age;
2. that the novitiate has been made validly;
3. that the profession be explicit and made without force, fear, or deceit;
4. that the profession be received by the Provincial Superior, personally or through another.

Upon completion of the novitiate, a novice will be admitted to temporary profession. The admission is decided by the Provincial Superior with the deliberative vote of the Council. When there are doubts concerning the vocation, either from the candidate or the Institute, the time of novitiate may be prolonged, but not for longer than a period of six months.
f: Cf. CIC, c 653 § 2.

t: The temporary profession will be made during the first four years for a period of one year each, and then for a two-year period. For those religious who are candidates to the priesthood, what is established in n. 256 must be taken into consideration. The Superior General, with the consent of his council and with just cause, can dispense from this norm so that a religious could be admitted to perpetual profession after completing the third year of temporal profession with due regard for what is established in canon 657 § 3.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 658 § 2.

t: The formula for temporary consecration is as follows:
For love
of the Father, first source and supreme end of consecrated
life;
of Christ, who calls us to His intimacy;
of the Holy Spirit, who disposes our soul to receive His inspi-
rations.
I, N., freely, make an oblation of my entire being to God:
to deepen, each time with a love more sincere and intense,
the gift of the evangelical counsels in a Trinitarian dimension;
to be a concrete imprint that the Trinity leaves on history
so that in this way, all mankind will discover an attraction
and longing for the divine beauty;
so that my life may be a living memory
of the way that Jesus, the Word made flesh (cf. Jn 1:14)
lived and behaved
before the Father and before mankind.
Therefore, I pledge all my strength
so as not to be elusive to the missionary adventure,
to inculturate the Gospel
in the diversity of all cultures,
to extend the Incarnation of the Word
“to all men, in the whole man,
and in all of the manifestations of man,”
assuming all that is authentically human,
in order to be like another humanity of Christ,
to carry out, with greater perfection,
the service of God and man.
Therefore, in the presence of God our Lord, and all His saints,
before N., Provincial Superior
of the Institute of the Incarnate Word
(or before N., who takes the place of the
Provincial Superior of the Institute of the Incarnate Word)
and in the presence of all the members of the Institute
and of the Servants of the Lord and of the Virgin of Matará,
I make a vow for … year/s to live
chaste, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,
poor, manifesting that God
is the only true wealth of mankind,
and obedient, even until death on the cross,
to follow more intimately the Incarnate Word
in His chastity, poverty, and obedience,
in accordance with the evangelical way
traced in the Constitutions
of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.
To fulfill this more perfectly,
I consecrate myself to Mary in filial slavery of love.
I request Our Lady, the Twelve Apostles,
and all the other patron saints to intercede for me,
and I also ask for the prayers
of my brothers in the Institute of the Incarnate Word
and the sisters of the Institute
of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará.
May the love and grace of the Most Holy Trinity
help me to be faithful to the work that He has begun. The one who is receiving the vows replies:
In the name of the Church
and the Institute of the Incarnate Word,
I welcome with great joy to our Religious Family
these brothers with temporal vows,
who have demonstrated their explicit desire
for a total conformity
to Christ, the Incarnate Word.
For perpetual profession to be valid, the candidate must be at least twenty-one years of age.

The religious who are candidates to the priesthood can be admitted to perpetual profession after at least five years of temporary profession, having completed their philosophical and theological studies prior to the diaconate. If there are doubts about suitability, or if the candidate himself asks for it, an additional period of up to three years with temporary vows can be permitted. At the end of this period, the candidate will either be admitted to the perpetual profession or dismissed.
The formula for perpetual profession will be the following:
For love
of the Father, first source and supreme end of consecrated
life;
of Christ, who calls us to His intimacy;
of the Holy Spirit, who disposes our soul
to receive His inspirations.
I, N., freely, make an oblation of my entire being to God:
to deepen, each time with a love more sincere and intense,
the gift of the evangelical counsels in a Trinitarian dimension;
to be a concrete imprint that the Trinity leaves on history
so that in this way, all mankind will discover an attraction
and longing for the divine beauty;
so that my life may be a living memory
of the way that Jesus, the Word made flesh (cf. Jn 1:14)
lived and behaved
before the Father and before mankind.
Therefore, I pledge all my strength
so as not to be elusive to the missionary adventure,
to inculturate the Gospel
in the diversity of all cultures,
to extend the Incarnation of the Word
“to all men, in the whole man,
and in all of the manifestations of man,”
assuming all that is authentically human,
in order to be like another humanity of Christ,
to carry out, with greater perfection,
the service of God and man.
Therefore, in the presence of God our Lord, and all His saints,
before N., Provincial Superior
of the Institute of the Incarnate Word
(or before N., who takes the place
of the Provincial Superior
of the Institute of the Incarnate Word),
and in the presence of all the members of the Institute,
and of the Servants of the Lord and of the Virgin of Matará,
I make a vow to forever live
chaste, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,
poor, manifesting that God is the only true wealth of
mankind,
and obedient, even until death on the cross,
to follow more intimately the Incarnate Word
in His chastity, poverty, and obedience,
in accordance with the evangelical way
traced in the Constitutions
of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.
To fulfill this more perfectly,
I consecrate myself to Mary in filial slavery of love.
I request Our Lady, the Twelve Apostles,
and all the other patron saints to intercede for me,
and I also ask for the prayers
of my brothers in the Institute of the Incarnate Word,
and the sisters of the Institute
of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará.
May the love and grace of the Most Holy Trinity
help me to be faithful to the work that He has begun.
The one who is receiving the vows replies:
In the name of the Church
and the Institute of the Incarnate Word,
I welcome with great joy to our Religious Family
these brothers with perpetual vows,
who have demonstrated their explicit desire
for a total conformity
to Christ, the Incarnate Word.

h: Article 5: Religious Seminary a. Seminary for Religious Who Are Candidates to the Priesthood
t: The Institute of the Incarnate Word is a clerical institute, wherein the majority of the members are priests. Upon finishing the novitiate, a new period of priestly formation begins, executed according to Canon Law for the formation of clerics and according to the documents of the Holy See, and always in accordance with the spirituality and mission of the Institute, so as to accomplish an authentic overall formation: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

h: Article 5: Religious Seminary a. Seminary for Religious Who Are Candidates to the Priesthood
t: According to our own charism, we strive to orient all our studies toward the evangelization of the culture, for which we will spare no efforts or means. We are not content with a merely superficial knowledge of philosophy and theology that is incapable of understanding the modern exercise of atheism in all its depth, and is thus incapable of providing a remedy for it.

h: b. Seminary of the Coadjutor Brothers
t: The Institute will also have religious called “coadjutor brothers.” They will dedicate themselves to serving the houses and to giving spiritual services that do not require the sacramental grace of Holy Orders.

h: b. Seminary of the Coadjutor Brothers
t: These brothers should complete formation in the seminary, where they will take some courses in philosophy and theology, “attending to the needs of the Church and the circumstances of men and the times, according to the end and the character of the Institute.” The coadjutor brothers will continue their formation, under the direct authority of the local superior, until their perpetual profession in the houses to which they are assigned. Their ongoing formation must be monitored.

Religious life is a process of continual conversion that does not end with the years of formation, but must be maintained and must grow every day. Regarding our pastoral work, this formation is an act of true and proper justice for God’s people, who always demand the most appropriate answer from us.
f: Cf. CONGREGATION FOR INSTITUTES OF CONSECRATED LIFE AND SOCIE- TIES OF APOSTOLIC LIFE, Directives on Formation in Religious Institutes, 66-68; CIC, c. 661. Cf. PDV 70.

t: Ongoing formation, not limited by the age or circumstances of the member, possesses four dimensions: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

We believe that permanent and ongoing formation is fundamental. To accomplish this, in addition to ordinary measures such as conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc., extraordinary measures should be taken whenever possible, for example: the 30day spiritual exercises every ten years, pilgrimages to the Holy Land and to great shrines of Christianity, etc.

In order to undertake this ongoing formation, we desire that all the members of our Institute take ecclesiastical or civil courses after the Seminary, according to their capacities and talents. These will be taken preferably in the pontifical universities of Rome or in those institutions recognized by the Holy See, so as to receive the qualifying degree of licentiate and doctorate. We already have a priestly community in Rome where two years are normally spent for this purpose. The formation in Rome implies the attainment of a Roman spirit, which entails a “crown of virtues: universal openness, fidelity to the Magisterium, a missionary spirit, endurance, and magnanimity.” Being in Rome is a “situation that permits [one] to live the supernatural reality of communion with the Church of Rome and with the Bishop of Rome. In the ecclesiastical experience [one] enters into the field of a new reality: [one] experiences the communion with all who are in communion with the Church of Rome.” Therefore, the opportunity to study in the Eternal City has a two-fold advantage: “It means having the advantage of living in a community either of priests or seminarians, and having access to the scholarship available in or through the Roman universities. It means being witnesses, day after day, to the living tradition of the faith as it is proclaimed in the See of Peter.”
f: Cf. CIC, c. 253 § 1. Cf. CIC, c. 660 § 1. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Homily during Vespers in the Capranica College of Rome, 5; January 21, 1992; OR (1/31/1992) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse at the North American Pontifical College of Rome, October 15, 1984; OR (12/2/1984) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse at the North American Pontifical College of Rome, October 15, 1984; OR (12/2/1984) Spanish Edition.

t: Therefore, the Church of Rome is the best place for this formation: “There is no other place with such an opportunity to form suitable priests as there is in the center of Christianity, next to the tombs of the two great Apostles, under the paternal solicitude of the Supreme Pontiff, who by his function as Vicar of Christ, is the common Father of all people and guardian and interpreter of the Catholic faith.”
f: LEO XIII, Benigna hominum parens, quote by BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse at the Armenian Pontifical College of Rome, July 7, 1984; OR (12/9/1984) Spanish Edition.

t: Roman-ness is “understood as the special spirit of communion with the Successor of Peter, visible Head of the Church of Christ, by means of unity of faith, and charity.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Speech to the Students and Alumni of the Capranica College of Rome, January 21, 1983; OR (4/10/1983) Spanish Edition.

t: These studies can also be undertaken in any scholastically prominent civil university according to the judgment of the Superior General and his Council.

Every superior should use any means necessary for all members of the community to obtain this ongoing formation: conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc. We must spend our whole life searching for the full truth: “If truth is not longed for with all the strengths of one’s soul, it cannot be found in any way.”
f: SAINT AUGUSTINE, The Gift of Perseverance, 20, 53.

h: Article 7: Those Responsible for the Formation
t: We will take special care preparing and choosing those priests in charge of the formation of seminarians, as the future of the Institute depends on it. This is what we mean by “to form a school”: that those priests in charge of the formation of our future priests must be able to transmit the heritage of our Institute, as opposed to forming a “solitary” priest, that is, one who would not contribute to the continuation of our work. In the work of evangelizing the culture, the efforts of one individual or one generation are not sufficient; rather, a great evangelical movement is necessary, one that will forever deepen and extend itself in this task. This is the work of those responsible for formation. Therefore, those in charge of formation must be formed themselves as men of suitable discernment who are rich in spirit.

h: Article 7: Those Responsible for the Formation
t: Besides sufficient knowledge of Catholic doctrine regarding faith and morals, the task of forming others demands certain conditions. These conditions are: human intuition and warmth, familiarity with God and prayer, wisdom, love for liturgy, necessary cultural competence, availability, and willingness to dedicate personal care to each of the seminarians individually, and not merely to the group. To accomplish this, one must have interior serenity, availability, patience, understanding, and true affection toward those who have been commended to him.
f: Cf. CONGREGATION FOR INSTITUTES OF CONSECRATED LIFE AND SOCIE- TIES OF APOSTOLIC LIFE, Directives on Formation in Religious Institutes, 30-32.

t: Anyone who may have legitimately left the Institute upon completing the novitiate, or even after profession, may be re-admitted by the Superior General with the consent of his Council, with no obligation to repeat the novitiate. The Superior General will determine the appropriate testing prior to temporary profession, as well as the duration of the vows prior to perpetual profession.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 690 § 1.

h: Introduction: The Religious Family of the Incarnate Word
t: The Institute of the Incarnate Word recognizes the primary and supreme authority of the Supreme Pontiff, and professes not only obedience to him, but also fidelity, filial submission, adherence, and disposition for the service of the universal Church.

h: Introduction: The Religious Family of the Incarnate Word
t: Ever docile to the will of God, superiors will regard the exercise of their authority as true service to the Church and will always remember that the primary obligation of the superior is to command well.

h: Article 1: Female Branch: The Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará
t: Both “the Institute of the Incarnate Word” and its female branch, “the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará” form the “Religious Family of the Incarnate Word.” Both Institutes are indissolubly united. Their union is spiritual, though legally independent. Their spiritual union is given essentially through possessing the same founder and twin Constitutions, by the Spiritual Father (elected by the women religious), and by the help of other priests of the Institute of the Incarnate Word (spiritual advisers, community advisers, spiritual directors, confessors, professors, etc.) who are appointed for these tasks by the competent authority.

The male contemplative branch is also part of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. It is comprised of those houses where the religious dedicate themselves to the contemplative life in conformity with the provisions of proper law.
Every monastery should have a superior designated by the Superior General with the consent of his council.
The monasteries are houses of the Institute belonging to the province in whose territory they are located.
The Institute of the Incarnate Word also has a Third Order. Third Order “members live in the world but share in the spirit of … [the] institute, under… [its] overall direction…”
f: Cf. CIC, c. 303.

t: The Third Order is structured on three levels, according to the degree of commitment which the members freely choose:

- First Degree: Lay associates who aspire to evangelical perfection according to the spirit of the Institute by participating in its mission, obligating themselves freely through private vows or some other sacred bond. - Second Degree: Lay associations of the faithful: groups or movements, each with its own structure, that want to participate in the spirit and purpose of the Institute.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 725.

t: - Third Degree: All faithful lay people related in different ways to the Institute, who want to share in its spirit: friends, acquaintances, benefactors, family members, etc.
The Third Order is united to and dependent upon our Religious Family in both aspects, in groups and individually.

The Superior General, with the deliberative vote of his Council, chooses the Major Adviser, the liaison between the Institute and the Third Order. Each Provincial Superior, in conjunction with the Provincial Superior of the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará, is the liaison in his province, and gives spiritual assistance to the tertiaries, according to the three levels of the Third Order.

The Superior General of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, or his delegate, will preside over the Central Coordinating Board, made up of: the Superior Generals of both Institutes; the superiors of each Institute, Movement, and Association of the Third Order. This board will coordinate the different apostolates, the foundations, the promotion of the spirit of the Institutes, etc. It will not possess any competence in the government of any branch.

The houses of the Institute will be grouped into provinces, vice-provinces, and delegations that can be established by the General Chapter and the Superior General together with his Council “ad referendum” of the General Chapter.

When a homogeneous group of houses does not meet the minimum conditions to constitute a province, then a viceprovince or a delegation can be established, according to the degree of development it may have reached. The vice-provinces and the delegations will be governed by a superior who possesses the necessary faculties and who is appointed by the Superior General with the consent of his Council.
The supreme governing body of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is the General Chapter, which shall be convoked according to the time and form established below.
General Chapters can be either ordinary or extraordinary.

The General Chapter is convoked ordinarily every six years in order to elect the Superior General and to deal with all matters established in canon 631 § 1, and other matters that may be necessary. Likewise, it is convoked extraordinarily to hold a new election on account of the death, resignation, or removal of the Superior General.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 194.

t: Pending due consent of his Council, the Superior General may convoke an Extraordinary Chapter to address grave matters of the utmost importance to the Institute.
The General Chapter will be convoked and presided over by the Superior General or his substitute. Also attending, with voice and deliberative vote, will be the following:
1) By reason of office:

- The former Superior Generals of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. - The General Councilors. - The Provincial Superiors and others who are their equals - The Rectors of the Major Seminaries. - The Rectors of duly established Clerical Colleges.
2) Delegates by Election:

- Priests under perpetual vows from each province and viceprovince, in proportion to the number of members of each jurisdiction, elected by an absolute majority of the perpetually professed members. The numerical proportion must be established in a pre-Chapter regulation.
- Two superiors of monasteries – for every six monasteries – elected as the Directory of Contemplative Life dictates.
With regard to the capacity and conditions of the voters and the votes, we will take into account what is established in Canon Law.
The number of Delegates by Election of the General Chapter must be higher than that of the Participants by Reason of their Office.
The President of the Chapter is the Superior General of the Institute or one who takes his place.
The Chapter Fathers will secretly vote for a Chapter Secretary, two auxiliaries and two auditors.

A profession of faith according to can. 833 will be made at the opening of the General Chapter. The General Secretary will then immediately record in the minutes the names of those in attendance. In the same way, he will record the name of the person elected Chapter Secretary, auxiliaries, and auditors. He will also record the agenda of the day.

At a suitable time, the Chapter will proceed to elect the Superior General by a vote that is free, secret, certain, and absolute, and by a two-thirds majority vote of the Chapter Fathers present. After two inefficient audits wherein the two-thirds majority has not been reached, there will be a third vote between the two candidates who obtained the highest number of votes; or, if there are more than two, the election will be held between the two longest professed; or, if they are equal in length of period of profession, the election will be between the two oldest. After the third audit, if a tie persists, the longest professed will be elected, and if they are equal in this amount of time, the older will be elected. The Superior-elect will be notified immediately. From that moment, the Superior-elect will have a period of eight working days to accept or reject the position, and if he accepts, to name the Vicar General, the General Secretary, and the Treasurer. Those designated by the Superior General will likewise have an equal length of time to accept or reject the appointment.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 119 § 1.

t: After electing the Superior General, the Chapter will proceed to elect, by absolute majority, two members who will be part of the General Council, and then to elect the first, second, and third substitute Councilors, also by absolute majority. In the event that the Superior General’s nominations include any members already elected by the Chapter to be Councilors or Substitutes, the nominations by the Superior General will take priority, and he himself will fill the missing positions. The members of the General Council, elected by the Chapter, will remain in their functions for the same period of time as the Superior General, and both the Superior General and council members can be re-elected.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 177.

t: Once the elections have been verified, the Chapter will hold the necessary sessions in which the new Superior General will be informed of the state of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. The other religious in attendance can make observations about things that they think are worthy of consideration for the well-being of the provinces and houses of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.
The main matters that will be addressed within the General Chapter are:

1) The defense of the patrimony of the Institute of the Incarnate Word; making adjustments and implementing renewal according to it, electing the Superior General, and promulgating the rules that bind for all Institute members.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 631 § 1.

t: 2) The amendment of a given point of the Constitutions, by a two-thirds consent of the General Chapter members, which then must be approved by the competent ecclesiastic authority.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 595 § 1.

t: 3) The revision and modification of the general Directories, Regulations, and other rules.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 587 § 4.

t: 4) The division of the Institute as a whole into provinces, viceprovinces, and delegations, and the cessation of the same.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 581. Cf. CIC, c. 585.

t: 5) Definition of the way in which the evangelical counsels will be observed.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 598 § 1.

t: 6) The handling of any other major topics, requests, and suggestions that may be freely contributed.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The Institute is permanently governed by a Superior General assisted by his Council of five Councilors. Of the six members of the General Government, the Superior General and at least two Councilors will be elected by the Chapter. The Vicar General, the General Secretary, and the General Treasurer are named by the Superior General.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The Superior General holds the highest rank in the Institute and exercises the functions of primary authority. He attends to the care and government of the Institute of the Incarnate Word and of all its members according to the present Constitutions and Canon Law.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The Superior General’s jurisdiction of authority is over the entire Institute of the Incarnate Word and over each of its members, both in the apostolic and contemplative houses.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: To be elected and to perform this office, he must possess ability, discretion, prudence, maturity, and the other virtues required for the sound performance of his duty.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: To be elected, the Superior General must be a priest with at least fifteen years of perpetual profession in the Institute of the Incarnate Word.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 623.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: He is elected for a period of six years and can be reelected.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: - The voters must be careful not to elect anyone who has desired or sought the office of Superior General. The same applies for choosing the other superiors.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: - The Superior General must avoid preferential treatment of members of the Institute. He must have the same attitude toward everyone, and avoid showing partiality. Preference of persons is a sin that opposes distributive justice – the principle of giving positions, offices, and responsibilities for the common good in proportion to the dignity or ability of each person. In justice, the person who is most suitable for each assignment must be chosen for the common good. Therefore, the person’s qualifications regarding his suitability must be considered. When we fail to do so, we commit the vice of partiality of persons. The person chosen in such a case is appointed because of who he is, and not because of his abilities; he therefore prevents the one who, in justice, should fill that office from doing so. This kind of injustice is expressly prohibited in Sacred Scripture. The Superior should be a father in the image of the Heavenly Father, Who shows no partiality (Acts 10:34).

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: - The Superior General is expected to be faithful to the Constitutions. He should not grant himself the authority to exempt anyone from honoring them even for minor reasons.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: - He is never to reprimand in anger. He is to be gentle with all and strict with himself. He is never to speak in praise of himself except with the hope of bringing about some good, and even then only with humility and acknowledgment of God’s gifts.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: - All functions and obligations flowing from his office as Superior General must be performed with a spirit of exceptional service. His authority is for service and his service is authoritative. He is to govern as one who serves, because he is obligated by reason of his office to serve by leading: Let the greatest among you be as the youngest, and the leader as the servant (Lk 22:26).

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: Faculties and duties of the Superior General are:

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 1st To govern the members as sons of God. The Superior General is to extend to them the same paternal charity that God has for them. He is also to have that fraternal charity desired by God in loving the other superiors and members. God also desires that they too love each other with the same fraternal charity.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 2nd To respect each human person because of his dignity as a person, and even more so because of the added dignity flowing from baptism and consecration. Moreover, he is to respect them because of the combination of inborn and acquired abilities which make up the uniqueness of each member.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 3rd To promote voluntary obedience, to foster willingness in obedience and submissive freedom. Whoever has freely professed obedience must voluntarily practice the specific acts of that counsel. The perfect attainment of this ideal will be the supernatural and human sign of the proper exercise of authority.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 4th To listen willingly. To listen is neither to assent, nor to hear with deaf ears; neither is it the attention of a disciple, nor the instruction of a teacher. Listening does not require giving an answer, for indeed, an answer may not exist. Nor may it be prudent or obligatory to give any answer. Nor is it his duty to reach an agreement on what he and any member may have been talking about, as this agreement is often non-existent or impossible to attain. Nor is it his duty to make a decision that accommodates the desires of a member.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 5th To foster his initiatives for the good of the Institute and the Church, because he is obligated to do so by his office, he must energetically resist any passivity, as if merely waiting for others to suggest initiatives.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 6th To decide and to order what should be done, taking into account the executive power given by Canon law.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 137 and concordant paragraphs.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The specific and proper functions of the Superior General, besides the ones already established by can. 619 of CIC, are the following:

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 1st To work for the preservation and growth of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 2nd To promote members’ knowledge and observance of the Holy See’s decrees relating to religious.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 3rd To oversee observance of the Constitutions and fidelity to the spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 4th To promote as much as possible the spiritual and temporal good of all the members of the Institute, and to ensure that everyone fulfills his respective duties and obligations.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 5th To preside over the sessions of the General Council and present therein all the matters to be addressed. The Superior General can seek advice from the Council any time he deems it necessary.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 6th To notify the Provincial Superiors, and when he deems it appropriate, to directly notify the Local Superiors, of the Council’s resolutions that they should be aware of.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 7th To visit all of the Provinces and houses of the Institute for inspection and general direction.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 8th To oversee all aspects of the spiritual and intellectual formation of religious.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 9th To convoke ordinary and extraordinary General Chapters, according to these Constitutions.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 10th To grant the license to publish writings related to religious or moral matters.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 832.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: 11th Within the limits of his proper competence, the Superior General can grant dispensations, that is, relaxations of merely ecclesiastical laws in a particular case, in every place, with respect to the members, and with respect to himself, according to the conditions demanded by Canon law.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 85. Cf. CIC, cc. 91 and 136. Cf. CIC, c. 90 and related canons.

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The Superior General also possesses other duties which he must execute together with his Council as determined in Chapter 4 (The Office of the General Chapter).

h: CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Superior General
t: The Superior General can be removed from his office for the reasons stated in the Code of Canon law.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 194.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: He is the second in authority in the Institute, whom all religious are obliged to obey after the Superior General. He will exercise his authority according to these Constitutions only when he replaces the Superior General or carries out the functions delegated by him.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: The appointments that are under the competence of the Superior General cannot be made by the Vicar General.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: In the case of vacancy or absence, the Vicar General can be replaced by whomever the Superior General designates.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: The priest who performs this office should have the necessary abilities and must be perpetually professed at least 10 years in the Institute.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: The Vicar General can be removed from his office for the same reasons as the Superior General. The same applies for all other superiors.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 194.

h: Article 2: Members of the General Council a. Vicar General
t: In addition to his obligations as Vicar General, he, as first General Councilor, will substitute for the Superior General in his absence, illness, or other impediments. Likewise, in case of death, resignation, or removal of the Superior General, the Vicar will temporarily undertake the governance of the Institute. However, the Vicar General may neither proceed to a new election, nor transfer, nor appoint any Provincial or Local Superior except in the case of necessity, for four months from the date of vacancy. After those four months, the Vicar General cannot defer the convocation for the election of the Superior General for longer than three more months.
This office will be performed by a priest with at least 10 years of perpetual profession in the Institute. He must also possess the qualities required by this office.
It is incumbent on the Secretary General:
- To record the minutes of Council sessions and those of the General Chapters.
- To send out all communications of the Superior General re-garding matters of the Superior General’s office.
- To take care of and update all of the Institute’s records concerning persons, houses, provinces, dealings with civil and religious organizations, contracts, statistics, etc.
The priest to whom the office of Treasurer General is given must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute and be qualified for this job.

The Treasurer General is responsible for the administration of the Institute under the authority of the Superior General and the supervision of his Council. He will take particular care of all documentation concerning goods and their custody.

The Treasurer General will register all income and expenses of funds and valuables. He will inform the Council regarding the state of the above-mentioned matters every three months and whenever the Council requires.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 636.

t: In addition to the priests already mentioned, two more priests will form part of the General Council. They will be given the name of General Councilors.

These priests must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute and have the prudence and all the other virtues necessary for the exercise of their office together with the other members of the Council.

To replace the General Councilors appointed by the Superior General, the Superior General himself will make the new appointments. The same applies to the replacement of those provincial or local councilors appointed by the provincial or local superior, respectively.

Whenever any Councilor from those elected by the General Chapter ceases to belong to the General Council because of resignation, removal, transfer, or any other cause, he will be re-placed by the first substitute, and successively thereafter.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: The General Council acting as a college. The Superior General is first among his equals with the same right to vote. The decision must be made as a college, and therefore its execution is binding for the members of the General Council. The college will be convoked according to can. 166 and requires a quorum of four. It is responsible for:
f: Cf. CIC, c. 127 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - approval of the Directories of the Institute, ad referendum of the General Chapter; modification of those Directories already approved, as needed, and also ad referendum of the General Chapter, to adapt them to the Church Magisterium’s new documents. Modification of the Directories is necessary to update them according to the new documents of the Magisterium of the Church. Any modification to the Directory of Monasteries will require two-thirds consent of the perpetually-professed members of the Contemplative Branch.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - Decree of dismissal by absolute majority of the present members.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 699 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: The General Council acting with deliberative vote. The Council acts according to can. 127, § 1 from the CIC, not as a college, but rather as a group of persons from whom consent is required. Decisions will be made by an absolute majority of those present. The final action will be the result of the personal choice and authority of the Superior, who may act according to the mentioned decision, or abstain from acting. The Council will be convoked as established in can. 166 of CIC, and will decide on:

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The establishment of provinces, vice-provinces and delegations ad referendum of the next General Chapter.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The appointment of Provincial Superiors, vice-provincials, and delegates. The appointment should be preceded by appropriate consultation. Individuals must be notified of the offices for which they have been appointed; they may accept or refuse their respective offices within a period of eight working days.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 625 § 3.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The appointment of superiors of houses of formation, namely, both major and minor seminaries, masters of novices, rectors of universities, and superiors of monasteries, after having consulted the Provincial Superior.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The agreement upon and the appointment of the priest elected by the female branch to be its spiritual father.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The appointment of the major adviser of the Third Order.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - Admission to the diaconate and priesthood.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The establishment of houses.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The establishment or cessation of novitiates, major seminaries, minor seminaries, and other houses of formation.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 647 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The cessation of houses.
f: Cf. CIC, cc. 585 and 616 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The approval of study plans for the houses of formation. - Material transactions.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 638 § 3.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The exception of making the novitiate in a different house.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 647 § 2.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - Change of institute.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 684 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The exclaustration of perpetually professed priests.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 686 § 1 and 3.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The indult of departure to temporarily professed religious.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 688 § 2.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - The re-admission of ex-members.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: The General Council acting with consultative vote. The Council acts as a group; everyone’s advice or opinion is necessary for an act to be valid. The final action will be the result of the personal choice and authority of the Superior, who can act even against what is unanimously advised if he has sufficient reason for doing so. The Council will be convoked according to Canon law to deal with the following matters:
f: Cf. CIC, c. 127 § 1.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - Approval of local regulations for the houses of formation and monasteries.

h: CHAPTER 4 THE OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNCIL Article 1: Faculties
t: - Approval of other general regulations.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: There will be two kinds of general council meetings: ordinary and extraordinary, both of which will be presided over by the Superior General, and in his absence, by the Vicar General or whoever takes his place.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: Ordinary meetings will be held each month, and the extraordinary meetings will be held when needed. Matters concerning the Institute will be dealt with and resolved in both types of meetings. Such matters will be presented by whoever presides. For meetings to be valid, a quorum of three is needed, except for what is established in paragraph 321 of these Constitutions.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: Council members have the right to present proposals concerning the following topics: formation, apostolate, discipline, spiritual life, and other proposals, all of which should be recorded in the minutes.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: Council members should present their opinions with fidelity and sincerity, and give their consent in matters of great importance.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: Except for cases in which the Council acts collegially, the Superior is outside and above his Council, which means that he is not to vote when consultation or consent are required as a group of persons, or as individual persons.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 127 § 1. Cf. CIC, c. 127 § 2.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: During the first three months of the year and in an ordinary meeting, the income and expense accounts of the Institute’s general administration will be submitted for examination and approval.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: Within the first three months of the year, the Institute’s Provinces and Houses are to prepare and submit the annual income and expense accounts of the previous year to the General Council; this does not prevent the Superior General or the Provincial Superior from examining the accounts of the provincial or local administrations on the occasion of the ordinary or extraordinary canonical visit.

h: Article 2: Meetings of the General Council
t: The Councilors are rigorously warned to keep all matters addressed during meetings confidential. Only the Superior General can communicate decisions with due discretion when appropriate.

h: CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces
t: To make governance of the Institute easier and more effective, territorial divisions called provinces are permanently established, according to the various conditions of people, places and time.

h: CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces
t: The General Chapter, and the Superior General ad referendum of the General Chapter, are responsible for the establishment or modification of province and vice-province boundaries, in accordance with established norms. The following norms must be considered:

h: CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces
t: a) In order for a territory or a group of houses to constitute a province, at least three canonically established houses of the Institute of the Incarnate Word are required.

h: CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces
t: b) As far as possible, homogeneity of the territory and its socio-cultural features will be taken into account, as will access to communications and administrative conveniences.

h: CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT Article 1: Provinces
t: Under the direction of the Superior General and his Council, each province is governed by a Provincial Superior, assisted by four provincial Councilors.

The priest appointed Provincial Superior must have the necessary physical and moral aptitude to execute the demands of this office, and must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute. The General Superior, with the consent of his Council, can dispense with this condition.
The Provincial Superior is appointed for three years, and may be reappointed for another three years in the same province, but ordinarily his appointment will not exceed this amount of time.

The Provincial Superior will exercise his authority over each and every house in the province under his jurisdiction, and also over the monasteries of contemplative life established in the same territory.
The faculties and obligations of the Provincial Superior are:

1st To exercise authority in the province, under the authority of the Superior General whose directives he will faithfully execute and whom he will appropriately inform regarding the life of the province.
2nd To appoint the first two members of the Provincial Council, that is, the vicar and the secretary.
3rd To appoint the local superiors with the consent of his Council.
4th To preside over the sessions of the provincial council and to propose the matters to be addressed therein. He can consult his council whenever he deems it necessary.
5th To communicate to the local superiors the resolutions and decrees that he receives from the general and provincial councils.

6th To resolve matters proposed by the house superiors or by religious, and also, according to the importance of these matters, to forward any appropriate issues to the Superior General and his Council.
7th To transmit to the Superior General all news and reports which will help him in appointing members for the positions that are under his competence.
8th To visit the houses of his province once a year and as many times as necessary.
9th To admit candidates to the novitiate and to temporary profession, after having consulted his Council. Similarly, to extend the period of temporal profession, with the consent of his Council.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 657 § 2.

t: 10th To admit candidates to perpetual profession with the consent of the provincial council.
11th To exclude members from subsequent profession, after consulting his Council.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 689 § 1.

t: 12th To grant permission for a prolonged absence from the community.
13th To grant permission in particular cases regarding the individual goods of those who are professing according to what is established in n. 70 of these Constitutions.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 668 § 2.

t: For the Superior General to be well-informed on the life and progress of the Institute, at the end of each year the Provincial Superiors will send an exact and detailed account on the financial and disciplinary state of the province and its government (in addition to the ordinary reports), together with the annual personal letter.

The Superior General, with the deliberative vote of his Council, will be able to grant the Provincial Superiors wider faculties within the norms of Canon law, principally to those located further away. However, those faculties granted to Provincial Superiors, ordinary as well as extraordinary, can in no way limit the authority and rights that belong to the Superior General and his Council according to the Constitutions.

h: Article 3: Members of the Provincial Council a. Provincial Vicar
t: The Provincial Vicar is appointed directly by the Provincial Superior. He shall exercise his authority over all members of the province when he substitutes for the Provincial Superior. He can also act with the functions delegated by the Provincial Superior.

h: Article 3: Members of the Provincial Council a. Provincial Vicar
t: In addition to possessing the aptitude required of his office, the Provincial Vicar must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute. After consulting his Council, the General Superior can dispense with this condition.

The provincial secretary is directly appointed by the Provincial Superior. He will perform the functions of secretary and provincial filing clerk, and the preservation of provincial documents as well as those of the provincial government archive will be entrusted to his care. For appointment to this office, the priest must have made perpetual vows.

The other provincial councilors, apart from the required aptitude for the office, must be religious with perpetual vows. They will be elected by the religious with perpetual vows who belong to the province (they will also elect three substitute councilors). When the majority of those who have been convoked are present, members who have the absolute majority of votes will be elected. After two inefficient audits, there will be another vote between the two candidates who obtained the highest number of votes; if there are more than two candidates, the election will be between the two longest professed. If they share the same amount of time professed, the election will be between the two oldest; after the third audit, if a tie persists, the longest professed will be elected, and if the candidates are equal in this, the older will be elected.
The provincial councilors will remain in their office for three years. Upon completion of their term, they can be reelected, but not normally for a third three-year term.
The Provincial Superior will choose the provincial treasurer from the two councilors. The priest so-appointed must possess the necessary ability to faithfully execute his office.

The administration and custody of the province’s goods belong to the provincial treasurer under the authority of his superiors. He will ensure the accuracy of all documents and ledgers of income and expenses. He will present his reports to the Provincial Superior and his council for their knowledge, revision, and approval every three months, and whenever required by competent authority.
The faculties and obligations of the provincial council are:
a) To handle cases within their competence, by means of consultative or deliberative vote, according to the rules of Canon law and the Institute’s proper law.
b) To examine and approve the accounts of the province.

c) To give the consultative vote for the admission of candidates to the Novitiate and temporary profession, and to give its consent for the admission of candidates to perpetual profession, by absolute majority of the quorum.

The provincial council must be convoked once a month and can convene for extraordinary sessions whenever the Provincial Superior, or his substitute, deems it appropriate. For validity, a session requires a quorum of two members in addition to the Provincial Superior. What is established in n. 328 applies to the Provincial Superior.

The Superior General must make an official visit to every province and house of the Institute at least once during his mandate, and whenever necessity demands it; unofficially, he must do so when he deems it appropriate.
In the event that he cannot perform this grave duty, he himself will appoint a religious as visitor.
By reason of his office, the Provincial Superior will visit each house of his province on three different occasions during his term of office, and as many times as special circumstances require.

Each house must have a sufficient number of religious to ensure community life and the practice of the evangelical counsels. That is why at least three religious must be assigned, except in special cases.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 610.

t: In every local community of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, there must be a priest who carries out the office of the local superior, assisted by a council with four members (except where this is not possible because of the number of priests), the first two of whom shall be directly elected by the local superior and who shall carry out the office of local vicar and secretary, re-spectively. The rest of the members shall be elected by simple majority of the priests who belong to the same community. One of them shall be elected by the local superior for the office of local treasurer.
The superior is the head of the family in each house; all the religious in that community must obey his orders with docility, exactness, and religious submission.

Naming a local superior must be preceded by appropriate consultation. To be appointed local superior, the religious must be a priest with perpetual vows, and must possess the ability to govern, a spirit of religiosity, a spirit of observance, and other re-quirements for the office.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 625 § 3. Cf. CIC, c. 625 § 3.

t: His term of office will be three years, and ordinarily he will not be reappointed for a third consecutive term in the same house.
The local superior has the following duties and tasks:
1) To govern the community, keeping in mind the purpose of religious life and the particular goals of the Institute.

2) To oversee the observance of the Constitutions; to see to it that the spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is maintained; and to dispense with some point of discipline in particular cases for a reasonable cause and in accordance with the norms established by the major superiors of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.
3) To promote the knowledge and observance of decrees of the Holy See related to religious, or those of interest among the community’s religious.

4) To name the second councilor, when possible, and to consult his immediate major superior, and those responsible for the various offices. Those who have been named will be notified, and they will have eight working days to accept or decline the office.
5) To regulate what he deems conducive to the order and service of the household, and whatever leads to the greater good of the family entrusted to his care and concern.
6) To preside over all activities of the house.

7) To resolve grave and urgent cases when it is impossible to appeal to the general or Provincial Superior, and to give an account of his resolution afterward to the competent major superior, indicating the motives for the resolution in question.

8) To meet with his councilors once a month and whenever necessary for their input, so that he may resolve what he deems more appropriate in the Lord. To be valid, the meeting must be attended by at least two members of the local council.

9) To write the local regulations with his council that will be submitted for approval of the Provincial Superior, except when the regulation must be approved by the Superior General according to proper law.

In cases requiring consultation and whenever else he deems it appropriate, he will contact the Provincial Superior. He will also submit to him an accurate report of the state of the house and its members at least every three months. He will also write to the Superior General at least once a year and as many times as he deems it necessary.

The first local councilor is also the vicar and substitutes for the superior during his absence, illness, or other impediment, outside of which he does not have any authority except for what the superior delegates to him. In the vicar’s absence, the councilor who is next in line will substitute for the local superior, according to the established order.
The second councilor, directly appointed by the local superior, will be the filing clerk responsible for handling and maintaining the house files.

A priest will hold the office of local treasurer in each house of the Institute; he will administer the goods of the house under the direction of the local superior. In fulfilling his duties he will oversee the funds and valuables that belong to the community. The local treasurer administers the goods of the community and is responsible for making ordinary purchases, according to the norms established by the local superior; he will carefully do the bookkeeping, and will give a report to the council of the house every month, every three months to the Provincial Superior, and as requested.
Besides possessing the necessary aptitude, those priests appointed for the local council must have taken perpetual vows. They remain in office for a renewable three-year term.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 627 § 1.

t: Local councilors are obligated to maintain complete confidentiality regarding the matters about which they are consulted. However, they must honestly inform the general or Provincial Superior if required to do so.

The goods of the Institute are the goods of the Church. Therefore, their administration must be according to Canon Law, these norms, and the Institute’s proper law. The Institute, as a juridical person, has the right to purchase, possess, administer, and sell temporal goods, according to Church Canon law.
Ultimately, the Superior General is responsible for all of the Congregation’s goods.
The Treasurer General, acting under the authority of the Superior General, administers all the goods of the Institute.
The respective treasurers administer the goods of the Institute, provinces, and houses under the authority of their immediate superiors, who will be informed of all matters concerning these goods.
The treasurers are to provide a regular account from their administration to their corresponding superior.
When acquiring assets, any resources consistent with the life of the Institute should be implemented, according to what is determined by the administration’s regulations.
The Superior General’s written consent will be re-quired to validate any act of disposing of or administering goods that has grave significance to the Institute.
“Any appearance of luxury, immoderate profit and accumulation of goods is to be avoided.”
f: Cf. CIC, c. 634.

t: Something will be set aside, as means allow, for the needs of the Church and sustenance of the poor.
f: Cf. CIC, c. 640.

t: The norms of Canon law will be followed in the case of separation from the Institute:
Transfer to another Institute: CIC, cc 684-685.
Departure from the Institute: CIC, cc 686-693.
Dismissal of members: CIC, cc 694-704.

h: PART 11 OBLIGATION TO OBSERVE THE CONSTITUTIONS
t: All members of the Institute must observe the evangelical counsels with the greatest possible perfection. They must also surrender to Jesus through Mary, and “direct their lives according to the Institute’s own law and so strive for the perfection of their state.”
f: Cf. CIC, c. 598 § 2.

h: PART 11 OBLIGATION TO OBSERVE THE CONSTITUTIONS
t: The Institute’s proper law is formed by: the Constitutions handed down by the founder; the Directories containing subsidiary and practical norms, which serve to apply the Constitutions; the Rules and Chapter norms and documents; the executive decisions of the superiors; traditions, good customs, and proper documents.

h: PART 11 OBLIGATION TO OBSERVE THE CONSTITUTIONS
t: May the Blessed Virgin Mary help us all to reach the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

h: PART 11 OBLIGATION TO OBSERVE THE CONSTITUTIONS
t: “God alone.”

h: CHAPTER 1 THE MYSTERY OF THE WORD Introduction
t: We want to be anchored in the sacrosanct mystery of the Incarnation which is “the first and fundamental mystery of Jesus Christ.” Rooted in this mystery that is truly present among us, we want to fervently set out to restore all things in Christ (Eph 1:10). We want to be another Incarnation of the Word so as to incarnate Him in all humanity.
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, September 9, 1981; OR (9/13/1981) Spanish Edition.

h: CHAPTER 1 THE MYSTERY OF THE WORD Introduction
t: Our religion “is a doctrine, but is above all an event: the event of the Incarnation, Jesus, the God-Man who recapitulated in himself the universe (Cf. Eph 1:10).” “It is impossible to find an entirely comparable example of the Godhead of Persons and of the mystery of the Incarnation.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Homily in the Cathedral of Oaxaca, January 29, 1979; OR (2/11/1979) Spanish Edition. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST III, 2, 6, ad 1.

h: CHAPTER 1 THE MYSTERY OF THE WORD Introduction
t: We always want to draw new light and strength from the redeeming Incarnation, since Jesus Christ is the inexhaustible source of Being, Truth, Kindness, Beauty, Life and Love.

We profess the preeminence of Christ, even as a man, over all creation. He has primacy over the souls and bodies of the members of His mystical Body, and also over all men through all ages. He is the Head of everyone – even of those not predestined to eternal life in heaven with Him, who will only stop being potential members of the Body of Christ when they leave this world. The Son is “the Father’s work of art.”
f: SAINT AUGUSTINE, De Trinitate VI, 10 (ML 34,148); cf. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST III, 59, 1, ad 2.

t: We profess that Christ is Head of the Church and of all men, and that He has triple primacy over them: a primacy of order, of perfection and of power. He has primacy of order because due to His closeness with God, His grace is the highest and the first – though not chronologically speaking. All who receive grace receive it in reference to His: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29). He has primacy of perfection because He possesses the fullness of grace: We have beheld his glory... full of grace and truth (Jn 1:14). He has primacy of power because He has all the power to communicate grace and glory to all the members of His Body: And from his fullness have we all received, grace upon grace (Jn 1:16).

Therefore, heresies throughout the ages have had and will have a common denominator: to diminish the dignity of Jesus Christ. Saint Leo the Great pointed out: “We are assured that hardly anyone (any heretic) has gone astray except if he has failed to believe the reality of Christ’s two natures, and to acknowledge one Person at the same time.” Saint Thomas teaches that, “When one considers the errors of heretics, it is apparent that their main objective is to diminish the dignity of Christ.” “No other mystery exists outside of Christ.” That is why Saint Philip Neri teaches, “Whosoever wants something besides Christ, does not know what he wants. Whosoever wishes for anything but Christ, does not know what he wishes for; whosoever asks for anything but Christ, does not know what he is asking for; whosoever works not for Christ, does not know what he is doing.”
f: SAINT LEO THE GREAT, Homily on the Nativity, 8, 4. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Opuscula Theologica, Contra errores Graecorum, Vol. I, Ed. Marietti, 1078. SAINT AUGUSTINE, Epistles, 187, 34. SAINT PHILIP NERI, Lo Spirito di San Filippo Neri nelle sua Massime e Ricordi, Roma 1988, 7.

h: Article 2: Love for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
t: Contemplation on the mystery of the Incarnation nurtures love for the Holy Trinity – Father, Son and Holy Spirit – who was the actual author of the Incarnation. This contemplation also ignites in us an ardent love for the Word who “for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven.” It also nourishes love for the Word in His preexistence, His entering the world, His earthly life (works and teachings), His leaving the world, His mystical life and His second coming.
f: COUNCIL OF NICEA I, The Nicene Creed.

t: a. Eternal Person. The person of the Word exists from all eternity: In the beginning was the Word... and the Word was God (Jn 1:1). By acknowledging the existence of the Word as coming before the Blessed Virgin and the creation of the world, we base our spirituality on the absoluteness of God before whom everything is like nothing. The exhortation of Saint Cyprian “to prefer nothing whatever to Christ” must always be of prime importance to us. We have to be convinced that “God loves Christ… more than He loves the entire created universe,” and, as Saint Teresa says, “God alone suffices.” In everything and for everything, we want to give primacy to the spiritual, and to surrender in holy abandonment to God’s “will of good-pleasure,” since as a response to the revelation of God, “man freely commits his entire self to God.”
f: Cf. Is 40:17. SAINT CYPRIAN, On the Lord’s Prayer, Chap. XIII-15, CSEL 3, 275-278. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST I, 20, 4, ad 1. SAINT TERESA OF JESUS, Poem “Nada te turbe” Obras Completas, BAC, Madrid 1979, 514. (Translation is ours). DV 5.

t: b. Distinct Person. And the Word was with God (Jn 1:1). The Word Incarnate is “the Word that proceeds from silence.” The distinction of Persons, the Word from the Father and from the Holy Spirit, moves us to give our whole life a Trinitarian imprint – the supreme mystery of God, the fullness of man and “the substance of the New Testament,” in Whom men, by means of the Son-made-flesh, have access to the Father in the Holy Spirit and become partakers of the divine nature (2 Pt 1:4). It must be a seal of honor to profess “three Persons equal in majesty, undivided in splendor, yet one Lord, one God.”
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF ANTIOCH, Epistle to the Magnesians, 8, 2. RM, Preface of the Holy Trinity.

t: c. Divine Person. And the Word was God (Jn 1:1). We recognize in Him the fullness of divinity with all the attributes of the divine being and the divine operations, and that all things came to be through him, and without him nothing came to be (Jn 1:3). In a particular way, we want to see ourselves and all men in Him, and to see ourselves created “in the image and likeness of God.” “For God and before God, the human being is always unique and unrepeatable; somebody thought of and chosen from eternity; someone called and identified by his own name.”
f: Cf. Gn 1:26. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Christmas Message, December 25, 1978; OR (12/31/1978) Spanish Edition.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: And the Word became flesh (Jn 1:14). The work of the Incarnation is shared among the three divine persons, but it is attributed to the Holy Spirit because: a) The supreme love of God is the cause of the Incarnation: For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (Jn 3:16). b) Human nature was not assumed by our own merit, but only by grace, which is attributed to the Holy Spirit: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit (1 Cor 12:4). c) Jesus Christ alone is holy and the only Son of God: The child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God (Lk 1:35); and because in Him we are made children of God: Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Gal 4:6); in Him we are sanctified, since He is the Spirit of holiness (Rom 1:4).

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: Based on the mystery of the Incarnation – the work of the Spirit in the Virgin Mary – we must always sing the mercies of God because “the immortality of blessedness becomes credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.” We must understand clearly that without Jesus Christ, we can do nothing, and that we must always be inclined to grow in virtue with all our strength.
f: Cf. Ps 89:1. SAINT AUGUSTINE, De Trinitate, 13, 9. Cf. Jn 15:5.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: Therefore, we must be moved by the Holy Spirit and have utter docility to Him. To obtain this we need:

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: a) Attention to the Holy Spirit’s inspirations like the Virgin, who was worthy to be visited by the Angel Gabriel and to listen to him because of her habitual attentiveness to the motions of the Spirit. Therefore, we must work against habitual dissipation, lack of mortification and disordered affections.
f: Cf. Lk 1:28.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: b) Discernment of spirits in order to accept and follow the motions of the Holy Spirit, and to reject those of the evil spirit. We must be very prudent, in imitation of the Virgin who considered in her mind what sort of greeting this might be (Lk 1:29).

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: c) Docility and readiness in the execution of the Holy Spirit’s requests, as the Virgin who arose and went with haste (Lk 1:39). “Indecision is foreign to the grace of the Holy Spirit.” We must always work against the temptation to delay, against the fear to sacrifice and totally surrender, and against the temptation to recover what we have given, seeking compensation or setting our hearts on things that are not of God.
f: SAINT AMBROSE, Commentary on Saint Luke, 2, 19. Cf. SAINT IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA, Spiritual Exercises, 322.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: Being in tune with the Holy Spirit must move us to live the Beatitudes, to allow ourselves to be led by the gifts of the Spirit acting in us, and to be fertile in producing the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22).

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: We must also consider the “yes” of the Most Holy Virgin: Let it be done to me according to your word (Lk 1:38). The Mother of God’s consent shows us that she was not “a mere passive instrument, but instead, she freely cooperated with the work of human salvation through faith and obedience.” Likewise, neither should we be passive instruments.
f: Cf. LG 56.

h: CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD Article 1: His First Coming
t: The Virgin gave her “yes” as a servant: I am the handmaid of the Lord (Lk 1:38), He has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid (Lk 1:48), and then the Word took the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7) in her pure womb. Therefore, our spirituality needs to be marked in a special way by professing a fourth vow of Marian slavery according to the spirit of Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, so as to “marianize” our whole life. When we reach the chapter that speaks about vows, we will discuss our Marian spirituality further.

Saint Peter’s confession has always been central to the Catholic faith: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mt 16:16). This confession must be central to our spirituality, too. As taught by the successor of Peter, Blessed John Paul II, “We are only redeemed if Jesus Christ can in his own person fully communicate the divine life.” On another occasion, Blessed Pope John Paul II said that when professing Jesus is Lord (Rom 10:9), “We break with everything that claims to set itself up as an absolute, and we destroy the idols of money, power, sex, and those [idols] that are hidden in ideologies, ‘lay religions’ with totalitarian ambitions.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the International Theological Commission, October 6, 1981; OR (10/25/1981) Spanish Edition. Cf. 1 Cor 12:3; Jn 20:28. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the Latin-American Episcopal Conference, July 7, 1980; OR (7/13/1980) Spanish Edition.

t: He is the “Way” to the Father, and nobody goes to the Father except through Him. His is the only name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). He is the one that makes the Church a “sacrament – a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of unity among all men.” He alone sustains all the Church’s dogmas since He is “the truth that contains all the others.” He alone reveals to us the primacy and weight of eternity above all temporal reality.
f: Cf. Jn 14:6. LG 1. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the Pontifical Antonianum University, January 16, 1982; OR (1/31/1982) Spanish Edition.

t: In addition, professing the divinity of Jesus Christ must move us to practice the virtues of transcendence: faith, hope and charity; and from practicing these, to the urgency of prayer and incessant contemplation, and to becoming conscious of the need to actively and passively purify the senses and the spirit.

In contemplating that the Incarnate Word is “God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father,” we want to put aside all attitudes of mere humanism (humanism without transcendence) that eventually annihilates man. We want to put aside all attitudes of false kenosis (emptying of oneself) that, based on an excuse of turning to that which is inferior, wind up emptying what is superior. “To be in the world” means that a person embraces the spirit of the world by emptying oneself and forgetting that Christians are in the world but not of the world (Jn 17:16). By “falling away from God altogether, [man] would cease to exist. For the glory of God is man fully alive; and man’s life consists of beholding God.”
f: COUNCIL OF NICEA I, The Nicene Creed. SAINT IRENAEUS, Against the Heresies, 4, 20, 7.

t: Saint John the Baptist foretold Jesus: After me comes a man (Jn 1:30); Saint Peter denied Jesus before the servant girl: I do not know the man (Mt 26:72); and Pilate presented Him to the crowd: Ecce homo (Behold the man) (Jn 19:5). We profess that Jesus is not only God, but also true man, as the centurion did: Truly this man was the Son of God (Mk 15:39).

Becoming man is “the first and fundamental mystery of Jesus Christ.” “God had never been so close to man – and never had man been so close to God – as in that very moment: in the instant of the Incarnation mystery!”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, September 6, 1981; OR (9/13/1981) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, August 2, 1981; OR (8/9/1981) Spanish Edition.

t: The Word that not only expresses the Father, but also expresses the being and the work of all creatures, and in particularly of all men, male or female, “manifests man fully, and man discovers himself in the sublimity of his vocation,” in such a way that “it is only in the mystery of the Incarnate Word that the mystery of man truly becomes clear.”
f: Cf. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST I, 34, 3; I-II, 93, 1, ad 2: “And among other things expressed by this Word, the eternal law itself is expressed thereby.” GS 22.

t: Derived from this, as from its root, is one of the main elements of our spirituality. As Terence said: “I am a man, and nothing human is alien to me.” Even more so, due to the Incarnation, nothing genuinely human is alien to us. Therefore, we must work to extend the Incarnation to all reality, specifically evangelizing the culture, because: “No human activity is foreign to the Gospel.”
f: “Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto” He auton timoroumenos, v. 77 (Translation is ours). BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Homily at Mass in Independence Square in Ghana, May 10, 1980; OR (5/25/1980) Spanish Edition.

t: For us Christ is mysteriously identified with each man. Each and every man can be comprehended only in Jesus Christ: “It was necessary for mankind that God became man in order to demonstrate the dignity of human nature to mankind.” On judgment day He will say: For I was hungry and you gave me food... (Mt 25:35). The poor are Christ: “They represent the role of the Son of God.” The pilgrims are Christ: “Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ.” The children are Christ: Whoever receives one child such as this in my name receives me (Mt 18:5). In every man, “Jesus is hidden in the depths of his soul.” Saint Augustine said: “In Him we are Christs and Christ.”
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Opuscula Theologica, Compendium of Theology, 381. SAINT VINCENT DE PAUL, Letters, 11, 32; ES XI, 725. SAINT BENEDICT, Holy Rule, 53, 1. SAINT THÉRÈSE OF LISIEUX, Story of a Soul, 9. SAINT AUGUSTINE, Exposition on the Book of Psalms, 26, 2, 2. CCL 38,154 ff.

t: All Christians, truly, should live a life in imitation of the Incarnate God. This truth is even greater for us, the religious of the family of the Incarnate Word.
