f: LG 23. CD 6. LG 23. CD 11. Cf. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the Roman Curia, December 20, 1990; OR (12/28/1990) Spanish Edition.

t: We do not belong to the universal Church through the mediation of a particular Church. By faith and baptism we are directly incorporated into the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, although entrance and life in the universal Church are necessarily carried out in a specific Church. Therefore, no one is a stranger in the Church. He who belongs to a particular Church belongs to all the Churches – without disrupting canonical dependence. Belonging to the Communion of the Church is never exclusively specific, but rather – due to its nature – is in itself always universal: “He who is in Rome deems the Indians as her members.”
f: Cf. Gal 3:28. Cf. CIC, can. 107. SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, Homilies on the Gospel of John, 65, 1. MG 59,361.

t: Since the universal Church is “the universal Sacrament of salvation,” she is open – not closed – to missionary and ecumenical dynamics; she has been sent to announce and to testify, to enact and to extend the mystery of the communion that is constitutive of her; to gather all and everything in Christ. As an image of the Church, our small Religious Family must never be closed off, but rather must be open like the arms of Christ on the Cross that were “dislocated” for love’s sake.

The Holy Spirit, present and acting in every time and place, acts “in the heart of every person, through the ‘seeds of the Word,’ to be found in human initiatives – including religious ones – and in mankind’s efforts to attain truth, goodness, and God Himself.” Our mission, therefore, is to joyfully and respectfully discover these seeds, so that men may awaken to a stronger desire of truth and charity, since “the Holy Spirit in a manner known only to God offers to every man the possibility of being associated with this paschal mystery.”
f: RMs 28. Cf. AG 11. GS 22.

t: This presence of the Spirit “affects not only individuals, but also society and history, peoples, cultures, and religions… [it] is the Spirit who sows the ‘seeds of the Word’ present in various customs and cultures, preparing them for full maturity in Christ,” because the Holy Spirit already worked in the world before Christ was glorified.
f: RMs 28. Cf. SAINT LEO THE GREAT, Sermon 76.

t: This work of the Holy Spirit is an evangelical preparation and “can only be understood in relation to Christ, the Word who took flesh by the power of the Spirit.” Consequently, it “is not to be separated from His particular activity within the body of Christ, the Church.”
f: RMs 29. RMs 29.

t: Therefore, the teaching of Saint Ambrose, “all that is true, said by any person, comes from the Holy Spirit,” will forever be like a torch that illuminates our work. The saints affirmed and believed that, “Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians”; “that all good Christians understand that whatever truth, wherever truth may be found, belongs to his Master”; “no one can say anything true [of his own accord], but only moved by the Holy Spirit who is Spirit of Truth”; “there is no knowledge of the truth but only in the Holy Spirit who works in the intelligence and preserves it”; “all which is good and all which is true is from the Holy Spirit.”
f: Quoted by SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, De Veritate, 1, 8 s. c. SAINT JUSTIN, Apologia 2, 13. SAINT AUGUSTINE, On the Christian Doctrine II, 18.28. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Super I ad Cor 11, 12, 1. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Commentary on the Book of Sentences, 28, 3, 1. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Reportationes ineditae Leoninae, 3, 12, 3.

t: Thanks to the teaching of Christ, we know that there is a humanity that opposes faith and the gift of grace, called the “world” by the Lord Himself. Facing this “world” – to which Christ sends us as sheep in the midst of wolves (Mt 10:16) – Saint Paul admonishes: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2). However, this difference from the “world” does not mean that we are afraid of the “world,” or contemptuous of it, since if one is conscious of what the Lord wants, the duty of evangelization and the urgency of the mission become apparent. Therefore, a merely conservative attitude is not enough, but rather the diffusion and the announcement of the deposit of the faith are necessary, according to the command of Christ. Dialogue is the name we give to “this internal drive of charity which seeks expression in the external gift of charity.”

This dialogue, which is a spiritual communication, has its transcendent origin in God Himself: “In the Incarnation and in the Gospel, it is God’s Word that speaks to us.” Such a dialogue of God with men is born from divine love and is directed to all men without forcing anyone.
f: ES 70.

t: We must know and “adopt the way of life of ordinary people in all that is human and honorable”, without succumbing to the danger of weakening or diminishing the truth, since “an immoderate desire to make peace and sink differences at all costs (irenism and syncretism) is ultimately nothing more than skepticism about the power and content of the Word of God which we desire to preach.” “The effective apostle is the man who is completely faithful to Christ’s teaching. He alone can remain unaffected by the errors of the world around him, the man who lives his Christian life to the full.”
f: ES 87. ES 88. ES 88.

t: Preaching has particular importance. It must always be “skillfully expressed, carefully thought-out, and zealously imparted. May it be supported by the evidence of real virtue. Progress must be its aim. It must concern itself with imparting a sure faith.”
f: ES 91.

t: Although this dialogue embraces all men, four environments, or “circles,” are distinguished in which this spiritual communication is carried out, according to the different attitudes of people:

The first circle is of those with whom we share human values, in order to elevate them to the supernatural and Christian level. Most striking in this environment is the problem of atheism, founded on false theories and not consisting of “a liberating force, but a catastrophic one, for it seeks to quench the light of the living God.” Dialogue is especially difficult in these circumstances, and “we must come to a prudent decision about them, and answer them effectively,” and we must know that there are many situations that are occasions for such dialogue.
f: Cf. ES 97. ES 100. ES 104.

t: The second circle is of those who worship one God. Among them are Jews, Muslims and the faithful from African and Asian religions. Aware that the true religion is Christianity, and yearning for all those who seek God to recognize it as such, we must recognize the many spiritual and moral values that they possess, and the ideals that can be promoted and defended in common.

The third circle “comprises all those who take their name from Christ. In our dialogues, we should first stress what unites us, and then what divides us.” We must demonstrate how those elements of the Church that may look like obstacles for union are fruits of the will of Christ for the benefit, unity and freedom of all. In particular, we need to demonstrate that the Primacy of Peter perpetuated in the Pope is not an obstacle: “Take away the sovereign Pontiff, and the Catholic Church would no longer be Catholic.” Without the Roman Pontiff “we shall have as many schisms in the Churches as there are priests.”
f: ES 110. SAINT JEROME, Dialogue against the Luciferians: ML 23, 164.

t: Finally, the fourth circle of dialogue is carried out among the Catholic faithful, children of God’s house. This dialogue “does not mean that the virtue of obedience is no longer operative. The right to command and the duty to obey must be present.” Rather, it presumes obedience, because “the very exercise of authority becomes, in the context of this dialogue, an exercise of obedience, the obedient performance of a service, a ministry of truth and charity.”

In order to be men of authentic dialogue, we must learn how to practice the following virtues: “Clarity before all else; the dialogue demands that what is said should be intelligible. We can think of it as a kind of thought transfusion… affability… It would indeed be a disgrace if our dialogue were marked by arrogance, the use of harsh words or offensive bitterness. What gives it authority is the fact that it affirms the truth, shares with others the gifts of charity, is itself an example of virtue, avoids peremptory language, makes no demands… Confidence is also necessary, confidence not only in the power of one’s own words, but also in the good will of both parties to dialogue. Hence dialogue promotes intimacy and friendship on both sides… Prudence of a teacher who is most careful to make allowances for the psychological and moral circumstances of his listener… The person who speaks always takes pains to learn the sensitivities of his audience, and if reason demands it, he adapts himself and the manner of his presentation to the susceptibilities and the degree of intelligence of his listeners.” “Moreover, the very fact that he engages in a dialogue of this sort is proof of his consideration and esteem for others, his understanding and his kindness. He detests bigotry and prejudice, malicious and indiscriminate hostility, and empty, boastful speech… True dialogue respects a man’s freedom and dignity… we nevertheless try to help him and to prepare him for a fuller sharing of ideas and convictions… Our dialogue, therefore, presupposes that we have a state of mind… that is characteristic of the man who realizes the seriousness of the apostolic mission…”
f: Cf. Mt 7:6. ES 81. Cf. ES 79-80.

t: We must also embrace the holy cause of ecumenism. There is a promise-prophecy of the Lord: There shall be one flock, one shepherd (Jn 10:16), and a prayer of the Lord, That they may all be one (Jn 17:21). By prayer, penance, study, dialogue, and collaboration, we must strive to reach full communion in the unity of the Church “which Christ bestowed on his Church from the beginning. We believe that this unity subsists in the Catholic Church as something she can never lose, and we hope that it will continue to increase until the end of time,” in order “that in a renewed conversion to the Lord, the following may become possible to all: to recognize the permanency of the Primacy of Peter in his successors, the Bishops of Rome, and that the Petrine ministry may be carried out just as it is understood by the Lord, as universal apostolic service, present in all the Churches from the inside, and that, preserving the substance of the Petrine ministry as a divine institution, it can be expressed in diverse ways...” The ecumenical commitment is to “pray and to work for reconciliation and for ecclesiastic unity according to the mind and heart of our Savior Jesus Christ.”
f: UR 4. CONGREGATION FOR THE DOCTRINE OF THE FAITH, Letter to the Bishops of the Catholic Church on some Aspects of the Church understood as Communion, 18. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse during the Ecumenical Meeting at the Cathedral of Canterbury, May 29, 1982; OR (6/6/1982) Spanish Edition.

t: Another exciting reality of the immeasurable mystery of the Church of the Incarnate Word is its apostolicity: founded upon the Apostles and perpetuated by apostolic succession.

Besides being based on faith, baptism and Eucharist, the communion among the particular Churches in the universal Church is based on the Episcopacy. Church unity is also rooted in the unity of the Episcopacy: in order that the Church “might be one and undivided, Christ put Peter at the head of the other apostles, and in him He set up a lasting and visible source and foundation of the unity of both faith and communion.”
f: LG 18.

t: “The individual bishops are the visible source and foundation of unity in their own particular Churches, which are established after the model of the universal Church.” For this to exist, the Church’s supreme authority, the College of Bishops “together with their head, the Supreme Pontiff, and never apart from him” must be present in the particular Church as a proper component. The Primacy of the Bishop of Rome and the College of Bishops are proper elements of the universal Church; they are not derived from the particular Churches, but are internal to each particular Church. “In the Pope we see Jesus Christ, we follow Jesus Christ, we love Jesus Christ. And in the Bishops? In the Bishops we see, we continue, we venerate and we love the successors of the Apostles.” Each one of the members of our Religious Family “wants to belong entirely to the Pope, the Bishops and the Church: worthless things, servants and obedient children of the Church, the Bishops and the Pope, in humility, with fidelity, with love without limits.”
f: LG 23. LG 22; cf. LG 19. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of July 15, 1936. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of July 15, 1936.

t: Therefore, we must have eyes of faith to always recognize those whom the Holy Spirit has made… overseers, to care for the church of the Lord (Acts 20:28). We must make the advice of Saint Ignatius of Antioch our own: “Neither do anything without the bishop and presbyters,” and even less so, something against them.
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF ANTIOCH, To the Magnesians, 7, 1.

t: The Saint Louis Orione also advised: “The Bishop’s state is the most perfect of all, even more than the religious state; to him the fullness of the priesthood; to him more than to any other is given the spirit of Faith, Wisdom and Fortitude... The Bishop doesn’t have enemies; to him all are but children. The smallest ones, the most humble and the most disgraced ones are dearer to him. He prays for everyone. He has words of everlasting life for everyone. For everyone he goes to the altar and offers the blood of the Immaculate Lamb that takes away the sins of the world… The Bishop is the Good Shepherd who watches over, who tends the sheep, who evangelizes, who knows how to suffer in silence, who knows how to give his life up for his sheep.” Church history offers us numerous examples of glorious figures of the Episcopate: bishops who evangelized and founded nations, defended and organized peoples, keeping the deposit of faith entrusted to them amid the cruelest of persecutions, and who reinforced the Church’s sound doctrine in the face of a multitude of errors and confusions. For this reason, “Let us love the Bishops!”
f: SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of February 6, 1935. Cf. 1 Tm 6:20. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of Pentecost, 1912.

t: Not only is communion with the Bishop necessary, but we must also strive for communion with other priests “under the authority of the bishop,” who is God’s steward (Ti 1:7). This communion forms a single presbytery based on the common participation of Christ’s Priesthood: “In virtue of their sacred ordination and of their common mission, all priests are united together by bonds of intimate brotherhood, which manifests itself in a spontaneously and gladly-given mutual help, whether spiritual or temporal, whether pastoral or personal.”
f: AG 20. LG 28.

t: Unity with other priests, both diocesan and religious, is primarily obtained in the “intimate sacramental brotherhood”; and from this we wish to establish close collaboration in pastoral work, since “even though they have diverse occupations, they exercise a single priestly ministry in the service of men.” For this reason, “Between the secular clergy and the religious communities, a renewed brotherhood and a bond of cooperation must be encouraged; having in great esteem certain mutual help and certain contacts... that help mutual trust, apostolic unanimity and fraternal concord in such a great way…”
f: PO 8. PO 8. SACRED CONGREGATION FOR RELIGIOUS AND FOR SECULAR INSTITUTES AND SACRED CONGREGATION FOR BISHOPS, Directives for the Mutual Relations between Bishops and Religious, 37.

t: This unity and cooperation which we want to establish with other members of the presbytery to whatever degree possible, leads us to preach Jesus Christ without any division, by word and example of life, and allows us to be aware that we are ministers of a new covenant, not in a written code but in the Spirit (2 Cor 3:6), and therefore it leads us to bear one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2) in this serious ministry.
f: Cf. 1 Cor 1:10.

t: Paraphrasing the Apostle, we want to do good always, to everyone, whenever possible, especially to our brothers in the priesthood bestowed by the laying on of hands.
f: Cf. Gal 6:10. Cf. 1 Tm 4:14.

t: God’s marvelous gift of consecrated life – priests, deacons, religious, missionaries and consecrated lay people – “affects the whole Church in her fundamental mark of apostolicity.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Regina Coeli Message, April 23, 1989; OR (4/23/1989) Spanish Edition.

t: The foundation of this essentially supernatural work resides in God’s very choice and call: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit (Jn 15:16); when choosing the Twelve, the Lord went up the mountain and summoned those whom he wanted, and they came to him (Mk 3:13). Vocations are God’s property: I pray for them. I do not pray for the world but for the ones you have given me, because they are yours, and everything of mine is yours and everything of yours is mine (Jn 17:9-10).

We would want God to give us the gift of being able to discover and to guide so many vocations that we would fill all the good seminaries and novitiates in the entire world, according to the Pope’s recommendation: “God calls who he wants, by his free initiative of love. But he wants to call through us... There shouldn’t be any fear in directly proposing the Lord’s call to a young person.” Therefore, vocational ministry should be active, constant, full of energy and vitality, undertaken and spurred forward by the charity of Christ, and definitely opposed to a mentality of “ordinary administration or bureaucratic slowness,” which carelessly hopes that vocations knock upon its door. God “sows seeds of vocation to full hands by grace.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Message to the XX World Day of Prayer for Vocations, April 24, 1983; OR (4/17/1983) Spanish Edition. Cf. 2 Cor 5:14. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to Priests and Religious at the Cathedral of Siena, April 14, 1980; OR (4/21/1980) Spanish Edition. Cf. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Message to the XXIX World Day of Prayer for Vocations, May 10, 1992; OR (12/20/1991) Spanish Edition.

t: The vitality of a community, and of the Church herself, can be measured by the vocations that God raises in it. Inseparably united with promoting vocations is the proper formation of those chosen; hence, we must recognize the importance “of making intense efforts to encourage vocations and to offer the best possible priestly formation in seminaries. An abundance of vocations and an effective formation of seminarians are two tests of the Church’s vitality.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Homily during the Mass celebrated at the Major Regional Seminary in Seoul, May 3, 1984; OR (5/13/1984) Spanish Edition.

t: The task of discovering and guiding vocations is achieved not only through an enthusiastic pastoral action, but essentially through prayer: Pray, therefore, the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Mt 9:38); I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Cor 3:6). One’s example and life testimony go together with prayer: “Where there is faith, prayer, charity, apostolate, Christian life, there the gifts of God multiply,” because “the religious and priests who live their vocation calmly day by day, faithful to their commitments, humble and hidden builders of the Kingdom of God from whose words, behavior, and life irradiates the luminous joy of the choice that they made... are in fact... those that by their example will stimulate many to welcome in their hearts the charism of vocation.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Message to the XX World Day of Prayer for Vocations, April 4, 1983; OR (4/17/1983) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the National Council and Regional Secretaries for the Work of Vocations, February 16, 1980; OR (3/23/1980) Spanish Edition.

t: Hence all anti-testimony, all incoherence between expressing values or ideals and living them, all looking out for oneself and not for the Kingdom of God and its justice, all falsification of the word of God, “are often strong obstacles for those who feel the call of Christ: Come and follow me.”
f: Cf. Mt 6:33. Cf. 2 Cor 4:2. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Discourse to the Bishops of the United States, February 22, 1980; OR (4/30/1989) Spanish Edition.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: Ecclesial communion has its root and its center in the Holy Eucharist. The Eucharist is the source and creative force of communion among the Church’s members because it unites each one with the same Christ: “Really sharing in the body of the Lord in the breaking of the Eucharistic bread, we are taken up into communion with Him and with one another. Because the bread is one, we, though many, are one body, all of us who partake of the one bread (1 Cor 10:17).” “The common spiritual good of the whole Church is contained substantially in the sacrament of the Eucharist itself,” “which is Christ.”
f: LG 7. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST III, 65, 3, 1. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST III, 79, 1; Cf. PO 5.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: The Church is the Body of Christ. This means that in the Eucharist, in which the Lord gives His Body and transforms us into one Body, the Church permanently expresses herself in her most essential form: present everywhere at the same time, one like Christ.
f: Cf. LG 3; 11.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: In the Eucharist all the faithful find themselves “in their own Church”, since in all valid Eucharistic celebrations, the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church becomes present. The faithful are indeed “in their own Church” even though, from a canonical point of view, they may or may not belong to the particular diocese, parish or community where the celebration is being carried out.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: Besides being based on faith, Baptism and Episcopacy, – the communion of specific Churches in the universal Church is fundamentally based upon the Eucharist. Since in the Eucharist we receive the Lord and His gift of salvation, the Eucharistic Sacrifice never belongs to a particular community. Each community is thereby manifested – beyond its visible particularity – as an image and true presence of the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church.
f: Cf. LG 26.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: The unity and indivisibility of the Eucharistic Body of the Lord implies the unity and indivisibility of the mystical Body of the Lord. Each Eucharist makes us surrender to the Lord, and integrates us into His one and undivided Body. That is why the Petrine ministry – the foundation of unity between the Episcopate and the universal Church – corresponds deeply with the Church’s Eucharistic dimension.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: Since Eucharist and Episcopate are realities essentially linked by the institution of Christ, the unity of the Eucharist and the unity of the Episcopacy “with Peter and under Peter” are not independent roots of the Church’s unity. The liturgy manifests this reality, since all Eucharistic celebrations are carried out in union with one’s own Bishop, the Pope, the universal Episcopate, the clergy and all the members of the People of God. All valid celebrations of the Eucharist either express this universal communion with Peter and with the whole Church, or at least claim it objectively, as in the case of the Churches separated from Rome.
f: Cf. LG 26. AG 38. AG 38. Cf. RM, Eucharistic Prayer III.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: Therefore, in the Eucharist, the perpetuation of the sacrifice of the Cross, we will always find the deepest foundation of our unity as a Religious Family. The Eucharist must be one of our great loves, since it is the undeniable sign of God’s immeasurable love for men, it is the sign of a God who wants to remain among men and who gives Himself up to man totally: “In the Sacrament, the logic of the Incarnation reaches its extreme consequences.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, July 19, 1981; OR (7/26/1981) Spanish Edition.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: The primary role of a priest is sacrifice: “A holy and unblemished sacrifice,” “acceptable... which brings salvation to the whole world” that “opens a way” toward the Father for us, “unique,” “of perfect reconciliation,” “ours,” “living.” Therefore, in the Eucharistic Liturgy Christ speaks, above all, with the strength of His Sacrifice. His speech is very concise but ardent. We must know how to listen to it attentively.
f: RM, Eucharistic Prayer I. RM, Eucharistic Prayer IV. RM, Eucharistic Prayer V. (Translation taken from the Roman Missal Spanish Edition). RM, Eucharistic Prayer for Reconciliation I. (Translation taken from the Roman Missal Spanish Edition). RM, Eucharistic Prayer for Reconciliation II. RM, Eucharistic Prayer for Masses with Children II. (Translation taken from the Roman Missal Spanish Edition). RM, Eucharistic Prayer III.

h: h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist
t: Every month a Holy Mass must be offered for the deceased members of the Institute, another one for the intentions of the General Superior, and a third one requesting the grace of final perseverance for all the members of our Institutes.

The Virgin Mary should be another one of our great loves because of her union with Christ and with the Church. Since She gave birth to the Head, She gave birth to us members as well. She was given to us as Mother when She was standing at the foot of the Cross: Behold, your son (Jn 19:26).

The Holy Virgin Mary is model of ecclesial communion “in the order of faith, charity, and perfect union with Christ”; She “is the image and beginning of the Church… She shines forth on earth, as a sign of sure hope and solace to the people of God during its sojourn on earth.”
f: LG 63. LG 68.

t: She is in the midst of the Apostles, at the very heart of the newborn Church: All these with one accord devoted themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers (Acts 1:14), and She is in the heart of the Church for all ages.

Indeed, “The Church was congregated in the upper part (of the cenacle) with Mary, who was the Mother of Jesus, and with his brethren. We cannot therefore speak of the Church unless Mary, the Mother of the Lord, is present there, with the Lord’s brethren.” The Marian dimension is as essential to the one Church of Christ as are the Eucharistic and Petrine dimensions.
f: SAINT CHROMATIUS OF AQUILEIA, Sermons, 30,1.

t: We must be apostles of Mary giving ourselves up to Her in a filial slavery of love, and doing everything “through Mary, with Mary, in Mary and for Mary.”
f: SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNION DE MONFORT, TD 257.

t: Always keep a memory of the Blessed Virgin in mind during eutrapelia and during cultural activities, because, after Jesus Christ, no one has done as much for the evangelization of culture as She did.

Our third great love must always be the “white figure” of the Pope. “Wherever Peter is, the Church is there,” and “Peter has spoken thus through Leo” (at the moment of the writing of this Directory, through Blessed John Paul II). After Simon gives testimony of Christ, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mt 16:16), Christ gives testimony of Simon: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Mt 16:18).
f: SAINT AMBROSE, Writings about the Psalms, 40, 30. Acclamation of the Conciliar Fathers of Calcedonia (451), concluding the reading of Saint Leo the Great’s Tomus ad Flavianum.

t: The idea of a Body of Churches demands the existence of a Head of these Churches. It is the Church of Rome, which “presides over the universal communion of love.” Peter’s Successor “is the perpetual and visible source and foundation” of the unity of the universal Church and of the unity of the Episcopate. Hence the Petrine ministry is not a service that reaches to the particular Churches “from outside,” but one “already belonging to the essence of each particular Church from inside.” The ministry of Primacy implies an Episcopal power – both as universal Bishop and as Bishop of the Diocese of Rome – and not merely an episcopal dignity, so that everything a Bishop can do in his parishes, the Pope can do in all of the local Churches. This ministry is a supreme power: no one possesses equal or greater power; it is a full power, not merely a principal part; it is immediate – the Pope can exercise this power over the Bishops and the faithful; it is universal, over all without excluding anyone; it is ordinary, derived directly from Jesus Christ; and “he can always exercise it unhindered.”
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF ANTIOCH, To the Romans, prologue. MG 5,685. LG 23. Cf. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the Bishops of the United States at the Minor Seminary of Our Lady of Los Angeles, September 16, 1987; OR (10/18/1987) Spanish Edition. LG 22.

t: The primordial task of the Roman Pontiff for the whole Church is to promote unity that is not contrary to promoting the diversification needed for proper communion.

We make the teaching of Saint Ignatius of Loyola our own: “If we wish to proceed securely in all things, we must hold fast to the following principle: What seems to me white, I will believe black if the hierarchical Church so defines.” Therefore, being certain that this is the will of Jesus Christ, “Let us remain deaf when someone speaks to us disregarding the Pope, or not explicitly in favor of the Pope, and when one is not in favor of the Church’s wholesome and precise doctrine; these are not fruits of the Heavenly Father, but wicked sprouts of heresies that produce murderous fruit.” Let us always remember “that the Pope should be loved in the cross; and whoever does not love him in the cross, does not seriously love him. To be in everything with the Pope means to be in everything with God; to love Jesus Christ and to love the Pope is the same love,” since “to love the Pope, to love the Church, is to love Jesus Christ.”
f: SAINT IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA, Spiritual Exercises 365. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of Pentecost of 1912. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letters, 1. cit. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Letter of July 1, 1936.

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: Jesus Christ came for the first time in humility and poverty. However, He will come a second time in power, greatness, dignity and majesty to demand an account and to judge.

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: The major signs of His second coming are three:

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: 1. the Gospel will be preached to the whole world;

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: 2. there will be a universal apostasy;
f: Cf. 2 Thes 2:3.

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: 3. the Antichrist will make His appearance.
f: Cf. 2 Thes 2:3-10.

h: Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs
t: There will come a time when men will go astray from the truth and will delight in iniquity, a time in which the majority will not have true faith in Jesus Christ. The certainty that this universal apostasy will happen one day must prevent us from joining the triumphant march of any movement or ideology that is set apart from Christ, although it may seem that the whole world is following it. We must always follow Christ, and even though the enemies seem to be in the majority, we must say: “We are surrounded everywhere, don’t let them escape.” “All creatures appear small to the soul that contemplates God.”
f: Cf. 2 Thes 2:12. SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, C 35; ML 66,200.

h: b. The Final and Universal Resurrection
t: At the end of time the resurrection of the body will take place. All men and women will resurrect by the power of God. We believe in the resurrection, and we are not afraid of persecutors who stalk the Church: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Mt 10:28).

h: b. The Final and Universal Resurrection
t: The time of this resurrection is hidden and “all those who had been misled to calculate the aforesaid time have so far proved to be untruthful.”
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST, Supplementum, 77, 2; cf. SAINT AUGUSTINE, The City of God, 18, 53.

h: b. The Final and Universal Resurrection
t: The soul will take up its own entire body, and will enjoy the gifts of impassibility, subtlety, agility and clarity – or beauty.

h: b. The Final and Universal Resurrection
t: Our trust and happiness from knowing that death has already been conquered should be so great! It has been conquered by the Incarnation of the Word and His redeeming Sacrifice. The Incarnation of the Word is the condition and guarantee for the whole universe: “The lack of life and salvation from despair for all men, the condition sine qua non and the guarantee for the whole universe are locked in the words, The Word was made flesh and the faith in these words.” “The Incarnation of the Son of God is the foundation, the source and the pattern of a new supernatural order of existence for all men; in fact, from this mystery they obtain the grace that sanctifies and saves them, and it is a foundation of Christian anthropology that is also projected in the natural sphere of thought and life, with its exaltation of man as person, placed in the center of society and, you can say, of the whole world.”
f: BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Speech to the Participants of the Colloquy about the “Common Christian Roots of the European Peoples”, November 5, 1981; OR (11/15/1981) Spanish Edition. BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Catechesis of the Pope in a General Audience, March 26, 1988; OR (3/27/1988) Spanish Edition.

h: c. The Parousia and the Final Judgment
t: Then, the Parousia of the Lord will happen: For the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (Jn 5:28). And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (Lk 21:27); the sign of the Son of man [the sign of the Cross] in heaven will appear (Mt 24:30). At that moment the universal judgment will take place. Christ, together with His chosen ones – you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Mt 19:28) – will separate the sheep from the goats; some will be put to His right, and others to His left; and He will say, Come, O blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom… (Mt 25:34), and depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire (Mt 25:41). And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Mt 25:46).

h: c. The Parousia and the Final Judgment
t: We must increasingly convince ourselves that we do not work for ephemeral or fleeting things, but “for the most divine work among the divine ones,” which is the eternal salvation of souls and the glorious resurrection of bodies. Aware that we are working for eternal life, we must say with Blessed Louis Orione, “Place me, Lord, on the mouth of hell, so that I, by your mercy, may close it.”
f: PSEUDO-DIONYSIOS, quoted by SAINT ALPHONSUS LIGUORI, Selva, 9, 1. SAINT LOUIS ORIONE, Points from February, 1939.

t: Then, the renewal of the entire material universe will take place. There will be a new heaven and a new earth (Is 65:17; Rev 21:1), so that the man resurrected in glory will be able to clearly see divinity with His senses, and somehow, he will see it in the corporeal world. The following words will be entirely true: “The heaven, and earth, and all that is therein, behold, on every side; they say that I should love You.”
f: SAINT AUGUSTINE, Confessions, 10, 4,6.

t: The quantity and mode of this renewal “is known to Him alone Who will bring it about.” There God…[will] be everything to everyone (1 Cor 15:28); matter will reach maximum dignity, manifesting the Divine Spirit, because it will be a perfect mirror of God.
f: SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST, Supplementum, 91, 3.

t: We only need to pray, work and wait, knowing that this world is passing away (1 Cor 7:31).
We finish this part of our fundamental code by summarizing what we want to be our spirituality:

Not Jesus or Mary; not Mary or Jesus. Neither Jesus without Mary; nor Mary without Jesus. Neither only Jesus, but also Mary; not only Mary, but also Jesus. Always Jesus and Mary; always Mary and Jesus.
To Mary through Jesus: Behold, your mother! (Jn 19:27).
To Jesus through Mary: Do whatever he tells you (Jn 2:5). First Jesus, the God man; then Mary, the Mother of God. He, the Head; She, the Neck; we, the Body.
Everything through Jesus and through Mary; with Jesus and with Mary; in Jesus and in Mary; for Jesus and for Mary.
In short, simply: Jesus and Mary; Mary and Jesus.
And through Christ, to the Father, in the Holy Spirit.

“Every liturgical celebration, because it is an action of Christ the High Priest and of His Body, the Church, is a sacred action surpassing all others; no other action of the Church can equal its efficacy by the same title and to the same degree.” This action is so, regarding the Holy Eucharist in which “the common spiritual good of the whole Church is substantially contained…  that is Christ Himself.”
f: SC 7. STh III,65,3,ad 3: “bonum commune spirituale totius Ecclesiae continetur substantialiter” STh III,79,1: “primo… et principaliter, ex eo quod in hoc sacramentum continetur, quod est Christus”. Cf. PO 5; Catech 1088.

t: At the liturgy, it is Christ Himself who continues to exercise His eternal Priesthood through those whom, in different ways, He has extended His own priesthood through Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders. “The liturgy is considered an exercise of the priestly office of Jesus Christ.”  “Through the liturgy Christ, our redeemer and high priest continues the work of our redemption in, with, and through his Church.”
f: SC 7. Cf. Pius XII, Mediator Dei, 2. 3. 12.13. Catech 1069.

h: Article 3: A Glorified God and Sanctified Men
t: In “this great work … God is perfectly glorified and men are sanctified.”   Thus “in the Liturgy, the whole public worship is performed by the Mystical Body of Jesus Christ, that is, by the Head and his members”; or, in other words, “the Church is His beloved Bride who calls to her Lord and through Him offers worship to the Eternal Father.”
f: SC 7. SC 7.

t: The Saving Work Christ entrusted to His Apostles is performed at the Liturgy “by means of sacrifice and sacraments, around which the liturgical life revolves.” It is particularly performed at the Eucharistic Sacrament – Sacrifice. The Eucharist is like “the consummation of the spiritual life and the pinnacle of all the other Sacraments.”
f: SC 6. STh .III,73,3: “Eucharistia vero est quasi consummatio spiritualis vitae, et omnium  sacramentorum finis” ; cf. III,65,3: “For all the other sacraments seem to be ordained to this one as to their end. For it is manifest that the sacrament of order is ordained to the consecration of the Eucharist: and the sacrament of Baptism to the reception of the Eucharist: while a man is perfected by Confirmation, so as not to fear to abstain from this sacrament. By Penance and Extreme Unction man is prepared to receive the Body of Christ worthily. And Matrimony at least in its signification, touches this sacrament; in so far as it signifies the union of Christ with the Church, of which union the Eucharist is a figure: hence the Apostle says (Eph. 5:32): "This is a great sacrament: but I speak in Christ and in the Church… For nearly all the sacraments terminate in the Eucharist, as Dionysius says - Eccl. Hier. Ii i - : thus those who have been ordained receive Holy Communion, as also do those who have been baptized, if they be adults." - PC 5; Catech 1324-1327.

t: The entire Universal Church offers the Sacrifice of the Mass  as She is also offered.  Through the Liturgy the Church manifests who She is. The Liturgy then, is the “Church’s Epiphany, since the Liturgy is the Church at prayer.”  “In the Liturgy, the Mystery of the Church is distinctively proclaimed, experienced and lived.”
f: Pius XII, Mystico Corporis Christi, 47. “…following in the footsteps of her Founder, the Church teaches, governs, and offers the divine Sacrifice”; Saint Robert Belarmino, De Missa, 1, 27: “The Sacrifice is offered principally in persona Christi; therefore the oblation that follows the consecration testifies that the whole Church accepts the oblation already accomplished by Christ and offers it with him”. Pius XII, Mystico Corporis Christi, 82: “He offers to the heavenly Father not only Himself as Head of the Church, but in Himself His mystical members also, since He holds them all, even those who are weak and ailing, in His most loving Heart”; St. Augustine, The City of God, 10, 6: “so we, being many, are one body in Christ… And this also is the sacrifice which the Church continually celebrates in the sacrament of the altar, known to the faithful, in which she teaches that she herself is offered in the offering she makes to God”. Cf. John Paul II, Vicesimus Quintus Annus, 9. John Paul II, Vicesimus Quintus Annus, 9.

t: The liturgy is also the action of Christ and of the Church:
- of Christ, because He is the unique and true High Priest (Heb 8:1);

- of the Church, because “in this great work… God is perfectly glorified and men are sanctified. The Church is His beloved Bride who calls to her Lord. Through Him, She offers worship to the Eternal Father.”
f: SC 7.

t: Since the liturgy is Christ and the Church’s action, it is therefore also the action of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary. “Mary shares a great intimacy with both Christ and the Church. Because of this intimacy, She can not be separated from Them. She is also united to each, first in what constitutes the very essence of the Liturgy itself, since the Liturgy is the sacramental celebration of Salvation for the glory of God and, second, in the sanctification of man. Mary is present at the memorial, the liturgical action, in the same way that she was with Christ during His Saving Work.
f: John Paul II, Alocution of 05/19/84: Maria’s presence in the liturgy celebration, OR (05/19/84)1.

t: “Since the Pope has the Peter’s ministry in the Church, he is associated with every celebration of the Eucharist, wherein he is named as the sign and servant of the unity of the universal Church. The bishop of the diocese or jurisdiction is always responsible for the Eucharist, even when another priest presides. The bishop’s name is mentioned to signify his presidency over the particular Church, in the midst of his presbyterium and with the assistance of deacons. The community intercedes also for all ministers who, for it and with it, offer the Eucharistic sacrifice.”undefined
f: Catech 1369.

t: The Purpose of this Directory

This Directory’s objective is not to present a liturgical theology, or to replace any approved instruction. Rather, its purpose is to mark a ‘style’ of worthy, sober, solemn, with a liturgical rhythm, festive, faithful and creative sacred celebrations. Our aim is not for banal or superficially noisy, nor secularized or unsacred, nor vulgar or childish, nor exaggerated or rigid celebrations. In addition, this Directory aspires to declare the religious and the educational importance of the Sacred Liturgy for our Religious Family  .
f: Cf. Isidro Gomá y Tomás, El valor educativo de la Liturgia Católica (Barcelona 1945).

t: An essential part of our Charisma is our commitment to highlight a style on our liturgical celebrations in which the Word is incarnated, sacramentally-incarnated. Celebrations which continually emphasize the prevailing presence and action of the Principal Priest,   celebrations in which it is perceived that the essential attitude of the secondary priest is an attitude of prayer, typical of someone who knows he is a mere instrument, imperfect and subordinated to the primary cause and its purposes, and celebrations in which all the visible elements help those who are in the presence of the Mystery to realize the splendorous presence of what is Invisible.
f: “Nothing of what we do in the Liturgy can appear more important than what in an unseen but real manner Christ accomplishes by the power of his Spirit” - John Paul II, Vicesimus Quintus Annus, 9.

t: Our liturgical celebrations must be an example: “by the rites, by the spiritual and pastoral tone, and by the due fidelity to the prescriptions and texts of liturgical books, as well as to norms issued by the Holy See and the Episcopal Conferences.”
f: Congregation for Catholic Education, Instruction on the liturgical formation, 16.

t: The Participation

The Church vehemently “wishes to guide all the faithful to take part totally, consciously, and actively (and ‘fruitfully’ ) in the liturgical celebrations.”  Total Participation means it should be manifested in the exterior postures: gestures, prayers, and songs, as well as in the interior: a firm will to be united with Christ and His Mystical Body. Conscious participation means to be fully aware of what one is doing and why, not merely ‘to be present’ in a negligent absentminded way. Active participation means everybody should take part: “They must not attend this mystery of faith… like strangers or silent spectators.”  It must be cultivated in the acclamations, responses, Psalms, antiphons, gestures, and bodily positions.  Fruitful participation is the perfect participation. It is the ‘completion’ of the liturgical participation. The Sacramental Communion constitutes the maximum and most effective way of participating.
f: SC 11. SC 14. SC 48. Cf. SC 30.

t: Liturgical renewal “cannot be restricted to the ceremonies, rites, texts, etc. Moreover, active participation does not consist solely of external activity, but, above all, of an internal and spiritual joining in the living and sacred participation of the celebration of the Paschal Mystery of Jesus Christ. ”
f: Cf. SC 11. Extraordinary Synod for Bishops of 1985, Final Relation, II, B, b, 1.

t: Our Liturgies must be lively and fully experienced by the community: lively, that is to say, vivacious, powerful, effective and radiant, and fully experienced by the community, full of life; an immediate experience of the Eucharistic Jesus. “The liturgy must foment the sense of the sacred and make it radiant. It must be filled with a spirit of reverence and God’s glorification.”
f: Extraordinary Synod for Bishops of 1985, Final Relation, II, B, b, 1.

h: Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation
t: The essential differences, not related to degree, that occur in the liturgical actions reside in the different sacramental characters. In fact, the Sacraments of the New Law are ordered for two aims: to be a remedy against sins and to perfect the soul regarding God’s worship according to the Christian Religion’s rites. However, as the Sacraments destine men to the spiritual service of God’s worship, they seal the Faithful with a certain spiritual character.

h: Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation
t: The sacramental character perfects the man in such a way that it makes him “divine and transmitter of the divine.”  Saint Thomas adds: “Since divine worship consists of receiving the divine mysteries or transmitting them to another one, a certain power is necessary for each one of these services: active, to transmit; passive, to receive. The character has, of its own, a spiritual power related to the divine rites.”
f: Pseudo Dionisio, Eccl. Hier., ch 2. STh III,63,2.

h: Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation
t: The sacramental character “is primarily a seal that characterizes something as ordered to a certain aim.” The Christian faithful are destined for two things: “first and principally for the enjoyment of glory… secondly, each of the faithful is deputed to receive or to bestow what is about God’s worship: and this, properly speaking, is the purpose of the sacramental character. Now the whole rite of the Christian religion is derived from Christ's priesthood. Consequently, it is clear that the sacramental character is Christ’s character, to whose priesthood the faithful are configured according the sacramental characters; these are  none other than certain participations of Christ's Priesthood, flowing from Christ Himself.”
f: STh III,63,3.

h: Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation
t: The sacrament ordered to provide ministers for the divine worship is Holy Orders. “By this sacrament, some men are destined to provide others with the rest of the Sacraments.”  The sacrament ordered to provide subjects for divine worship is Baptism. “Through the virtue of this sacrament, man is enabled to receive the rest of the Church’s sacraments …. In a certain way, it is the same for Confirmation….”
f: STh III,63,6. STh III,63,6.

h: Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation
t: For this reason it is established in our Constitutions: “This participation in Christ’s Priesthood is the essence of the sacramental character that begins with Baptism, is perfected with Confirmation and achieves its plenitude in Holy Orders.”
Priesthood and Participation

“The baptismal character empowers us to receive the other sacraments. It empowers the lay faithful to act as their own proper ministers in the sacrament of Marriage which is the maximal realization of the common priesthood. How we should nurture our soul with the reality of our Baptism! How we should teach this reality to the Christian lay faithful!”

“The baptismal character enables all the baptized to specially offer the Eucharistic Sacrifice. This grandiose and amazing prerogative should be insistently taught especially to all the members of our Institutes who are not ministerial priests. The baptized participate, though without carrying out the liturgical rite themselves, in the oblation to the Father of the Altar’s Victim in two ways: 1st they offer the Sacrifice by means of the visible priest, since he offers on behalf of all the members when acting in Persona Christi (the Person of Christ) as Head and Shepherd; 2nd they also offer the Sacrifice together with the visible priest when they unite to this Sacrifice their vows of praise, supplication, and atonement.”

First, then, by means of the visible priest, at each Mass that is celebrated, in the offering of the Church, all its members, all the baptized ones, including the shepherds, offer the Sacrifice through the hands of the main priest. This priest, acting in persona Christi, the Head,  offers the Sacrifice in the name of all the Christian faithful, as it is read in the anaphora: “Remember, Lord, your people...;  accept this offering from your whole family”;  and still: “we offer you this sacrifice of praise for ourselves .…”  These words clearly show that, by means of the visible priest, all the baptized offer the Sacrifice, men,  women, children and the elderly, seculars and consecrated men and women.
f: “In persona Christi capitis”- LG 10.28; SC 33; CD 11; PO 2.6;  cf. STh III,22,4. Roman Missal, Roman Canon, 45 Roman Missal, Roman Canon, 47 Roman Missal, Roman Canon, 52

t: Because of their baptismal character, it is presumed that all the faithful give consent in all the Sacrifices the Church offers. They virtually want these Sacrifices to be offered in their name also, through the visible priest. In addition, they consent to be recipients, as it is proper to them, of the fruits of each Mass that is celebrated anywhere in the world and at every hour. For this reason Pope Innocent III taught: “Not only the priests offer [the Sacrifice], but the faithful also, since what is particularly carried out through the ministry of the priests is also universally carried out through the faithful’s baptismal vows.”  For this reason the ministerial priest was chosen publicly to offer the Sacrifice in the name of all.
f: De sacro Altaris Mysterio, 2, 6

t: Second, along with that offering of the visible priest, the faithful unite their act of praises and vows so that in the same oblation of the Victim and the external rite of the visible priest, they are  truly presented and offered to God the Father “as living, holy and pleasing hosts to God.” (Rom 12:1)

“The character of Confirmation, through the comforting or corroborative grace, enables us to confess our faith in Christ with courage and fortitude and to defend it against its opponents with greater ease and naturalness.”

“The character of Holy Orders configures the ministerial priest with Christ-the-Head, giving him power over the physical and mystical Body of Christ. It allows him to act ‘in persona Christi.’   His main role is in the immolation and oblation of the Sacrifice of the Mass. It is also his office to bless, preside, preach, baptize, to hear confessions, etc. The ministerial priest-members of our Institute should return again and again to that ineffable reality which operated in them to change ontologically through their configuration to Christ-the-Head. No ‘secular spirituality’ should shrink their ‘priestly spirituality’.”
f: Saint Thomas Aquinas, In IV Sententiarum d. 8, 22, 5, 2.3.4; STh III,22,2,ad 4; 82,2,2; 82,3; 82,7,ad 3; Super Ev Matthaei 26, 1; Super Ev. Johannis 6, 6; Super I2 ad Cor. 2 2. {133}

t: Without a doubt, the liturgical celebrations will generally be what the celebrant “wants” and “is”. He must be vigilant that every detail in the celebration is what it should be. He is to celebrate with unction but without affectation, with solemnity but without pomposity, with fidelity, without excepting a sane creativity, with devotion but without false piety, with the conscience that the principal operator is Jesus Christ, the principal Priest, showing Christ transparently, not an opaque membrane obstructing the people’s vision to Christ.

As blessed Pope John XXIII remarked, Saint John Maria Vianney, the holy Priest of Ars, is an example of this required spirit. Saint John would say, “The reason for the relaxation in many priests’ moral lives is because they do not offer the Sacrifice with attention and piety.”
f: John XXIII, Sacerdotii Nostri Primordia, 58.

t: “He did everything there was to be done to stir up the reverence and love of the faithful for Christ hidden in the Sacrament of the Eucharist and to bring them to be nurtured by Holy Communion. The example of his devotion was ever before them. To be convinced of this, a witness says, it was enough to see him celebrating the Holy Mass or simply doing genuflection when passing in front of the tabernacle.”
f: John XXIII, Sacerdotii Nostri Primordia, 47.

t: Words and Gestures

The visible elements have great importance in the liturgy. The pronunciation of the words should be observed with a certain rhythm, neither fast nor slow, neither blaring nor dim in voice, said with expression, without theatricality, with sincerity, clarity, precision, originality, unction. It should evoke in those participating that which God says or hears. We must keep in mind through the pronunciation of the words God becomes present and is made manifest.
f: Cf. SC 7.

t: The liturgical gestures must be full, not unnecessarily repeated, ordered, human, not like coming from automatons. Gestures are not to be omitted. The quality of our celebrations must be meticulously scrutinized even to the smallest details; neglected, loose, unprepared, hurried, verbose-wordy, anodyne and dull celebrations debilitate the faith of those participating.

The necessity of remote and proximate preparation for the Holy Mass will never be over-emphasized. In fact, our day should be divided in two: one is for preparation, the other for thanksgiving. There is nothing more important in our Christian life than the Mass. When we celebrate or participate in It, the day is already won. For this reason, in some sacristies, we find that wise warning: “Celebrate this Mass as it would be the first one, the last one, and the only one.”
f: Saint Alphonsus de Liguori, Misa y oficio atropellados, Obras ascéticas 2 (Madrid 1972) 399-442.

h: Article 2: Three Examples of Full Gesture
t: The first of these full gestures is Concelebration: “Through Concelebration the Sacrifice and the Priesthood’s unities are suitably expressed. Moreover, when the faithful actively participate in it, the unity of the People of God shines extraordinarily. It also signifies and fortifies brotherly bonds among the priests.…”  It is preferred that in conventual or ‘communitarian’ Masses all priests concelebrate in It: “It is desirable then, in these cases, that all priests who have no obligation to celebrate individually for the faithful, should concelebrate in these Masses. Moreover, all the priests belonging to a Community, who have the obligation to celebrate individually for the faithful, can concelebrate the same day in the conventual or ‘communitarian’ Mass.”  In a special way at the seminaries: “...the Mass must be celebrated by all the Seminary’s community in which each one is to participate according to his rank. For this reason it is fitting that priests who live at the seminary and who have no obligation to celebrate elsewhere by pastoral office, concelebrate at the communitarian Mass. Deacons, acolytes and readers are to exercise their own functions.”
f: Instruction Eucharisticum Mysterium, 47. General Ordination of the Roman Missal, 114. Inter Missas autem ab aliquibus communitatibus celebratas peculiarem locum obtinet Missa conventualis, quae pars est Officii cotidiani, aut Missa, quae " communitatis ", dicitur. Et quamvis hae Missae nullam specialem formam celebrationis prae se ferant, maxime tamen decet eas cum cantu fieri, praecipue cum plena participatione omnium sodalium communitatis sive religiosorum sive canonicorum. In iis proinde munus suum exerceant singuli iuxta Ordinem vel ministerium receptum. Expedit ideo ut omnes sacerdotes qui pro utilitate pastorali fidelium singulariter celebrare non tenentur, in iis, quantum fieri potest, concelebrent. Omnes insuper ad eam communitatem pertinentes sacerdotes qui officio in bonum pastorale fidelium singulariter celebrandi tenentur, Missam quoque conventualem aut "communitatis" eadem die concelebrare possunt. Praestat enim presbyteros, qui celebrationi eucharisticae intersunt, nisi iusta causa excusentur, munus proprii ordinis de more exercere et proinde uti concelebrantes participare, sacris vestibus indutos. Congregation for Catholic Education, Instruction on the liturgical formation, 23.

h: Article 2: Three Examples of Full Gesture
t: A second example of full gesture is the Communion under both species, when it is permitted, since “it acquires a bountiful form as a sign… the sign of the Eucharistic banquet is more perfectly shown and that Will, which ratifies the New and eternal Covenant in the Blood of Christ and the bond between the Eucharistic and the eschatological banquet in the Kingdom of the Father (cfr. Mat 26:27-29), is more clearly expressed.”  “Communion under both species, which if considered as a sign, presents a more bountiful form and is recommended at the seminary.”
f: Congregation for Catholic Education, Instruction on the liturgical formation, 32. Congregation for Catholic Education, Instruction on the liturgical formation, 32.

h: Article 2: Three Examples of Full Gesture
t: A third example of full gestures is receiving Communion with hosts consecrated at the same Mass: “Let it be offered at the altar as much holocaust as sufficient for the people.…” “...At Mass, the priest gives (in Communion) part of the same Victim offered by himself... and satisfies the piety and the right petition of those who, attending the Mass, ask to be admitted at the participation of the same Sacrifice….”  “Worthy of praise are those who, being present at the Sacrifice, receive hosts consecrated in It….” “It is specially recommended the most perfect form of participation at Holy Mass, which consists of receiving, the faithful, after the priest’s personal communion, the Body of the Lord from the same Sacrifice.” “It should be procured that the faithful receive hosts consecrated at the same Mass that, through this sign, Communion as a participation at the same celebrated Sacrifice be more perfectly shown.”
f: Saint Clement, De consecra., dist. II. Cn. 23. Benedict XI, Enc. Certiores effecti. Pius XII, Enc. Mediator Dei, 74 SC 55 Ins. Eucharisticum Mysterium, 31; cf. General Introduction to the Roman Missal, 85. Valde optandum est, ut fideles, sicut et ipse sacerdos facere tenetur, ex hostiis, in eadem Missa consecratis, Corpus dominicum accipiant et in casibus praevisis calicem (cf. n. 283) participent, quo etiam per signa Communio melius appareat participatio sacrificii, quod actu celebratur.

t: “The liturgical action acquires a nobler form when celebrated with song... Prayer adopts then, a more penetrating expression.” Through singing “the mystery of the Liturgy is more clearly manifest.”
f: MS 5. MS 5.

t: Song is a “necessary or integral part of the solemn liturgy.” Even more “song is a sign of euphoria, joy, happiness of the heart. From here Saint Agustin rightly affirms: “Singing is proper to the lover.”” For that reason the one who loves not, who is absorbed in himself, does not sing. Song, then, is not merely ornamentation as something external to prayer.
f: SC 112 General Introduction to the Roman Missal, 39. Cantus enim est signum exsultationis cordis (cf. Act 2, 46). Unde S. Augustinus recte dicit: " cantare amantis est " (Serm. 336,1) ,et iam antiquitus in proverbium venit: " bis orat qui bene cantat ".

t: The great values of singing in the liturgy are:

1) Song expresses and shapes inner attitudes: song expresses ideas, feelings, attitudes, and desires. It is a universal language -together with the word, the gesture, the movement, and the dance-. It is a sign of expression of sorrow, happiness, triumph, protest. It often reaches where the single word does not.

It also shapes the inner attitude. It brings to life the inner feelings and feeds them. It moves us and, somehow, is an incarnation of our inner attitudes. It makes prayer more complete. It encompasses the whole of the person in prayer since it touches his feelings and esthetical capacity.
2) Song creates Community. “Through the union of voices a more total union of hearts is made possible.” In a fuller and perfect way it manifests “the communitarian nature of the Christian worship.”
f: MS, 5. General Introduction of the Liturgy of Hours, 270.

t: Singing creates a harmonious atmosphere and is a sign of solidarity and communion. Singing helps to get out of ourselves, surpassing merely personal perspectives and so be incorporated into the communitarian perspectives.
We are a community, and singing is one of its most prevalent signs and cause of our common sensitivity.

The reluctance of some for singing is often due to a false individualism, selfishness, since singing with others helps us leave ourselves and adhere to the communitarian expression in a unique celebration.
3) Singing brings out a festive celebration:
- it shapes a more festive or solemn atmosphere
- it expresses prayer with much gentleness
- it fosters unity
- it enriches the sacred rites with a greater solemnity
f: SC 112

t: - it is the clearest prefiguring of the joy of the heavenly liturgy

Solemnity and festivity are manifested in the community that takes part in singing. When the celebration is in common and sung, then that is the real festival: “there is nothing more festive and pleasing... than a whole assembly who expresses its faith and piety through singing.”
f: MS 16.

t: For that reason it is proposed to us “to sing with joy the liturgy of the Hours.” “Blessed are the people who know the festal shout.”
f: General Introduction of the Liturgy of Hours, 270 Salt 89 [88]:15; cf also Ef. 5:19; Col. 3:16-17

t: 4) Singing has a “ministerial function,” the result of singing in the liturgy, is not owed to its own musical nature, nor to its being received in Tradition, nor to its pedagogical value. Rather, it comes from the celebration itself, considered as a liturgical rite with its proper identity and laws, and from the celebrant community.

Singing must lead this particular community to celebrate in unity. For this reason singing is not ‘independent’ but ‘ministerially’ serves the Rite celebrated by the gathered community. This is the reason why each song’s exigencies must be respected if it is an acclamation, a processional song, a song for meditation, litanic response, hymn of glory, etc.
“The more intimately linked to the liturgical action a song is, the holier it becomes.”
5) Singing is like a sacrament; at the celebration, the song and the music are certain efficacious signs of the inner event.

It is the “incarnation” of a mystery taking place at deeper levels: a God who speaks and creates His gift, and a Community who responds with faith, praise and pleas. Singing is one of the effective signs of this “encounter”. Even more than this, it is an efficacious sign of the praise of all humanity and the cosmos: “United with them, and in the name of every creature under heaven, we too praise your glory as we sing….”
f: Eucharistic prayer IV. The Spanish version ends ‘sing’; the English version ends ‘say’

t: A singing Community is also sign of Christ’s presence: “Who is present when the Church pleads and sings psalms”. It is ‘the bride’s voice’ united to the Bridegroom in the sacrificium laudis (sacrifice of praise).
f: SC 7

t: Other Liturgical Celebrations

It is also necessary to recognize the importance of the pious and devout prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours, previously known as the Divine Office or Breviary. A helpful document for understanding its importance is the “Laudis Canticum.” It is also necessary to recognize its importance as a preparation and prolongation of the Holy Mass.
f: Paul VI, November 1st, 1970 General Introduction of the Liturgy of Hours, 270

t: The main Hours of the Divine Office ordinarily are to be prayed in community.
In our communities, as far as possible, penance celebrations should take place every week, on a fixed day, according to the Ritual of Penance.
f: Roman Rituals of the Sacraments, C.E.A., Ed. Regina, 1987, Ap. II., pp. 762-826.

t: The different liturgical seasons are to be celebrated as rightfully due. In a special way, the celebration of the Octave of Easter as a Great Sunday is an ongoing tradition among us. Solemnities scheduled in the Canonical Right Code and every Apostle’s Feast are also to be observed.

Maximum attention must be given concerning reverential care for tidiness in regards to the altar and the celebrant’s trousseau. The ornaments are to be worthy and beautiful. The chalice cup should preferably be made of silver; the altar, made of stone; the celebrant and reader’s pulpits are to be fixed. All material is to be ‘noble,’ including the images. Let’s have no concern about spending money for the splendor of the worship. Philip II was reproached for his bedroom’s floor at the Escorial, made of brick; and he answered: “A palace for God, a hut for the king.”
f: Catech 1162

t: Much attention is to be paid concerning the different liturgical ministries:  the ministry of hosting (perhaps it would be more biblically correct to call it ‘hospitality’), the guide, the offering collectors, the servers or acolytes, the readers.… Attention should be paid, in a very special way, to the people guiding the sacred music and songs, whether it be a polyphonic choir or Gregorian, the psalmist or the soloist.
Permanent Formation

Taking into consideration all that has been stated here, it is essential to include into our permanent formation’s programs, time for the study of the Liturgy. Every year, the following documents should be read and/or carefully reviewed:

- A good book on the Eucharist, a review on the General Introduction for the Roman Missal, a review on the Primary Notes to the different sacraments’ rituals and to the Lectionary, the Norms for the liturgical year and the universal Calendar, the norms for the Liturgy of the Hours, and the norms for the Sacramentals, etc.
f: Roman Rituals of the Sacraments, C.E.A., Ed. Regina, 1987, pp. 11-45, 139-166, 423-427, 451-471, 525-538, 665-693, 935-942, 997-1018, etc. Lectionary I, CEA, Ed. Regina, Spain, 1987, 13-63 Lectionary I, CEA, Ed. Regina, Spain, 1987, 93-121 Liturgy of the Hours, Preliminary Documents, CEA, 1979 Blessing, Liturgical Coeditors, 1986

t: It is even advisable, considering the advancements in modern technology, to record on video some of our Masses, and so have the advantage of watching ourselves in the way people see us. Perhaps we would be surprised to see certain ‘tics’ or ‘faults’ in our gestures, words, or attitudes, and the lack of observance of norms: in the exterior and in the spirit with which they are to be observed. We should probably answer to blessed John XXIII’s invitation: “With fatherly affection we ask our dear priests to examine from time to time the way they celebrate the divine mysteries.…” It is also useful to attend or to see a video of Masses presided by other priests, specially by Our Holy Father the Pope, since He is a living example of how the liturgy should be celebrated... Every liturgy should be, as far as possible, cathedraly.
f: Enc. Sacerdotii Nostri Primordia, n° 39

t: Diverse Rites and Cultures

Everyone who has a genuine catholic soul should learn to appreciate the diversity of liturgical rites that show the catholicity of the Church, its sane pluriformity, the wonderful richness of its more pure traditions. It is necessary to learn how to breathe using both lungs: “one can not breathe like a Christian, or better said as a Catholic, with a single lung; it is necessary to have two lungs, that is to say, the Eastern and the Western.” It is also important to know and help, as far as possible, those Eastern and Western liturgical traditions that are in most need of it. For that reason, we already have an Eastern branch in our Congregation.
f: {260. John Paul II, Speech of no catholic Christian communities of Paris, 05/13/1980

t: Since we want to reach every man with the Gospel, we want to inculturate and adapt the liturgy if it is required. “The celebration of the liturgy must correspond to the mind set and the culture of the different people. In order to make the Mystery of Christ ‘known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of the faith’ (Rom. 16, 26), this Mystery should be announced and lived in all the cultures; and these are not abolished but rescued by It.”
f: SC 37-40: SC 37. Even in the liturgy, the Church has no wish to impose a rigid uniformity in matters which do not implicate the faith or the good of the whole community; rather does she respect and foster the genius and talents of the various races and peoples. CT 53 Catech

t: The inculturation, understood as “the incarnation of the Gospel in the different regional cultures and at the same time the introduction of these cultures into the life of the Church,” has its own place in the Cult as in other fields of the Church’s life. A liturgy taking root in diverse cultures “constitutes one of the aspects of the Gospel’s inculturation, that which demands a true integration of the permanent values of a culture at the life of faith of each nation, rather than the transient ones. This work must, then, be inseparably united to a vast action and a harmonized pastoral that considers all the aspects of the human condition.”
f: Slavorum Apostoli, 21 (June 2nd,1985): AAS 77 (1985), 802-803 “The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation”; in L’OR 8/4/1994, p. 5-9. The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation

t: For the inculturation and adaptation of the liturgy we are to consider the principles exposed by the Church: “At the liturgy, above all the sacramental, there is an immutable part of a divine institution for which the Church is only its guardian. There are also parts susceptible to change, of which the Church has the power, and sometimes the duty, to adapt to the cultures of the recently evangelized nations.”
f: SC 21 John Paul II, Vicemus quintus annus, Catholic Church Catechism, n°1205

t: Other considerations in our study and inculturation of the Roman rite are the proper AIM of Inculturation, the Substantial UNITY of the Roman rite, and the Competent AUTHORITY.
f: The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation , n°34

t: a) “The aim that must guide the inculturation of the Roman rite is the same that the Second Vatican Council has set as a foundation for the general restoration of the liturgy: to order the texts and the rites in such a way that they express, with more clarity, the holy things they signify, and as far as possible, that the Christian people may easily understand them and so participate in these rites through a full, active, and communitarian celebration.”
f: The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation , n°35

t: b) “…The process of inculturation will be implemented in keeping with the substantial unity of the Roman rite. This unity is actually expressed in the approved liturgical books published under the authority of the Holy Father and books sanctioned by the Episcopal Conferences for their respective countries and confirmed by the Holy See. Our study of the inculturation should not search for the inclusion of families of new rites; since an adaptation, due to the necessities of a certain culture, means to have these new adaptations as part of the Roman rite also, not out of it.”
f: The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation , n°36

t: c) …The adaptations of the Roman rite, also considering inculturation, depends solely upon the authority of the Church. This authority resides in the Holy See and is exercised through the Congregation for the Divine Worship and the discipline of the sacraments, within the limits established by the Canon Law, the Episcopal Conferences, and the diocesan bishop.… The inculturation, therefore, is not left to the personal initiative of the celebrant or the common initiative of the Christian assembly.”
f: The Roman Liturgy and the inculturation , n°37

t: All the efforts we make to improve our liturgies will always be minuscule, considering the greatness of the Mystery which we celebrate, the greatness of the fruits we receive, and the produced effects. After praying for what he needed, at the celebration of the Holy Mass, Saint Leopold Mandic would respectfully say: “Now refuse to answer my prayers if you are able to, Oh Lord.”
f: P.E. Bernardi, Leopoldo Mandic, Saint of the Reconciliation, Sanctuary, Padua, 1988, p.58; Pietro Bernardi de Valdipono, Father Leopoldo, Martyr of confessionary and Apostle of “ecumenism”, (Sanguesa 1983) 328.

t: Directory of Spiritual Direction

It has always been a custom in the Church, to grow under the shadow of the Apostles, of the fathers of the desert, of the saints, of the spiritual men. Not any the less does the Church nowadays recommend the practice of spiritual direction. It is enough to quote the CVII. There it is recommended, above all, to the future priests. “The spiritual training should be closely connected with the doctrinal and pastoral, and, with the special help of the spiritual director, should be imparted in such a way that the students might learn to live in an intimate and unceasing union with the Father through His Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit.”. In order that the priests may fulfill their ministry with fidelity, it is recommended, among other means, “a visit to and veneration of the Most Holy Eucharist, spiritual retreats and spiritual direction”. In the formation of the religious, it is said that “superiors are also obliged to see to it that directors, spiritual fathers, and professors are carefully chosen and thoroughly trained”. Spiritual direction is also recommended in the formation of all laymen.
f: 80 OT, 8 PO, 18 PC, 18 See GE, 10

t: Our constitutions say: “The priest must be above all, a father, because he engenders sons by the cross, by the prayer, by the apostolic zeal, by the predication. In this ministry Christ was the first, that is why He is called Eternal Father (Is 9, 5). The other priests are fathers due to their participation in his fatherhood: they are fathers, “by Him, and with Him, and in Him”.
f: Const (439)

t: One of the privileged moments during which the priest may exercise this spiritual fatherhood is in the spiritual direction.
With this directory it is sought to revive the conscience of our priests as regards the importance of spiritual direction.

Nowadays spiritual direction is in crisis, while other phenomena that have certain analogy with it grow parallel and tend to replace it or at least, stand as obvious alternatives, even among the consecrated religious lives, such as the yoga, the psychoanalysis, the parapsychology, and other oriental practices.
Some of the causes of this crisis may be stated in the following terms.
The mentality of these times, the outstanding tendency of the groups, where:
An authority is not admitted.
A vertical dependence is avoided.
A true fatherhood has not been experienced.
This mentality helps a lack of disposition in the directed people, who as they don’t reach “the third pair of men” they would not like to devote themselves wholly to God.

The priests, who, perhaps owed to a personal disappointment, to the lack of understanding of the nature of spiritual direction or to unsuccessful experiences, have lead to deforming practices and abuses in the spiritual direction, such as:
Domination by the director

Certain absolutism manifested in that the directed person tells and consults the director, all the subjects, even those which are not matter of spiritual direction, creating, thus, a harmful dependence in the directed person upon the director.
Organization of the life of the directed person by the director
A director imposed since the childhood.
A direction focused only in the directed person, with oblivion of the community, the family, the Church and the world.
Perfectionist priests, formal, rigorist, restrictive, abandoning, ignorant, meddlesome, hesitant, demagogic.
These causes have lead to a misunderstanding of the spiritual direction and thus formed bad directors:
Directors who thought that they knew all.
Directors that imposed their authority without any possibilities of appeal.
Directors that solved everything with prayer.
Directors that restricted the freedom of the directed persons as if they belonged to them
Directors that fell in a camouflaged Pelagianism.
Directors that lived in an angelistic quietism.

h: Chapter 1: The spiritual direction in the Revelation
t: Although spiritual direction is based remotely on the social dimension of human being, spiritual direction itself appears in the revealed religion. From the Revelation, we must then, extract the elements that show the nature of spiritual direction.

h: Chapter 1: The spiritual direction in the Revelation
t: Nevertheless, spiritual direction must be focused mainly in the New Testament:

h: Chapter 1: The spiritual direction in the Revelation
t: The New Testament, is above all, a New Alliance, which consists in serving the Father in spirit and truth, through an intimate communication with Him, in the Holy Spirit.
f: Cf. Jn 4, 23

h: Chapter 1: The spiritual direction in the Revelation
