Precisely then do all the inhabitants feel sacred fear, and moreover, those who go to the mission, and at least during this time, would not interfere by tempting the others, because they know very well that they could not find accomplices. But, supposing the case that there was a libertine man who would dare to tempt a girl, would the events of the mission have to be omitted just because they finish at night? It is said that one should not do wrong so that good would come; holy and good; but it is one thing to do wrong and another to allow it. If it were necessary to omit all good things to avoid all possible danger of evil things, we would have to prohibit all the saints’ feasts, processions, pilgrimages to shrines, because some disorder will always emanate from them; in the same way, we would have to prohibit confessions, communions, attendance at Mass, because there are also scandals and sacrileges from them. It is known that the Church not only permits these things, but she approves and imposes them. But, our contradictor replies: as it is preached at night, so it results that the mission is the cause of these sins. I respond in turn: would they stop committing sins without the mission? If the mission were not preached, bad habits, fights, blasphemies and all the existent scandals would continue, but if it is preached, thousands of sins would be avoided at least while it lasts.”

In the fourth place: “certain missionaries speak imprudently from the pulpit about sins heard in confession, which contributes to people conceiving an aversion for the confessional, and, for fear of being humiliated in public, they omit confessing their sins. I am amazed that the afore-mentioned pastor repeats what people of bad conscience, who dislike the mission, allege. When missionaries arrive at any place, the first thing they do is to become informed by the most prudent men about the sins that reign above all in the population.  so that the morality of the sermons could frequently deal with them, and they take much care not to speak about certain particular acts that could have a special relation with what they had heard in confession. Therefore, with what will they occupy themselves from the pulpit? Perhaps ecstasy, raptures, visions or revelations? The most common sins which are ordinarily committed by habit everywhere, such as impure acts, blasphemy, hate, theft, and other similar ones will be treated and spoken about.”

In the fifth place: “he [the pastor] has not requested the mission because to request it gives rise to the people suspecting that the pastor does not carry out his duty since he is asking for outside help. It can be said that this difficulty, or better said, this excuse, is mixed with his pride. I think entirely the contrary: there is not the least dishonor in the parish priest requesting the mission, but there is dishonor in not requesting it, because omitting the care to request the mission in his parish gives rise to thinking that the he is afraid that his own faults will be discovered. On the other hand, when the pastor fulfills his obligation well, the missionaries will praise his behavior not only in the town, but also before the bishop."

In the sixth place: “his parish had a mission three years ago and scarce fruits are reported from missions when they are frequent, because the people become accustomed to them, so that they do not make an impression: I answer that, regularly, the mission should not be repeated after a short period of time in the same place, but that three years is not a short period of time; ordinarily, after that interval, many have forgotten the sermons, many are those who have also relapsed and many more are those who have become cold, and with a new mission, some of them will revive their fervor and others will raise themselves up from their fall. Apart from that, it is not true that the repetition of missions ceases to produce fruits; when the mission is repeated in the same place, even when that lively compunction is not noticed that was noticed in the first one, all the same, the fruit which the town can take from it will not fail to be great, because, as I already mentioned, many sinners rise from their relapses, many cold souls revive their fervor, and many, at least, reaffirm with steadiness the good way.“

Another objection against popular Missions that is widespread is the economic cost. According to our experience, the Missions pay for themselves. An economic problem does not exist if the popular Mission is done well. God will not be outdone in generosity! He it is who said: Mine is the silver, mine is the gold, says the Lord  (Ag 2:9 ).

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: We can talk about a so-called “pre-history” of popular missions, if we keep in mind the contributions inherited from the magisterial experience of the Church that has contributed to its systematization.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: In the beginning, what stands out as an exemplary model of all popular missions is the missionary action of the Prophets and the Apostles, which, over and above the ordinary ministry carried out in order to maintain faith and grace, stood out in an extraordinary mission that had as its goal winning souls for Christ. In the book of Acts, elements which will systematize the Popular Missions can be corroborated.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: Subsequently, the epoch of persecutions and of the first heresies produced great preachers who - with the strength of their words and even with the signature of their miracles - won souls for Christ in special missions, which in their kind will continue to solidify the popular missions. This preaching was the best means to confront heresies, which consisted in instructing the faithful who many times found themselves abandoned by their shepherds.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: Some examples of these are the missions carried out by Saints Ireneus of Lyon, Cyprian, Gregory Thaumaturgy, Gregory Nazianzen, Anthony Abbot, Pacomio, Columba, Eusebius of Vercelli, Hilario of Poitiers; especially those who “while passing through town” preached about the end times, mercy, and Christian customs.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: During the Middle Ages, we find an important phase for the systematization in the preaching especially motivated by the promulgations of the crusades. Each crusade was preceded by the preaching of great orators, such as Peter the Hermit or Saint Bernard, and these masters of the Word did not work according to a determined plan, but, obliged by the circumstances of the moment, carried out for this occasion a kind of popular mission for the crusaders as for the town. In this way, it was possible to awaken the spirit of Christian penance and a holy enthusiasm for the Holy Land in the society, a powerful impulse that animated Christendom throughout the centuries.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: It is in the XII century when popular missions began to appear, highlighting the figures of Saint Bernard - preacher of the Crusade and renowned refuter of the heresies of his time - and Saint Robert - who insisted in penance and in the vanity of worldly things. The themes are always constant: penance, conversion, novisimos, mercy...

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: The missions begin to be more frequent until they are transformed into a very effective element for the conversion of the people, moving them to confession, to charity to pay for the crusades, to acts of charity, and to constancy in receiving the other sacraments.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: After the XI and XII centuries, reacting against the relaxation of the priests in the active life, the canons regular arose, secular priests who united themselves to take on a life in common according to the rule of Saint Augustine. With this goal, in 1120 Saint Norbert founded the Premonstratensians, fully dedicated to apostolic preaching.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: Nevertheless, before the XIII century, with the exception of the great shepherds of souls, the people were driven away by preaching that was, at best, theological dispute.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: The necessity to expose in a simple form the essence of the true faith grew with the appearance of the heresies of the “cataros and valdenses.”  As a result, the mendicant orders arose as an authentic reformation that, through the testimony of evangelical poverty and preaching outside of the parochial environment, achieved great successes in their missions.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: The fourth Lateran Council (1215), gave stability to the type of life offered by mendicant orders.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: By then, the Franciscan preachers had in mind the advice of Honorio III, when, in 1223, he wrote to them to confirm their Order: "would that your elocution be purified and corrected for the utility and edification of the people, announcing to your listeners vices and virtues, sorrows and glories, the sermon with brevity because it is an abridged word that our Lord has made over the earth."

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: 85.The Dominicans, according to the purpose of their order, and approved in 1216, forged prepared preachers with a firm theology in order to defend the faith from the attacks of heretics.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: To make a principle task of the ministry of the word of God, and the reason for being from a religious society, were completely new things in the Church. From the beginning, this idea was revealed as very fertile.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: In the new dedication that these orders conceded to preaching, behind the figure of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic shined that of Saint Anthony of Padua  (X 1231), and of Berthold of Ratisbona (X 1272).

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: During this period it is admired how public activities ceased when the missionaries passed. An author from that epoch relates: "all, the young and the old with banners at front, went to the city to listen to the sermon and to sing the praises of God. They preached morning, noon, and night...The Way of the Cross was made in Churches and squares..."

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: Here, the pious theater, solemn entrances, processions of penitents, and representations of the Passion are joined as resources for preaching.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: When Boniface VIII instituted the Holy Year for the jubilee of 1300, the special preaching of indulgences prevailed in the pulpits with the thematic logic of the reform of customs.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: Some years later the three immediate forerunners of the Popular Missions arose:

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: *Saint Vincent Ferrer (1419): he consecrated himself as prototype of Popular Missions in France, Spain and Italy. He preached about sin, death, hell, and especially about the universal judgment, which he considered to be near. He celebrated Mass and heard confessions early, and at night, he organized processions for penitents and flagellants.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: *Saint Bernardine of Siena (1444): disciple of Saint Vincent, he also used external elements and ceremonies, for example: bonfires of worldly things, the reconciliation of enemies...Many of those who came later imitated his method and repeated the written sermons he left.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: *Saint John of Capistrano (1456): he inherited Saint Bernardine's style. The “sermo ad status” arose during these years, pointing to the execution of the duty of the particular state.

h: Article 1: Pre-history of the Popular Missions
t: The preaching in general was very simple and moving, adapted to the public, and for this reason efficacious. They usually worried about recording forever in memory the truths of faith which had been preached by using songs, it was the spirit of the alive emotion of the end of the Middle Ages.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The XVI century opened with the Protestant reformation, which was the culmination of an anticlerical ferment. But the same Counter reformation, at

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: the moment of the Council of Trent, gathered the desires for fervent renewal inside the Church in a  great number of souls. The Popular Mission came about as a fruit of the missionary experience of the Church throughout the centuries.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The triumph of the Catholic reformation (1545-1563), was mainly due to the work of the popular missions. It was necessary to reform the customs of the clergy first, for which new congregations of clergy regulars were particularly consecrated:

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The “Teatinos,” founded by Saint Cajetan of Thiene, aimed at the reform o f the clergy, but were also adapted to preaching.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The Barnabites, founded by Saint Anthony Mary Zachariah, exhorted people to penance and the sacraments, for which they carried a big cross on their habits and they preached with a rope tied around their necks.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The Jesuits, who in the missions utilized all possible means, by mandate from Saint Ignatius who, from the beginning, considered the popular mission as one of the best means for the apostolate of his Society.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: Saint Ignatious poured fourth many instructions in his “Rules for those who live in missions"; he insisted on the formation of the missionaries, he asked that they give talks and sermons during the missions, that they give catechism to children and adults, and that they administer the sacraments.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: Moreover, in 1590, Father Acquaviva, Superior General of the Society, gave very profitable norms: to discover the more common sins and vices of the town visited; to use many examples; to make solemn and lively processions; to go two by two; a minimum of eight missionaries in each center; to speak about the peace of God and the means to reach it in the initial speech; to use the influence of teachers and authorities; to converse personally with people during free times; to pin point the places where more profit could be obtained; to extend what is necessary to prepare consciences for confession; each priest should do a mission at least once a year; to renew baptismal promises, to concede indulgences at the end of the mission; to do controversies, because one learns by repetition,  etc.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The Oblates of Saint Ambrose, analogous to the Jesuits, were founded in 1578, by Saint Charles Borromeo; they are those who give the specific name of “mission” to this form of evangelization. They required a total disposition for the mission: "To carry out any ecclesiastical mission in any Church..." Saint Charles Borrromeo indicated the characteristics of missionary preaching: "You will use any means to touch your listeners, that they cry for their sins and repent; try to separate them from their vices and from their crimes, frightening them with the sight of the tortures of the eternal fire; to recommend them to the recompense of the life in heaven, informing them about zeal by means of the virtues and above all by the love of God and neighbor.”

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: The Capuchins, founded in 1528 by Bernardino D`Asti, were characterized by their simple and popular preaching.

h: Article 2: The Popular Mission Properly Speaking
t: 104.The popular mission, as we know it today, was born during the time of the Catholic Counter-reformation, by the work of the regular canons and clergymen. They aimed at reinforcing the faith of the people, reforming the customs, banishing heresies... For this reason, they preached over all of the ultimate end of man, penance and the sacraments. They especially stressed general confessions and the solemn renewal of the promises of Baptism at the end of the mission. Their duration oscillated between some days and some months, according to the circumstances. With Trent, the preaching of Catechism was given the first place among the ministries.

After the Protestant heresy, popular missions were aquiring a more serene and systematic character: to combat heresy and to confirm the religious and moral life of the Catholics. But in other countries, the popular mission has developed quickly until it becomes a specific institution consecrated to the extraordinary ministry and provided with an own character and structure.

a) In Spain: for example, Father Jerónimo López (1658), introduced some variations such as the penitential procession through the city with sermons along the way, preaching with a skull in hand and a “dialogue” with it, the act of contrition or “feeling of night," the solemn communion of the whole town, etc.

b) In Italy: Father Landini, S. J., asked that, upon arrival to a city, the missionaries make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, give vigorous sermons and discipline to men..." the discipline is,” he used to say, “in some manner,  the practical confirmation of what is speculatively taught in the sermons." He was concerned that the Blessed Sacrament be exposed and devotion to the Passion be spread. He focused on immediate conversion. “The mission should not last more than ten days, in order that fervor not be lost, but after, the missionaries can stay to preach a retreat to priests, and to see those who were not able to attend...."

Father Segneri, S.J (1694), used to begin the missions on Monday and finished them Sunday. The Mission included sermons, catechesis, penitential processions and a general communion. The topics were: the value of the soul, malice of the sin, death, eternity, the Sacraments, etc. At the end, people were vehemently urged to persevere in good. This priest was the one who systematized the method among the Jesuits.

Cardinal Caraffa (1633), who later would be Paul IV, founded the congregation of the “Pii Operarii” in 1601: secular priests who lived in community to preach missions to towns and villages with the principal end of “teaching to all the way to salvation." Their missions lasted 10 days, because “he who does not allow himself to be affected in that time will never allow himself to be affected.” He Insisted on walking the streets inviting people, and the procession culminated with a great sermon in the afternoon.

Saint Alphonsus Marie of Liguori founded the Congregation of the Holy Redeemer (Redemptorists) in 1732, with the purpose of giving missions, obliging themselves to it by simple vows. He insisted on some topics that he considered to be principle ones: mortal sin, death-judgement-hell, the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, confession, trust in Mary, prayer. He also put as optional topics:  mercy, God’s calls, the vanity of things, perseverance.

Saint Leonard of Porto Maurizio OFM (1751), “the celestial patron of popular missions," according to Pius XI, in 1923, combined action and contemplation perfectly: "mission being always busy for God, solitude being always busy in God.” He abandoned his monastery to dedicate himself to the “campaign against the devil,” as he called the missions. He placed a good confession as the principle end of the missions. The first day, he placed the crucifix in a very visible place and said: "Here is a summary of what we will preach to you in these holy days: Jesus Crucified. “ In the morning, he gave instruction that lasted one hour; exposition of a relic of the Virgin with a few words about the Mother of God and finally a blessing given with the relic ended this exercise. In the afternoon, he gathered the town in procession singing songs of the mission; after came the exposition of the Holy Sacrament, a colloquy with the Eucharistic Christ and benediction. Then, the saint gave the great sermon of the afternoon; everything lasted about two hours. During the course of the mission two penitential processions were made; communion was distributed on several days... "I want to die on mission, with the sword in my hand against hell,” he said, and so it happened.

c). In France: Saint Vincent de Paul (1581-1660), founded the “Congregation of the Mission,” or “Lazaristas,” to be devoted to the missions among peasants and to the formation of the clergy. He gave great importance to the teaching of catechism; he used to say: "The whole world will agree with the fact that the fruit taken from the mission comes through the catechism.” He established a day so that the missionaries could rest. In thirty years the Lazaristas gave more than 1,000 missions in France.

Other important missionaries were: Father Le Nobletz, who took advantage of songs and drawings; Father Maunoir, S.J., whose missions were like the outline of the Exercises of Saint Ignatius. Father Condren; Monsignor Olier, founder of Saint Sulpicio; Saint John Eudes, founder of the Apostolic Missionaries of Jesus and Mary, who proposed much more duration to ensure the fruits of the mission: two months or more.

Saint Louis Marie Grignion of Monfort founded, in 1705, the Missionary Fathers of the Company of Mary, characterized by their Marian devotion and their apostolic zeal. Saint Louis Marie always carried a cross  and a statuette of the Virgin which he accommodated at Mass, in the confession box, in his room, etc. He especially used processions and songs. He also returned after a time to ensure the fruits; after the mission, his “return to the mission” lasted one week.
The French Revolution with its wars extinguished the popular missions; but the storm ended and they began their rebirth.
New congregations and great missionaries were born like: Monsignor Mazenod and the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, Saint Gaspar of Buffalo, Saint Vicent Palotti, and many others.
d) In America: some figures are highlighted among others: Saint Francis Solano, Saint Toribio of Mogrovejo, Saint Roque Gonzalez, and a multitude of Jesuits, Franciscans, Mercedaries, etc

During the XIX century, “Propaganda Fidei” is founded, and later on Pontifical Missionary Works. During this century Saint Thérèse is named as patron of the missions, and with that purpose, Pope Pius XI publishes an important document about the theme. The figures of Saint Anthony Marie Claret (1870), and Charles of Foucauld (1916), are highlighted.
The universal Patrons of the missions are: Saint Francis Xavier (1506-1552), and Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus (1873-1897). The Patron of Popular Missions is Saint Leonard de Porto Maurizio.

The praxis of the Popular Mission is very varied and rich, and depends for the most part on the missionary's charisma. But, without getting bogged down on minor details, we consider that it has three well-marked phases, they are: 1st the Pre - mission, 2nd the Mission itself; and 3rd the Post-mission.

The Pre-mission is of capital importance due to the best organization of the Mission, since beginning a Mission with everything ready is to possess, already at the beginning, the success of the whole Mission, because this is to ensure its fruits. On the contrary, not preparing the Mission is to tempt God. The collaboration of the pastor is fundamental for this preparation.
This preparation certainly has its requirements, such as:

- To determine the area for the mission, the date, the plane of the area and to have maps for all of the missionaries, defining the zone of each one. To keep in mind celebrations which are characteristic of the area, and also the climate. In the plan, to divide into zones, to mark the routes for the processions; with that, to calculate the number of the faithful; the possible places to begin the procession before the missionary act.

To know the area. To determine social structures, the religious situation, (attendance at Mass, vices, etc.), the pastoral attention and social problems that condition the religious life (work in a factory), etc.

To advertise. For example, to make contests for Mission advertisement, of its slogan, its hymn and logo. The Mission should be announced, it should awaken interest, it should be favorably welcomed and interpreted well.

To have campaigns for prayer and penance. To have a list of all the missionaries and of the lay people who help them; to organize adoration of the Most Holy Sacrament, the Holy Rosary; to request prayers from contemplatives and the sick, etc.
Economy. To organize the expenses to pay for the food for the missionaries, images, rosaries, catechisms, song books, catechetical pamphlets, missals, Gospels, etc.
Acceptance. To have the catholic spirit, that is to say, to accept the solidarity of other preachers and missionaries.

The search for militants. To look for people to help in some aspect of the Mission: it is a way to seek their conversion, making them useful for the missionaries (for example: to look for chauffeurs, cooks, missionaries' companions, people in charge of publicity and propaganda, people who look for donations, people in charge of the sound system, etc.).

Appointment of commissions. To divide the work: liturgy, catechism, entertainment, the children's Mission, the Mission to the sick, extraordinary ministers of the Eucharist, liturgical and popular choir, etc.

Planning. To fix objectives, to choose blocks, to study the content of what is going to be transmitted, to determine the centers of the mission and to be familiar with them before the Mission, to determine special centers: for children (schools), for young people (clubs). To organize collective acts (processions). To form the group of lay and consecrated missionaries.
The Mission itself consists in three principle elements, they are:
- The visits to families
- The schedule of every day of the Mission and
- The missionary act of every day.

In the first place, the home visits should be primary. This centrifugal action, from the center to the periphery, is the search for the “lost sheep" (Lk 15:6). It is through the home visits that the spiritual situation of each of the faithful is known, in order to be able to do pre-sacrament catechesis, if it were necessary, in their homes. It is necessary to attend preferentially to the adults.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: At the same time, such an expansion of the missionaries seeks to develop a centripetal action, from the periphery to the center, because bringing people to the missionary center is the objective of, where the following should take place:

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: - The opening acts with the missionary mandate;

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: - The missionary acts of every day;

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: - The closing acts;

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: - The special acts during each day of the mission.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: For example, during the Eucharistic day, the bells should be rung every half hour, in order to remember that that day the Sacramental Jesus is being adored in the Church, and it brings the people to participation from their homes through ejaculatory prayers and acts of adoration. At night the Most Holy Sacrament is carried in procession, like in  “Corpus." It produces many spiritual fruits and is very much appreciated by the people.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: Likewise, one day should be dedicated to the Virgin, that day can be a Saturday, adorning her image with flowers, and also organizing a continuous Rosary at the Church with shifts of thirty minutes to pray it in the church, for example.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: One day should be dedicated to the deceased, it is convenient to do it twice,  at the beginning of the mission, to attract the people, and another at the end, with a visit and prayer for the dead in the cemetery, if possible.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: One day can be dedicated to the families, with the blessing of future mothers, marriages, homes, etc., where the Gospel of the family can be preached; and other days can be devoted to children, to youth, to workers, where there can be preaching about the Gospel of work, etc.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: There should also be a penitential day, in which confessions are heard for the whole day. Strictly speaking, it is ideal that a missionary Priest stay always in the missionary center and that people know that he is at their  disposal from the first day of the Mission.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: These special dedications for each day have as objective to concentrate on each type of person in particular, and to highlight the most important things, transmitting the Gospel to them in a more specific way.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: During the development of the mission, it is a custom of great profit to have the “Rosary of the Dawn," which is carried out early in the morning, in which people songs and “saetas” are inserted between the mysteries; also, the path taken each day can be varied with great profit.

h: b. The Program of the Whole Mission
t: The “saeta” is a little sententious and moral verse that is used in the missionary sermons, or in any other act of devotion, and the mission is the suitable moment to use it, both in the sermons and in the processions. As the true “saetas” are high pitched, swift and of long flight, they differ from the ejaculatory prayers in that the latter go from man to God, on the contrary the former go from God to man through the missionary; they contain eternal truths about: divine mercy, justice, the final judgment, sin, man's end, etc, and they have their origin in Sacred Scripture. The Holy Fathers also used them (Saint Jerome, Saint Cyril, Saint John Chrysostom, etc). They are not songs; they are not a hymns... The saeta wounds to kill. It should be sonorous, harmonic, it should not be affected. Although it has verse and meter, it does not try to be poetry. Many people, for the pleasant sound of the “saeta,” have passed from the sensible to the spiritual plane of the will. The missionaries of old used it with much profit. It is what is now, in a secular way, the " jingle."
f: Cf.Is 49, 2;  Sal 7,14 Job 6,4. Cf. P. Nicholas Gremon, Saetario, compilation and study, Ed. A. Biffignandi, Cordoba, 1927. “Tinkling, jingle bell….rhyme…”, in Collins Spanish, Gem Dictionary, 8º edition Great Britain, 1963.

t: It is convenient to have the central act at an appropriate hour; not with the Mass if possible, it should not be together with the Mass because the Mission is fundamentally the preaching of the Word of God, and thanks to it, people will draw close to the sacraments. The structure of the missionary act generally consists in ten acts:
The procession;
A point of catechism;
The controversy;
The most important : the missionary Sermon;
The offering of flowers to the Virgin;
The Collective Prayer;
Communion;
Announcements about the Mission;
The Final blessing;
10.  The Farewell and cultural act.

1st The Procession: by which external testimony of the interior faith is given; in order that those who do not participate because of laziness or shame are attracted, by praying the Rosary and singing songs after each mystery, by carrying the images of saints to whom the people of the mission site have more devotion, and also others. We begin carrying the principle image, and then the others are collected that children, teens, women, men, etc., carry. Children usually make the procession of candles. We make a procession each day of the Mission, for 30 minutes, walking about 800 meters. At arriving to the Church, the children go to an appropriate place for the Children’s Mission.

2nd The Point of Catechism: We usually call it the “doctrinal cartridge” to show that it should impress the audience. It is a brief (about 5 minutes) and clear exhibition of some point of Catholic doctrine. It is directed to the intelligence and should be more formative than persuasive. Its net purpose is catechetical. The topics should be those that the people need most.

3rd The Controversy: it is a discussion in which one defends the Catholic doctrine and another attacks it using the more common arguments which people use in order not to go to Church. The attacker should be the interpreter of the people; they should identify with him, so that when the attacker is refuted, the audience is being refuted. The purpose is not to destroy the attacker, but to correct with charity. It lasts about 10 or 15 minutes.

-It could be convenient to dramatize the discussion. The topics should be those that catch people’s attention most, by their present interest, by being topics which people are most ignorant about or are most questioning, these can be: the meaning of suffering, the problem of alcoholism, drugs, priestly celibacy, the reasons why bad things happen to good people and good things happen to bad people, superstitions, confession, the richness of the Vatican, priestly salary, those that sustain the most virulent sects in the area, bad in the Church, consumerism, hedonism, permissiveness, “ethical night,”  divorce, abortion,  bioethics, etc.
f: Some time ago, in the case of the preaching of only one, it was called the sermon of  the apparatus and that, modernizing it, in the case of only one or in that of the controversy, it can give a lot of fruit. It is necessary to be very prudent in the use of this technique, because from the worthy to the ridiculous there is little distance.

t: 4th-The missionary sermon: or of the end, or of shock, is the most important part of the missionary act because it is the moment in which people’s will should be moved to the practice of the virtues. It should last 30 minutes or more. Those who say that it should be shorter are those who are bad preachers, who improvise and who are not capable of developing a topic with interest, who are not convinced of the truth and of the effectiveness of Christian preaching. They bored even though they preach only a minute, and the feeling they leave is that they spoke too much.  Yes, too many empty words. For this issue they should use the Directory of Preaching.

5th- Flowers to the Virgin: at the end of the missionary Sermon, homage should be paid to the Virgin, for which it is convenient that children enter in procession carrying flowers which they place before the image. It is a very touching moment and does much good.

6th -Then the collect prayer is made, which can be a novena, or from the title [or patron] of the parish or chapel, or any other appropriate prayer. In some places a collection for charity is made (it is convenient that many people pass the basket around).
7th - Communion is distributed according to the corresponding Ritual.
8th - The announcements of the Mission are clearly given, especially those for the following day, reiterating the most important from previous days.
9th - The final blessing is given.

10th- The faithful of the Church are dismissed, inviting those who would like to, to participate in a reception or show in the atrium or another appropriate place, with folk songs, videos of the Holy Rosary, or videos of debates, etc. The participation of the people is great and with this, the esteem and appreciation for the missionaries increase

- The Mission does not finish with the departure of the missionaries, on the contrary, it should be the beginning of a better Christian life or of conversion. For that reason, the permanent formation of the people should continue through the organization of different groups, confession, spiritual direction, attention to the sick, catechesis, courses about Catholic culture, spiritual exercises, conferences, monthly retreats, the use of media to defend the Gospel, parish associations, confraternities, nocturnal adoration, holy hours, Sunday schools, meditation and prayer in community, epistolary apostolate, etc.
The " tornate "  is a brief mission of one, two or three days which is made after two or more months, to revive the fire kindled in the Holy Mission.
f: These renovations of Mission, peculiar of the Redemptorists, are called" tornate ". "After no more than four or five months have passed, return to the places that the Congregation gave missions,  in order to do any other shorter public exercise of preaching, but with a less number of subjects, with the purpose of consolidating the fruit of the Mission given previously."

t: May God grant us many and holy preachers, true “authentic apostles," “burning,"  who will spend and be utterly spent for your sakes. (2 Cor 12:15).
f: Saint Louis Marie Grignion de Monfort, VD, 56-58, Works, B.A.C., Madrid, 1984, p.296-297.

t: “Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1).  Therefore, in our spirituality we should never dialectically separate teaching from work or work from teaching.  It is always necessary to unite integrity of doctrine with rectitude of life, orthodoxy with orthopraxis.  In all of revelation word and work – dabar and barah – are inseparably united.”
f: Dir. of Spirituality 109

t: “We will devote ourselves especially to preaching the Word of God... in all its forms by studying and teaching Sacred Scripture... [and] catechisis,” participating in the prophetic office of Christ.
f: Const. 16 Cf. Dir. of Spirituality 33

t: As a Congregation, we must have always present the words of the Holy Father to religious: “I wholeheartedly exhort you, whose religious consecration should make you even more readily available for the Church's service, to prepare as well as possible for the task of catechesis according to the differing vocations of your institutes and the missions entrusted to you, and to carry this concern everywhere. Let the communities dedicate as much as possible of what ability and means they have to the specific work of catechesis.”
f: CT 65

t: To dedicate all of our energies in this work we must also be interiorly convicted that: “The more the Church, whether on the local or the universal level, gives catechesis priority… the more she finds in catechesis a strengthening of her internal life as a community of believers and of her external activity as a missionary Church. As the 20th century draws to a close, the Church is bidden by God and by events - each of them a call from Him - to renew her trust in catechetical activity as a prime aspect of her mission. She is bidden to offer catechesis her best resources in people and energy, without sparing effort, toil or material means, in order to organize it better and to train qualified personnel. This is no mere human calculation; it is an attitude of faith. And an attitude of faith always has reference to the faithfulness of God, who never fails to respond.”
f: CT 15

t: We will develop… the essential elements that we will have to have in mind in order to complete this fundamental mission that the Church has entrusted to us.  To do this we have tried to respond to the questions: What is catechesis and its history in the Church?  What should be the content of catechesis?  How ought one organize and present this material?  How must we transmit this material?  Who should teach catechesis?  How should catechists be prepared?  Who will be the addressees of such teaching?  What are the demands of a catechesis that truly begins in “the life in Christ”?

We have taken our exposition of these points from the abundance of that magnificent document of John Paul II, the encyclical Catechesi Tradendae.  We also have always had present the Catechism of the Catholic Church.

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: The principal urgency and necessity of catechesis derive from the mandate that Jesus Christ Himself gave before His Ascension: “Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Mt 28:19-20).

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: The Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent tells us in the first section for parish priests that “man, abandoned to his own power, can attain neither true wisdom nor sure means of attaining happiness.” From this we see the need for catechesis so that man can effectively reach his end.  We ought to put into practice what is expressed in the Constitutions: “They will work so that the principles of the Gospel effectively influence the lives of men…and they will combat error with all their strength.”
f: Const. 178

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: On the other hand the pressing reality that the contemporary world presents shows us that: “Today, the human race is involved in a new stage of history. Profound and rapid changes are spreading by degrees around the whole world. …  Hence we can already speak of a true cultural and social transformation, one which has repercussions on man's religious life as well,” resulting in the generation of distinct problems:
f: GS 4

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: the cultural tradition was more favorable in the past than it is today for the transmission of the faith;

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: in order that the Christian faith profoundly penetrates cultures not yet evangelized, new forms of expression are needed, as long as the fundamental postulations remain the same;

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: pluralism and moral relativism reign in society;

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: also, there is a growing indifferentism on the part of persons;

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: and the enslavement of the means of communication, to the point that “in particular, the younger generation is growing up in a world conditioned by the mass media.”
f: Const. 168

h: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
t: This dynamism proper to our time should in no way regulate the principles of the Christian faith; to the contrary, it ought to urge us to make an analysis of this reality in order to show to men the danger that encircles them and the solution that the Gospel message proposes to us; for this we must “assume the responsibility of teaching catechism to children and adults.”
f: Const. 181

t: We do not find in the New Testament the noun “catechesis,” but we do find the verb “katechein” with the ordinary sense of “to tell”, “to instruct”, “to teach” in a religious sense.  Such was the catechesis in the first Christian community and, in this sense, it is clear that the primitive Church was born from the teaching of the faith and from the catechesis done by the Apostles, because, “How can they believe in Him of Whom they have not heard?”

The fundamental importance of the theme is evident since it treats of the transmission of the doctrine of the faith. “The Church has always considered catechesis one of her primary tasks, for, before Christ ascended to His Father after His resurrection, He gave the Apostles a final command - to make disciples of all nations and to teach them to observe all that He had commanded.”

“Very soon the name of catechesis was given to the whole of the efforts within the Church to make disciples, to help people to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, so that believing they might have life in His name, and to educate and instruct them in this life and thus build up the Body of Christ. The Church has not ceased to devote her energy to this task.”
f: Cf. Jn 20: 31 CT 1

t: “Some of the most impressive Bishops and pastors, especially in the third and fourth centuries considered it an important part of their episcopal ministry to deliver catechetical instructions and write treatises. It was the age of Cyril of Jerusalem and John Chrysostom, of Ambrose and Augustine, the age that saw the flowering, from the pen of numerous Fathers of the Church, of works that are still models for us.”
f: CT 12

t: The Councils were always a fount of energy for catechesis.  We ought to remember the Council of Trent and its Roman Catechism, and in particular, as a fruit of Vatican II, The Catechism of the Catholic Church, a providential gift for our times.  On this point, the Holy Father expressed that: “Following the renewal of the Liturgy and the new codification of the canon law of the Latin Church and that of the Oriental Catholic Churches, this catechism will make a very important contribution to that work of renewing the whole life of the Church, as desired and begun by the Second Vatican Council.”
f: John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution “Fidei Depositum” I

t: John Paul II asks “the Church's Pastors and the Christian faithful to receive this catechism in a spirit of communion and to use it assiduously in fulfilling their mission of proclaiming the faith and calling people to the Gospel life. This catechism is given to them that it may be a sure and authentic reference text for teaching Catholic doctrine and particularly for preparing local catechisms.”
f: Ibid IV

t: Also bear in mind the General Directory for Catechesis promoted by the Sacred Congregation for the Clergy, since it : “provides the basic principles of pastoral theology taken from the Magisterium of the Church, and in a special way from the Second Vatican Council by which pastoral action in the ministry of the word can be more fittingly directed and governed.  Both instruments [the Catechism of the Catholic Church and the General Directory for Catechesis], each taken in accordance with its specific nature and authority, are mutually complementary.”
f: DGC 120

t: Thus, in a specific sense, “All in all, it can be taken here that catechesis is an education of children, young people and adults in the faith, which includes especially the teaching of Christian doctrine imparted, generally speaking, in an organic and systematic way, with a view to initiating the hearers into the fullness of Christian life.”
f: CT 18

t: With regard to the content of the faith that is transmitted in catechesis, it is clear that it concerns the unique message of eternal salvation that directs all men of all cultures and of all times.  The respect for the integrity of this content is the indispensable condition of Catholic catechesis.  “In order that the sacrificial offering of his or her faith (cf. Phil 2:17) should be perfect, the person who becomes a disciple of Christ has the right to receive "the word of faith"(Rom 10:8) not in mutilated, falsified or diminished form, but whole and entire, in all its rigor and vigor. … Thus, no true catechist can lawfully, on his own initiative, make a selection of what he considers important in the deposit of faith as opposed to what he considers unimportant, so as to teach the one and reject the other.”
f: CT 30

t: “A catechism should faithfully and systematically present the teaching of Sacred Scripture, the living Tradition in the Church and the authentic Magisterium, as well as the spiritual heritage of the Fathers, Doctors, and saints of the Church, to allow for a better knowledge of the Christian mystery and for enlivening the faith of the People of God.  It should take into account the doctrinal statements which the Holy Spirit has intimated to his Church down the centuries.  It should help to illumine with the light of faith the new situations and problems which had not yet emerged in the past.”
f: FD 2 For our Institute the Catechism of the Catholic Church will be a valuable instrument, since it has been known as an “organic exposition of all the Catholic Faith” (CI 18), of an understanding of the four pillars: baptismal profession of faith, the sacraments of the faith, the life of faith, and prayer of the believer (cf. CI 13).   This catechism constitutes a service that the successor of Peter wants to give to the Holy Catholic Church, in order to support and confirm the faith of all the disciples of the Lord, as bonds of unity in the same apostolic faith.

t: All catechetical formation must include a liturgical aspect.  The same sacred signs are a fountain of catechetical formation.  “Catechesis is intrinsically bound to every liturgical and sacramental action.  Frequently however, the practice of catechetics testifies to a weak and fragmentary link with the liturgy: limited attention to liturgical symbols and rites, scant use of the liturgical fonts, catechetical courses with little or no connection with the liturgical year; [and] the marginalization of liturgical celebrations in catechetical programs.”
f: DGC 30

t: “Catechetical instruction is to be given by using all helps, teaching aids, and instruments of social communication which seem more effective so that the faithful, in a manner adapted to their character, capabilities and age, and conditions of life, are able to learn Catholic doctrine more fully and put it into practice more suitably.”
f: CIC c. 779

t: We must pay attention to two poles: the means to use and the diversity of those we will teach.

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: In the catechetical field there is not one unique method of transmitting revealed truth.  One must have in mind that “The end is always higher than the things that are ordered to it.”  Therefore be attentive to utilize in the transmission of the faith all the suitable means for its best understanding and dissemination; just as one makes sure that a particular method of writing a catechism, or of explaining it, does not result in harm to the contents that one wants to teach or for the end that the catechesis proposes with this teaching.  This harm not only has repercussions in scientific errors, but also in something that is graver: the salvation of souls.  Therefore, to refer to the means that the catechist has to employ, the General Directory for Catechesis says that one has to use that which is best for obtaining the spiritual ends that one pursues.
f: S.Th. I-II, 3, 5 (Translated from Spanish)

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: The election of methods, then, will be valid “to the extent that far from being dictated by more or less subjective theories or prejudices stamped with a certain ideology, it is inspired by the humble concern to stay closer to a content that must remain intact.”  If not, it will fall into the vanity of which St. Thomas spoke, since “a man is called vain who, lead by a wrong rule, does not reach the right end.”
f: CT 31 St. Thomas Aquinas, Super Epistolam ad Ephesios, III, 4. (Translated from Spanish)

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: Catechesis is to form the faith of children, youth, and adults, by means of an organic and systematic instruction, aiming at initiating them into the fullness of Christian life.
f: cf. CT 21

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: We must categorically affirm, therefore, that catechesis “must be systematic, not improvised but programmed to reach a precise goal; it must deal with essentials, without any claim to tackle all disputed questions or to transform itself into theological research or scientific exegesis; it must nevertheless be sufficiently complete, not stopping short at the initial proclamation of the Christian mystery such as we have in the kerygma; [and] it must be an integral Christian initiation, open to all the other factors of Christian life.”
f: Ibid.

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: After this very clear affirmation, the Holy Father stressed anew “the need for organic and systematic Christian instruction, because of the tendency in various quarters to minimize its importance.”  And he sums up those tendencies, disqualifying them with all clarity: “It is useless to play off orthopraxis against orthodoxy: Christianity is inseparably both. … It is also quite useless to campaign for the abandonment of serious and orderly study of the message of Christ in the name of a method concentrating on life experience. … Nor is any opposition to be set up between a catechesis taking life as its point of departure and a traditional doctrinal and systematic catechesis.  Authentic catechesis is always an orderly and systematic initiation into the revelation that God has given of Himself to humanity in Christ Jesus, a revelation stored in the depths of the Church's memory and in Sacred Scripture, and constantly communicated from one generation to the next by a living, active tradition. This revelation is not however isolated from life or artificially juxtaposed to it. It is concerned with the ultimate meaning of life and it illumines the whole of life with the light of the Gospel, to inspire it or to question it.”
f: Ibid. CT 22

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: The desire to spread the faith in order that it become more alive and efficacious in men, will lead, of course, to utilizing all the resources that the discoveries of human sciences offer.  “In fact, it is natural that techniques perfected and tested for education in general should be adapted for the service of education in the faith. However, account must always be taken of the absolute originality of faith. Pedagogy of faith is not a question of transmitting human knowledge, even of the highest kind; it is a question of communicating God's revelation in its entirety. Throughout sacred history, especially in the Gospel, God Himself used a pedagogy that must continue to be a model for the pedagogy of faith.”
f: CT 58

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: The most elementary of whatever catechetical system and method, to our understanding, must have in mind the following:

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: it must expound in simple and appropriate language the essentials of the deposit of the faith;

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: this exposition of the deposit of the faith must be done in an ordered way, in order to show the necessary connections existing between the truths of the faith;

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: it must make sure that the fundamentals of the faith be memorized, since they will live the rest of their life a good part of Christians;

h: Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
t: and, through these truths, it must move each person to rectify his conduct, by an exacting application of the faith to all the circumstances of his life, whether in his relationship with God directly, or in all his human relationships, that have to be also dealt with God.
The diversity of persons to which catechism is directed demands a necessary adaptation in all cases.

“He who instructs [should] become all things to all men (1 Cor 9:22), and be able to gain all to Christ. …Nor let him imagine that those committed to his care are of all equal capacity or like dispositions, so as to enable him to apply the same course of instruction, to lead all to knowledge and piety; for some are, “as it were new-born infants,” others grown up in Christ, and others in some sort, of full maturity. …all who are called to this ministry [should] understand that in announcing the mysteries of faith and in inculcating the precepts of morality, the instruction is to be accommodated to the capacity and intelligence of the hearers.”
f: Catechism of the Council of Trent (CR), Preface.  Translation by Rev. J. Donovan, 1829.

t: “The age and the intellectual development of Christians, their degree of ecclesial and spiritual maturity and many other personal circumstances demand that catechesis should adopt widely differing methods for the attainment of its specific aim: education in the faith. On a more general level, this variety is also demanded by the social and cultural milieu in which the Church carries out her catechetical work.”
f: CT 51

t: Nevertheless, one must always remember in choosing a method and the most suitable language to use, that “the choice made will be a valid one to the extent that, far from being dictated by more or less subjective theories or prejudices stamped with a certain ideology, it is inspired by the humble concern to stay closer to a content that must remain intact. The method and language used must truly be means for communicating the whole and not just a part of ‘the words of eternal life’ ( Jn. 6:69; cf. Acts 5:20; 7:38) and the ‘ways of life’ (Acts 2:28, quoting Ps. 16:11).”
f: CT 31

t: In this work of necessary adaptation, “the first question of a general kind that presents itself here concerns the danger and the temptation to mix catechetical teaching unduly with overt or masked ideological views, especially political and social ones, or with personal political options.”  The catechist must always stand firm over these unilateral options and for him, “it is on the basis of revelation that catechesis will try to set its course, revelation as transmitted by the universal Magisterium of the Church, in its solemn or ordinary form.”
f: CT 52 Ibid.

t: Another great challenge for catechesis is the incarnation of the message in cultures.  “We can say of catechesis, as well as of evangelization in general, that it is called to bring the power of the Gospel into the very heart of culture and cultures.  For this purpose, catechesis will seek to know these cultures and their essential components… and help them to bring forth, from their own living tradition, original expressions of Christian life, celebration and thought.”  In this work one must remember that “on the one hand the Gospel message cannot be purely and simply isolated from the culture in which it was first inserted…nor…the cultures in which it has already been expressed down the centuries.  On the other hand, the power of the Gospel everywhere transforms and regenerates. When that power enters into a culture, it is no surprise that it rectifies many of its elements. There would be no catechesis if it were the Gospel that had to change when it came into contact with the cultures.”  One of the works with which our Institute can collaborate in this infusion of the Gospel into cultures will be the translation, publication, diffusion and teaching of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, especially in the places of mission.
f: CT 53 Ibid.

t: “It is a proper and grave duty especially of pastors of souls to take care of the catechesis of the Christian people so that the living faith of the faithful becomes manifest and active through doctrinal instruction and the experience of Christian life.”
f: CIC c. 773

t: In the first place, the exhortation of the Holy Father in Catechesi Tradendae direcs the bishops whose principal commitment must be “to bring about and maintain” in the local churches a “a real passion for catechesis, a passion embodied in a pertinent and effective organization, putting into operation the necessary personnel, means and equipment, and also financial resources.”
f: CT 63

t: Then the Holy Father tells the priests how to immediately assist the bishops: “with all my strength I beg you, ministers of Jesus Christ: Do not, for lack of zeal or because of some unfortunate preconceived idea, leave the faithful without catechesis. Let it not be said that ‘the children beg for food, but no one gives to them’ (Lam 4:4).”
f: CT 64

t: “By virtue of his function, a pastor is bound to take care of the catechetical formation of adults, youth, and children, to which purpose he is to use the help of the clerics attached to the parish, of members of institutes of consecrated life and of societies of apostolic life, taking into account the character of each institute, and of lay members of the Christian faithful, especially of catechists.”
f: CIC c. 776

t: Thus, the Holy Father entrusts catechesis to religious and to the faithful laity, and then  reminds us of most excellent place for catechesis: the Parish.  We must be convinced that the center of catechesis is the Parish and the parish priest must consider it as one of his most important responsibilities.  “It is true that catechesis can be given anywhere, but I wish to stress…that the parish community must continue to be the prime mover and preeminent place for catechesis.”  An adequate catechesis, in its different levels, especially for children, constitutes the central apostolate of the Parish.  And it is precisely the parish that must promote the great work of catechesis in families, in schools and in the movements of the faithful, etc.
f: CT 67

t: Keep in mind what our Constitutions say:  “Religious who assist in parishes should give priority, in an enthusiastic pastoral action, to the…responsibility of teaching catechism to children and adults.”
f: Const. 181 In this work the parish priest will be helped by his assistants.

t: Inasmuch as the faithful laity do not encounter legitimate impediments, “parents above others are obliged to form their children by word and example in faith and in the practice of Christian life; sponsors and those who take the place of parents are bound by an equal obligation.”

This right that parents posses cannot enter into conflict with the responsibility conferred by the Church on legitimate pastors who are in charge of organizing and keeping watch over catechesis.  “Family catechesis precedes, accompanies, and enriches other forms of instruction in the faith. Parents have the mission of teaching their children to pray and to discover their vocation as children of God.  The parish is the Eucharistic community and the heart of the liturgical life of Christian families; it is a privileged place for the catechesis of children and parents.”
f: CCC 2226

t: Make use of the various means of social communication:  bulletins and newsletters, reviews and magazines, radio or television programs, videos, etc… by these, catechism can reach more people, environments, families…

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: The great Spanish catechist, Mons. Manuel González, sums up this important question on the necessary intellectual and spiritual preparation of catechists in one principle and three proverbs.

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: First of all, the principle: “Catechesis is the catechist.”  He explains: “Give me a catechist with vocation…, with adequate intellectual preparation, who treats first with the Heart of Jesus in the Sanctuary, who next treats with children and who, above all, loves these children with the love drawn from the Sanctuary, give me a catechist like this and do not tell me that this catechist cannot teach, cannot do his job, because he lacks educational material like posters, projectors, valuable rewards, attractive outings, etc.  This catechist that you have described will be able to manage so that the expressions of his face and the form and contortions of his body substitute for and surpass posters or projectors, and will give great value to and more than make up for, with his smile and his warm word, the affection, trinket or trifle of which in his poverty he prepares for prizes.  In other words, the problem of Christian instruction and education of the people, more than a problem of laws, of organization, or of works, is a problem of man.”

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: And in three proverbs, he leaves us fundamental pedagogical principles which sum up the most important things to take into account in catechesis with children, as in all catechesis.
f: Cf. Cartilla del Catequista Cabal.

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: a) “No one gives what he does not have.”  “Whoever does not possess Jesus cannot give Jesus.”  Whoever wants to give to his students the clear and exact knowledge of Jesus Christ and His doctrine must, before all, posses such knowledge through responsible study and prayer.  Whoever wants to transmit the liking and love for that which he teaches must begin by the imitation of the same.  And finally, if the catechist wishes the children to come with enthusiasm to the doctrine, “to listen attentively to him with happiness and without fear or dissipation or disturbance, and to go with a desire to return,” he must begin by teaching in this way.  If the catechist does not carry out these conditions, now he knows the cause of his failures.

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: b) “Children are children.”  The catechist must exert himself to adapt his teaching to the age and condition of the students and cannot expect from them what they cannot give.  Thus, for example, he cannot ask the seriousness and immobility of a class of adults from a class of children.

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: c) “Eyes that don’t see, heart that does not feel.”  “While children see and understand better that which is explained to them, then their hearts will be more interested and will more deeply understand what is being taught.”  For him, Mons. Manuel González proposes: “Give them more Sacred History or Gospels than lessons from the catechism text.  Seek that they know first who is Jesus, what He did, where He lived and what He taught with His word.  The holier the ideas, the more necessary it is to understand them thoroughly in order to love them.  It is enough to know a good person a little in order to love him/her.  It has been disgracefully forgotten that those who know more Theology are not necessarily better Christians, but those who more firmly believe and more loyally unite themselves to and love Jesus.”

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: Local superiors and especially parish priests (and their assistants) should pay close attention to the formation of catechists through fruitful participation in the Sunday Liturgy, courses, Spiritual Exercises, etc.

h: The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists
t: Pay special attention to promoting, supporting, and collaborating with all the initiatives on the diocesan level by starting schools or institutions for theological formation for laity, seeking that which imparts a competent catechesis.  If such an institute of this nature already exists, offer members of our Religious Family to collaborate in it.
“Attentive to the norms established by the diocesan bishop, a pastor is to take care in a special way:
that suitable catechesis is imparted for the celebration of the sacraments;

that through catechetical instruction imparted for an appropriate period of time, children are prepared properly for the first reception of the sacraments of penance and the Most Holy Eucharist and for the sacrament of confirmation;
that having received first communion, these children are enriched more fully and deeply through catechetical formation;
that catechetical instruction is given also to those who are physically or mentally impeded, insofar as their condition permits;
that the faith of youth and adults is strengthened, enlightened, and developed through various means and endeavors.”
f: CIC c. 777

t: If we consider catechesis as the initiation into the sacramental life of the Church, according to the distinct conditions of the students, we must take into account in our parishes:
a) Catechism for children in First Communion and Confirmation classes

From infancy, the child should receive an organic formation in the faith.  It is the stage of the student, the stage of cementing vital principles, of direction by parents, godparents, and catechists, of sowing good seeds on fertile soil.

Therefore, systematic or gradual catechesis is a fount of inspiration and formation in the faith and religiosity of children.  It is a means of forming persons, directing moral criteria, and  cultivating virtues.
In First Communion classes, teach them the principal mysteries of the faith and prepare them for a fruitful reception of the sacraments of Confession and Eucharist.
Prepare the children and adolescents who will receive the sacrament of Confirmation so that they not only strengthen their faith but also can defend it and proclaim it with works and words.

In our time it is common that children find themselves abandoned, suffer a spiritual abandonment, and even are abandoned by their own parents.  In addition, the culture of death seeks to take away from them the most valuable thing they possess, the grace of God.

The work of the one dedicated to the apostolate with children must help them to grow spiritually so that they become saints, that is to say that they know and love Jesus very much.  “Central aspects of the formation of children are training in prayer and introduction to Sacred Scripture”
f: DCG 178

t: We should note some of the characteristics of children with their negative and positive aspects:
Negative aspects:

Take into account the influence of television.  The images, music, and words strongly impress in sensibility of children that do not yet have critical judgment.  Television increases the activity of the senses, diminishes intellectual activity, and conditions the conduct of the child.  In addition, TV and video games impedes their ability to dedicate themselves to an activity that requires more attention, such as lectures or talks.
Take into account that familial problems, including broken families, the absence of the father or mother, etc. make it difficult for children to understand the paternity of God.
Patience must be practiced to the extreme because of the crisis of authority that exists today, in order to discover the best way to speak to children.
Positive aspects:

The generosity of children enables them to give that which to them is most precious.  They are simple, unsophisticated, natural, without complications; they do not suffer from the miseries of grown-ups; they do not act with duplicity or hypocrisy.
In order to succeed in this, encourage the preaching of retreats for children, penitential para-liturgies, Masses for children with preaching themes adapted for them, popular missions, etc.
For the perseverance of children and youth, encourage oratories.
b) Catechesis for youth

The age of youth is very rich in dynamisms that strongly drive them to action.  It is necessary to discover through this dynamism the values that move youth, for example, the search for security, authenticity, conquering self, relationships with others, service…

It is necessary to further orient them in the discovery of their vocation and of their cultivation.  Implement a vocational catechesis, presenting the ideals of consecrated life as well as those of the matrimonial life.

In this age, youth demand a solid foundation in the faith, not so much with apologetical demonstrations, but rather the testimony of the Christian life which is capable of loving in truth and of radiating this love.

In this age, catechesis must be achieved by means of the dynamics of groups, in which an authentic friendship and spirituality provide youth with a real experience of Christian unity, founded on the charity of Christ.

We must also have systematic catechetical formation which should occupy the first place in the schools of our Institute.  The principal object of our educational Institutes is the formation of good Christians; without this, they are meaningless.

We should be aware of different religious situations: unbaptized youth, baptized youth who have not been catechized or completed their Christian initiation, youth who encounter a crisis of faith, oftentimes grave, others who might have the option of faith, or others who have made an act of faith and hope to be helped.

Useful means for an efficacious catechesis include: a well oriented community action group, educational youth associations, and personal accompaniment of the youth, in which spiritual direction is highlighted.

One of the greatest difficulties that is confronted and should be responded to is the difference in language (mentality, sensibility, likes, style, vocabulary) between the youth and the Church (catechesis and catechists).  It is important to insist on the necessity of an adaptation of catechesis to youth, knowing how to translate the message of Jesus Christ into their language “with patience and good will, without betraying it.”
Take advantage of the invitations given to members of our Religious Family to give talks in state or secular schools.
c) Catechism for adults

“From infancy until the threshold of maturity, catechesis is thus a permanent school of the faith and follows the major stages of life, like a beacon lighting the path of the child, the adolescent and the young person.”  Also adults, since “for catechesis to be effective, it must be permanent, and it would be quite useless if it stopped short at the threshold of maturity, since catechesis, admittedly under another form, proves no less necessary for adults.”
f: CT 39 CT 43

t: It should form Christians of enlightened faith, firm and faithfully lived, that is to say, capable of fully assuming life in all its realism, with its responsibilities and duties, in all the fields of human activity.
In particular the duties of catechesis with adults are:
Promote formation and maturation of life in the spirit of the resurrected Christ, with adequate means like sacramental pedagogy, retreats, and spiritual direction.
Educate in order to be able to objectively judge the socio-cultural changes of our society in the light of faith.
Give response to religious and moral questions of today (eg: public and individual morals).
Form them to assume responsibilities in the mission of the Church and to know how to give Christian testimony in society.

When dealing with adults who haven’t even received the sacraments, propose to them, by means of a prudently adapted catechesis, the necessary aids for them to receive them.  They will them try to continue their formation.
d) Catechesis for the elderly

“Not infrequently the old are seen as passive objects and possibly even as an encumbrance. In the light of faith, however, they must be understood as a gift of God to the Church and to society, and must also be given adequate catechetical care. In catechesis, they have the same rights and duties as all Christians. … Catechesis for the aged pays particular attention to certain aspects of their condition of faith. An aged person may have a rich and solid faith, in which case catechesis, in a certain sense, brings to fulfillment a journey of faith in an attitude of thanksgiving and hopeful expectation. Others live a faith weakened by poor Christian practice. In this case, catechesis becomes a moment of new light and religious experience. Sometimes people reach old age profoundly wounded in body and soul. In these circumstances, catechesis can help them to live their condition in an attitude of prayer, forgiveness and inner peace.  At any rate, the condition of the old calls for a catechesis of hope, which derives from the certainty of finally meeting God.”
e) Catechesis for the sick

Those who have the apostolate with the sick should instruct them on the substantial reason for sufferings and on the justifications of the present condition, about the medicinal and expiatory value of the cross.  Teach them also to participate through their sufferings in the great apostolate of the parish and of the Church.  Encourage them to exercise themselves in patience and to prepare themselves for eternity.
f: cf. Dpar, 145; cf. Const. [193]

t: f) Catechesis for the handicapped

Take special care of these.  “Every Christian community considers those who suffer handicaps, physical or mental, as well as other forms of disability—especially children—as persons particularly beloved of the Lord.  A growth in social and ecclesial consciousness, together with undeniable progress in specialized pedagogy, makes it possible for the family and other formative centers to provide adequate catechesis for these people, who, as baptized, have this right and, if non-baptized, because they are called to salvation. … [This catechesis] is most effectively carried out in the context of the integral education of the person.  On the other hand, the risk must be avoided of separating this specialized catechesis from the general pastoral care of the community. … The particular demands of this catechesis require a special competence from catechists and render their service all the more deserving.”
f: DCG 189

t: We should give privileged attention to the sick and handicapped, for in them we discover the face of the suffering Christ.

We reproduce a magnificent and rich text of the Catechism of the Catholic Church which gives us a summary of that which catechesis ought to be in order not to remain in the letter “which kills” but that introduces one truly into the mystery of the divine life which the Son of God has come to transmit to us by His Incarnation.
Catechesis has to reveal in all clarity the joy and the demands of the way of Christ (cf. CT 29).  Catechesis for the “newness of life” in him (cf. Rom. 6:4) should be:
“a) a catechesis of the Holy Spirit, the interior Master of life according to Christ, a gentle guest and friend who inspires, guides, corrects, and strengthens this life;
“b) a catechesis of grace, for it is by grace that we are saved and again it is by grace that our works can bear fruit for eternal life;”
f: CCC 1697

t: c) a catechesis oriented to the sacraments.  “Attentive to the norms established by the diocesan bishop, a pastor is to take care in a special way:
that suitable catechesis is imparted for the celebration of the sacraments;

that through catechetical instruction imparted for an appropriate period of time children are prepared properly for the first reception of the Sacraments of Penance and the Most Holy Eucharist and for the Sacrament of Confirmation.”
f: CIC c. 777

t: “d) a catechesis of the beatitudes, for the way of Christ is summed up in the beatitudes, the only path that leads to the eternal beatitude for which the human heart longs;

“e) a catechesis of sin and forgiveness, for unless man acknowledges that he is a sinner he cannot know the truth about himself, which is a condition for acting justly; and without the offer of forgiveness he would not be able to bear this truth;
“f) a catechesis of the human virtues which causes one to grasp the beauty and attraction of right dispositions towards goodness;
“g) a catechesis of the Christian virtues of faith, hope, and charity, generously inspired by the example of the saints;

“h) a catechesis of the twofold commandment of charity set forth in the Decalogue.”  “Before his Passion, Christ, interrogated by an expert of the Law about was the greatest and first commandment, said: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; this is the greatest and first commandment (Mt 22:38).  And certainly it is the greatest, most noble and useful of all the commandments… then in this is fulfilled all the commandments.”  “Two are the roots of all the commandments…: The love of God and of neighbor.”
f: CCC 1697 St. Thomas, Duo Praecepta Caritatis, Opuscula Theologica, Marietti, vol. II, 2o edición, 1972, p. 249, no 1160.  (translated from Spanish) Ibidem, p. 261, no 1332. (translated from Spanish)

t: “i) an ecclesial catechesis, for it is through the manifold exchanges of “spiritual goods” in the “communion of saints” that Christian life can grow, develop, and be communicated.”
f: CCC 1697
