In the oratorian climate each one ought to “work in every way possible to infuse into the hearts of the youth the love of God, respect for sacred things, the value of frequenting the sacraments, a filial devotion to the Blessed Virgin, and all that constitutes true piety.”  This fruitful environment will not be achieved if it is not supported by or built on true piety and the practice of Christian virtues.
f: Cap. I de la parte, arts. 1 y 7.

t: In order for the environment of religious practice to be foundational, frequenting the sacraments of Confession and Eucharist must be insisted upon.  “Frequent confession and communion and daily Mass are the columns that must sustain the educational edifice if intimidation and the stick are to be kept far away.”  “Remember that the first method of education is good confessions and good communions.”  The Oratory should be a place where all “… can have the convenience to fulfill their religious duties and, at the same time, receive instruction, orientation, and advice, so as to direct their life in a Christian and honest manner.”
f: Cf. Const. 181 St. John Bosco, El sistema preventive en la educación de la juventud. Memorias Biográficas, IV, 555. Circular letter of Dicember 10, 1851.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: All need to save their soul and body.  The Oratory must be universal, like the salvific will of God.  The student should be surrounded by a constant, kind, and solicitous assistance.  The Oratory must be open to all.  It should take into account all the values of the youth and of all.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: “The festive Oratory of Don Bosco is an institution totally his, that differs from whatever other similar institution as much as by the end that it pursues as by the means that it uses.  According to Don Bosco, the Oratory is not for a determined category of youth in preference to others, but for all without distinction, from the age of seven up; there is no impediment stemming from the family situation or from the parents’ presentation of the youth: the only condition to be admitted is to come with a good will to have fun, be instructed, and to fulfill with all the others their religious duties.  The cause of a youth’s expulsion from the Oratory can neither be the vivacity of his temperament, nor the occasional rebellion, nor the lack of education, nor what ever juvenile defect caused by frivolity or natural stubbornness; but only systematic and contagious insubordination, blasphemy, bad conversations and scandal.  With the exception of these cases, the tolerance of the director should be unlimited.  All the youth, especially the most abandoned and miserable, must understand that the Oratory is for them the paternal house, the refuge, the ark of salvation, the secure way to become better under the transforming action of the affection of the Director, more than his paternity.”
f: Albera, P., Circular Letter, Gli Oratori Festivi, le missioni le vocazioni, p. 112.  Cited by Pablo Sivak, op. cit. 318.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: The Oratory does not have schedules; it should fill to the brim the free hours of a youth’s life, “to saturate it with possibilities, with joy, with human and heavenly values, with formation and fun, with instruction and edification.”  The Oratory tends to prolong itself, in one way or another, throughout the week.
f: Op. cit. p. 318 In the Memorias Biográficas and in the Memorias del Oratorio you can find detailed notes about the origin and the activities of the diverse courses: for the illiterate (Memorias Biográficas 3, 499; 2, 347-348, 55-557; Memorias del Oratorio 182-183), for drawing and arithmetic (Memorias Biográficas 2, 347-348, 560), for music and singing (Memorias Biográficas 2, 561, and Memorias del Oratorio 186-187, 194-195). Pablo Sivak, op. cit. 322.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: All have the right to receive moral and religious assistance: “However, the poor, most abandoned and most ignorant are admitted and attended to preferentially, because they have the most need of assistance in order to maintain themselves in the way of eternal salvation.” “To entertain the most abandoned youth,” repeats Don Bosco in his Memoirs.
f: Regolamento, parte II, cap. II, art. 2 Memorias del Oratorio de S. Francisco de Sales, 142.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: The conditions for acceptance are broad: “All are free to frequent this Oratory.  But all must submit themselves to the orders of those in charge and observe the proper behavior in recreation, in the church, and outside the Oratory.”
f: Ibid.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: “The boy that enters the Oratory should be persuaded that this is a place of religion, where we desire to form good Christians and honest citizens.  For this reason it is rigorously prohibited to blaspheme or to have conversations against good customs or against the Holy Catholic religion.  Whoever commits one of these faults will be paternally warned the first time, and if he does not amend, the Director will be notified, who will expel him from the Oratory….  Disobedient youth can also be admitted, provided that they do not give scandal and that they manifest the will to better their conduct.”
f: Regolamento, parte II, cap. II.  Cited by Pablo Sivak, ibid.

h: Article 3: An Environment that is Open to All and that Embraces All
t: The Oratory is a complete program of material help and family support, of evangelization and of conviviality, of culture and of mission, finally, a community where one can be with friends and be happy.

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: The festive Oratory is a “free” educative system in which the obligation and regulation are substituted by the attraction of the festive environment and of charity.  An environment of novelty and joyful saturation of the youth should be created through games: “a diversity of games according to the ages of the children and the customs of the place is recommended – these constitute one of the most efficacious means of attracting the youth to the Oratory.  It helps encourage frequent attendance and good behavior at the festive Oratories if prizes are distributed at determined times, for example, books, objects of devotion, clothing; as well as lotteries, outings, skits and moral plays, music classes, little parties, etc.”  The activities that can be carried out in the Oratory should not only be amusing, but also, when possible, they should be constructive.
f: Memorias Biográficas, 3, XII, pp. 136-143; Memorias del Oratorio de S. Francisco de Sales, 155-157, 175-178, cited by Pablo Sivak, op. cit. p. 320. Memorias Biográficas, 18, 703, cited by Pablo Sivak, op. cit. ibid.

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: Joy is essential to the spirit of the Oratory.  The Christian life is to prepare for a feast, and to live the heavenly feast while still on earth.  Joy springs from possessing that which it loves.  One is truly joyful when one is joyful in love: “where charity rejoices, there is festivity.”  And this is because every feast implies a existential richness that in its turn is born of a renunciation, for one cannot have a time of feasting if one has not denied oneself something.  And this renunciation implies love, for there is no renunciation where there is no love.  Don Bosco saw in dreams how the spirit of long ago had decayed: “shouts and songs of jubilation are not heard” from which “the coldness in many when approaching the holy sacraments originates, and negligence in the practices of piety in the church and outside of it…”
f: St. John Chrysostom, cited by Josef Pieper, Una teoría de la fiesta, p. 33. Cf. Josef Pieper, Una teoría de la fiesta, p. 30. Fierro, R., Biografia y Escritos de San Juan Bosco, Madrid 1967, p. 448. Op. cit. p. 449.

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: Freedom has its source in charity as well, therefore if we surrender our heart to Love Himself, nothing an no one can impede us from coming to be with the Lord, for we are no longer two but one: What will separate us from the love of Christ?  Will tribulation, or anguish, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? …  No, in all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through Him who loved us.  For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor present things, nor future things, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:35, 37-39).  Love is that to which we are called and in what we find true freedom, not carnal freedom: For you were called to freedom, brothers.  But do not use this freedom as an opportunity for the flesh; rather, serve one another through love.  For the whole law is fulfilled in one statement, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal 5:13-14).  It is the freedom of the one who, solely for love of God and of neighbor, does good and avoids evil.

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: In our oratories there should not be a vigilance of the police type, but rather a paternal watchfulness, for all the members of our Religious Family are none other than children of God, who rejoice in the freedom proper to the children of God, because to rejoice in freedom, Christ set us free (Gal 5:1).  The spirit of family that is instilled in our oratories lives in a climate of freedom.

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: The Oratory is of itself a “fragile” institution, since its attendance is totally free – it is based on voluntary attendance.  This voluntary aspect has a most important role: “this voluntary aspect is that which makes the action of the leaders much more varied, elastic, dynamic, and rich in initiatives, so that they are not limited to waiting and receiving, but like Don Bosco, organize “raids” of collection, true peaceful “searches” (in city squares, streets, bars, neighborhoods, etc.).

h: Article 4: Environment of joy and freedom
t: “Making festive each Sunday at the Oratory should be one of the most elemental preoccupations of the educators that work in it.”  The variety that attracts and enthuses the youth should be a great preoccupation: “in this is the whole secret and the success of the Oratory.  When a Director is not able, with holy industries, to make festive the Sundays of his Oratory or, when, even having great plans, does not know how to communicate them to his assistants, except in spurts and only at the time of putting them into effect, then the Oratory will become a little Babel and the youth will begin to be tired and stop coming.”
f: Albera, Don Paolo, Lett. Circ., p. 117.  Cited by Pablo Sivak ibid.

t: The life of the Oratory should be interwoven with the Christian virtues of piety and joy, but above all the divine and human bond that establishes charity and true love must exist.  Charity should pedagogically be transformed into “amorevolezza,” as St. John Bosco masterfully teaches.  Charity should always appear, become visible, transform into a human means of attraction and conquest.
f: Cf. Pablo Sivak, op. cit. p. 321.

t: The spirit of our communities must be founded in charity that be transformed, as Don Bosco says, into “amorevolezza.”  This is a typical expression of the saint, that does not have a satisfactory translation in English and that signifies: kindness, love, the affection of a father or older brother.  This “amorevolezza” is described perfectly in the Circular Letter on Punishments, a quote that can be analogically applied to every religious: “Before all, if we want to present ourselves as friends of the authentic good of all our students, if we want to oblige them to fulfill their duties, we should never forget that we represent the parents of these beloved youth….  If then you have to be true parents of your students, it is necessary that you have the hearts of parents and never use repression and punishment without reason;” and further on, “Stay firm in looking for good and in preventing evil; be, nevertheless, always gentle and prudent.  Be persevering and kind, and you will see how God will make you lords over the least docile hearts…”  Remember the religious that “over all must be mother since she bears children by the cross, by prayer, by apostolic zeal, by example, and by announcement.”  The saint finishes by recalling that the work is God’s: “remember that education is the business of hearts and that God is the Lord of the hearts.  We can do nothing if God does not teach us the art and we do not put the keys in His hand.”

Every community will really be such if they live the words of St. Paul: Charity is patient and kind…. It bears all things, hopes all things, believes all things, endures all things (1 Cor 13:4, 7).  The effectiveness of this life is that it always has a spirit of sacrifice, a great patience, charity, benevolence towards all, “works, community duties, contradictions… harshness, all these are little to her who immolates herself with generosity and unlimited confidence in God.”  All in them must be expressed in the language of love, including punishments themselves.  Through charity we show our knowledge of and desire to unite ourselves with God Who has first loved us.
f: St. Francis Xavier Cabrini, “Pensamientos y Propósitos,” p. 191. Cf. 1 Jn 4:19.

t: To achieve this environment of charity it is necessary that the students not only be loved but also feel love.  On this the saintly pedagogue insisted frequently; in writing to the directors he described a dream he had and said that in their Oratories the best is lacking: love, in such a way “that the youth be not only loved but give an account of those who love them.”  In the same letter he reminds that if in those moments there was no joy and liveliness it is because there was no charity.  It is for this that Superiors should always appear like fathers: “who love what the youth like, and the youth love what pleases the Superiors.  In this way the work will be very bearable.  The cause of the present change in the Oratory is that a good number of youth do not have confidence in the Superiors.  Formerly all hearts were open to the Superiors, because of which the youth loved and obeyed promptly.  But now the Superiors are considered only as such and not as fathers, brothers, friends.”  Much to the contrary, “if we want to present ourselves as friends of the authentic good of all our students, if we want to oblige them to fulfill their duties, we should never forget that we represent the parents of these beloved youth…”  It is the same for the religious.
f: Carta sobre el espíritu de familia, OF, p. 614. Ibid, p. 615-616. Carta circular sobre los castigos, OF, p. 598.

t: Because of this, the Superiors must be those tried in virtue and possessed of a great charity: “Those in charge of this Oratory, since all exercise the title of charity, should fulfill it for each with zeal, since it is a tribute that lends itself to the divine Majesty; therefore they should all mutually encourage one another to persevere in their respective positions and to fulfill their duties conscientiously.”
f: Reglamento, part II, ch. 1, art. 1.  Cited by Pablo Sivak, op. cit. p. 321.

t: Your presence should be seen only as that of a father concerned for his children.  Therefore better than words are deeds that move, and thus: “the Superior must be all things for all people, always ready to listen to every doubt or lament of the youth, all eyes to paternally watch over his conduct, all heart to seek the spiritual good of his subordinates and the temporal welfare of those whom providence has entrusted to his care.”
f: Carta sobre el espíritu de la familia, OF, p. 617.

t: If this love reigns, punishments are not necessary since those who have to obey have the same mind as the superiors in love.  In those moved by love, there is no room for fear, since there is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; for fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not reached perfection in love (Jn 4:18).  And when punishment is necessary, they themselves see the necessity of this punishment and the benefit meant by it.  Still, when punishing we must show the love of Mothers, showing to them in it that we seek their good, and thus what Don Bosco teaches is perfectly applicable to the religious: “If then you have been true fathers of your students, it is because you have the hearts of fathers and never use repression and punishment without reason, without justice, but only as one who resigns himself to it by necessity and to fulfill a painful duty.”  For this reason the Superiors must try to make them love more than fear, since by charity the most obstinate and rebellious hearts yield: “charity and patience accompany you faithfully when you order and when you correct, and work with such fortune that all know by your deeds and words that you seek the good of souls.”  “Try, then, to attract them with love, moderation, or charity, not with arrogance or harshness, having with them the kindness that is suitable for every spiritual mother, according to the words of Our Lord: “Learn from Me for I am meek and humble of heart” (Mt. 11:29), imitating God of Whom we read: He disposed all things gently, avoiding principally imposing with violence our authority: God, in effect, has given us all freedom, and for this, he does not force anyone, but limits Himself to showing, to persuading.  Sometimes, nevertheless, it will be necessary to act with authority and severity, when it is reasonably required by the circumstances and personal needs, but even in this case, the only thing that must move us in charity and zeal for souls.”
f: “In general the system that we have to employ is called preventative, which consists in disposing in such a way the soul of the students, that without violence they yield to our desires.  In reminding you, then, of this system, I am trying to show you that you don’t have to use coercive means, but those of persuasion and charity (amorevolezza)” Carta circular sobre los castigos, OF, p. 598. Carta circular sobre los castigos, OF, p. 598. Recuerdo confidenciales a los Directores, OF, p. 550. Brevario de la Conferencia episcopal argentina, del testamento spiritual de Sta. Angela de Mérici, Virgen, II Lectura, 27 de Enero, p. 1346, tomo III.

t: Just as the soul behaves in the first act, principle of all the vital movements of man, by which we live, feel, and understand, so must be charity in the spiritual life: the first act, the principle by which all works are accomplished: “love is formally the life of the soul, like the soul is the life of the body.”  Love should be the life of the soul in such a way that the activities and all works be carried out are ordered to God, since all done in the spirit of charity does not seek anything other than His greater glory.
f: S.Th. II-II, 23, 2 ad 2.

t: In the Letter on the Spirit of Family, Don Bosco shows how the Oratory was no longer what it was before; it had neither joy nor liveliness because it did not have charity.  And the cause of all this change, including in what was religious, was because there was no trust between the Superiors and the youth, that is to say, because there was not familiarity: “the cause of the present change in the Oratory is that a good number of the youth do not trust the Superiors.  Once hearts were open to the Superiors, and because of this the youth loved and obeyed promptly.  But now the Superiors are considered only as such, not as fathers, brothers, and friends; therefore they are more feared than loved.”
f: Carta sobre el espíritu de familia, OF p. 615-6.

t: The solution is in breaking this distrust with true family spirit that has to live in the Oratory, which must be like the extension of a good family in which the youth grow: “familiarity with the youth, especially in recreation.  Without familiarity, affection cannot be demonstrated and without this demonstration there cannot be trust.  He that wishes to be loved must demonstrate that he loves.  Jesus Christ became little like the little ones and bore our infirmities.  Here is the teacher of familiarity!”
f: Ibid.

t: Only in the spirit of family, only in the spirit of trust that exists between parents, children, and siblings can the educative, religious, open to all, charitable, joyful and free environment live: “He that knows he is loved, loves, and he that is loved obtains all, especially from the youth.  This trust establishes itself like an electric current between youth and Superiors.  Hearts open and make known their needs and manifest their defects.  This love makes it so the Superiors can bear the fatigues, dislikes, ingratitude, lack of discipline, flippancy, and negligence of the youth.  Jesus Christ did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick.  Here we have our model.  Then there will not be one who works for vainglory; nor one who punishes to avenge his offended self-love; nor one who withdraws from the field of service for fear that others will have predominance; nor one who gossips about others to be loved and esteemed by the youth, to the exclusion of the other Superiors…; nor those who because of love of their own comfort, scorns the duty of attendance; nor those who for false human respect abstain from admonishing those who need to be admonished.  If this effective love exists, it will not look for anything more than the glory of God and the good of souls.”

Charity and patience are recommended to be practiced by all towards one another so as to bear each other's defects, and that it be preferred to fasts and penances. The charity of those who order and the charity of those who obey should make an environment like that of the little family of Nazareth reign, where there was no place for rumors, anger, sadness, envy, conflicts, or quarrels proper to those who do not have the spirit of Christ.  If there is someone who is not disposed to live in this way, he should be removed from the Oratory, since being in it, he is not of it:  “charity and patience with one another in order to bear with the defects of others, to promote the good reputation of the Oratory, of those in charge, and to encourage all to esteem and trust the Rector, are things that are insistently recommended to all; without them we will not succeed in maintaining order or in advancing the glory or God and the good of souls.
f: “Avoid austerity in food.  Your mortifications should consist in the faithful completion of your duties and in bearing the defects of others” Recuerdo confidenciales a los Directores, OF, p. 550. Reglamento, part II, ch. II, art. 4.  Cited by Pablo Sivak, op. cit., p. 321.

h: Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory
t: Following in the footsteps of Don Bosco, regarding the Oratory, we must see the creative genius who knew well the different situations of the youth and gave them an adequate answer moved by an eminent pastoral charity.

h: Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory
t: Because of this we must know how to be docile and creative, resolute and reflective at the same time.  We should how to be attentive to the situations of our time: “it is necessary to try to know our time and adapt ourselves to it.”
f: Memorias Biográficas, XVI, p. 416.

h: Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory
t: We must return to the spirit the oratory had in the time of its creator since it should be “a house for those who lack one…”

h: Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory
t: Don Bosco uses these pastoral categories referring to other enterprises: “I propose to enter their houses...bring them to church (parish)...sit next to them in school...be their friend during the hours of recreation.”
f: Epistolano, vol. IV, p. 320.

h: Chapter 5: Qualities of Those who Work in the Oratory
t: To grasp in depth that which an authentic Oratory should be – or to form our activities according to the spirit of the Oratory – means to know how to constantly adapt the works and activities to the condition of the youth and to the cultural transformations that shake the world of the youth.  That is to say, to be docile to the will of the Lord and to the mission received of transmitting the Gospel, especially to the youth.  And this search should be holy and enthusiastic (santamente apasionada).
f: Cfr. Iuvenum Patris, 1: " La Iglesia en este período cercano al año 2000, se siente interpelada por su Señor, a mirar a los jóvenes con especial amor y esperanza, viendo su educación como una de sus primeras responsabilidades pastorales".

t: Now we will treat of the Oratory in its broad sense, that which we can call “the oratorian spirit.”

In this sense we consider that the “first Oratory” should be the family.  Every good family should see that the children do not have idle hours, but that they amuse themselves virtuously, after having completed their daily duties, and on feast days, their religious duties.
The high schools, elementary and middle schools, etc.  that are like a second home, should stand out because of its oratorian spirit, forming “good Christians and honest citizens.”
f: Reglamento, part II, ch. II, art. 6.

t: Each community of our little Religious Family also should live this spirit of healthy recreation and contagious joy, founded on the fulfillment of religious duties. Consider always that “God is the first served.”
f: San Benito, cited by John Paul II, San Benito, patrono y protector de Europa: su mensaje para nuestro tiempo, (Sept. 29, 1980); OR (Oct. 5, 1980).

t: It is also the spirit that must live in the popular missions, especially in the Children's and Youth Misssions, but also, in its own way, in the other forms of mission.

In a special way this oratorian spirit should live in our aspirancies, postulancies, novitiates, and juniorates.  It lives when in these the first place, the most important, is give to God and to His Kingdom.  It lives when it works, taking advantage of the present time (Eph 5:16; Col 4:5), in its educative, religious, and all-embracing environment, an environment of joy and freedom, of charity, and of true family.
Likewise this oratorian spirit should live in the times of rest or recreation like: convivencias, camps, field trips, outings, conferences, congresses, floral games, etc.

For example, for us it is inconceivable for us to organize camps that are not “schools of life,” that is to say, without discipline, without a strong religious mark.  Usually we organize them with two intense periods of prayer: in the morning, Holy Mass; in the afternoon, Eucharistic Adoration, or the Rosary if they are laity.  At night, give them “good nights.”  This simple plan works for all the other activities.

h: Chapter 2: Applications of the Oratorian Spirit
t: Finally, we consider that this oratorian environment, climate, or spirituality is nothing other than the expression of our spirituality “of the Incarnate Word” in concrete environments.  At its roots, it is nothing other than the prolongation of a good Catholic family in these environments.

h: Chapter 2: Applications of the Oratorian Spirit
t: In other words, similar to the Christian family, the oratorian spirit is like a “spiritual womb.”  Just as the family is a community of persons in love, a communion in love, so our houses must be communities of charity, to the point that one could say that in them lives Christ Himself.

h: Chapter 2: Applications of the Oratorian Spirit
t: We consider that this oratorian spirit, in order to be molded of our spirituality, should be lived principally in the families from where  it is extracted as way of life, in religious communities, in our schools, in seminaries, in times of rest, and finally in festive or daily oratories in imitation of Don Bosco.
Directory of Works of Mercy

We know through Sacred Scripture that “God is love” (1 Jn 4: 16). He loves himself as highest good.  But we also know that his good tends to communicate itself, it is for that that God, infinite goodness, created the universe. By this work of his love, God not only participate being to the creature, but makes her fertile, giving her the power to diffuse that good by virtue of his same Love, the Holy Spirit: “the Spirit of God swept over the waters” (Gen 1:2). In this way, the universe will be able to reach the end for which it was created.

Within the goods participated by God to the creature is Freedom. It is given to spiritual beings, who by contrast to material beings, must reach their end freely. Moreover, with freedom appears the possibility of not reaching that end, or of the existential breakdown.

This possibility is made actual through sin, which is no other than the rejection of God and of his love. First a certain number of angels fell in sin, “because the devil has sinned from the beginning” (1 Jn 3: 8), afterwards, our first parents also fell, and through them, all the human race: “just as through one person sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and thus death came to all, inasmuch as all sinned” (Rom 5:12).

Before the lack of love of man, God answers with love, well then, he logically applied his justice in order to reestablish the alternated order: “The LORD God therefore banished him from the garden of Eden” (Gen 3: 23), also he was merciful when he promised a redeemer to the offspring of Eve. “In God, the Spirit of love changes the dimension of the human sin in a new gift of salvific love”. Therefore then, before the misery of the creature, the answer of God is mercy, who “in the preaching of the prophets signifies a special potency of love which is prevalent over sin and the infidelity of the chosen people.
It is interesting to recover this iidea of the divine mercy as potency of the love which conquers evil throughout the length of the history of mankind.

Our Father, who is a God “rich in Mercy” (Eph 2: 4), had mercy on the people of the covenant. From the deeds most worthy of praise of the Old Testament, we can record: the beginning of the history of the Jews, where the Israelites fall into idolatry, and in consequence are burdened by their enemies, therefore they called on Yahweh, and obtained his mercy; the prayer of Salomon at the inauguration of the temple; a part of the propheti intervention of Micah: “[he] does not persist in anger forever, but delights rather in clemency, and will again have compassion on us, treading underfoot our guilt” (Mic 7: 18-19); the securities offered by Isaiah; The supplication of the exiled; the renovation of the covenant after the exile. Physical evil as much as moral evil make the children of Israel have recourse to mercy. That is what David does for the gravity of his sin, Job in his disgrace, Esther before the threat for her people, etc….

When the fullness of time had come, by the work of the Holy Spirit, the Word was made flesh. “Christ is the revelation and the incarnation of the mercy of the Father, he then comes to reveal and to incarnate his merciful love. He reveals and incarnates therefore the mercy of God which is the potency of the love which conquers evil, by means of the greatest work of mercy ever know which is the redemption of humankind by the blood of his cross, with which he kills the root of all evil, which is sin. Work which eliminates even the effects of sin. When St. John sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?” (Lk 7:19), our Lord answers: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind regain their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the good news proclaimed to them” (Lk 7:22).

In this way, “Christ manifested man to man in the revelation of the mystery of the Father”. Our redeemer then reveals the mercy of God in accepting the cross, with which the  love of the Father is concretely shown. As the old Adam rejected the love of God, so Christ is the new Adam who teaches man that only in accepting the mercy of God can he love the Father.
Our religious family, another prolongation of the Incarnation of the Word, “to incarnated in all of man”, humbly desires by means of the works of mercy to:

Continue to reveal to men the merciful love of God for mankind, and continue to incarnate it through all types of works of benevolence and with it, to alleviate many evils which befalls upon the actual man. So that moreover by the testimony ofcharity many brothers may know God “so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your heavenly Father” (Mt. 5:16).
To love God, well then the concrete love of brothers is the unique way possible to love God, as the apostle moreover affirms: “he that says he loves God, and does not love his brothers is a liar”.

Our institute by this, desires to follow the wheel of the Incarnate Word, who not only came to redeem us from sin, but subjected himself to its effects, given that he passed through this world, healing men from their physical and spiritual miseries, through which he gave a concrete proof of his mercy and of his love for thee Father.
“Mary is the one who in a singular and exceptional way experienced…mercy…and has made it possible with the sacrifice of her heart the proper participation of the revelation of Divine Mercy.

“This maternity of Mary is the economy of the grace always strong since the assent… in the Annunciation which remained without change at the foot of the Cross until the perpetual consummation of the elects.
Therefore the religious, who must have the charge of a work of mercy, whether corporal or spiritual, must imitate the Blessed Virgin Mary in her Merciful maternity.

The specific and singular end of the institute of the Incarnate Word is the evangelization of culture, and it is precisely the spiritual works of mercy that are more in symphony with this end, and are the ones that diffuse better the good.

But like the redemption of our Lord Jesus Christ reaches all of man, our mission will be to “prolong the Incarnation ton all man, in all of man, and in all the manifestations of man”. And because as Redeemer He did as such, we would like to also practice the corporal works of mercy. Those in which, giving a concrete testimony of charity will win many men for the kingdom of Christ, giving glory to God and saving many souls, fulfilling in this manner our universal end. Fulfilling as well with the specific end of our family, “as testimony, firstly, to all the members of our religious institutes that “charity, and only charity will save the world. Blessed are those who have the grace of being victims of charity” and of that charity is indispensable for the evangelization of the culture, as the end worked for, and the end of the work, in any contrary case, one will never reach “the civilization of love”.

The religious of our Institute who dedicates herself specifically to the works of mercy much bring forth to its fullness a fertile spiritual maternity, …this maternity will be able to express itself as a solicitude for men, especially for the most needy: the sick, the handicaps, the abandoned, the orphans, the elderly, the children, the youth, the homebound, etc…

A consecrated woman encounters in this way the Bridegroom, different and unique, in all and each one, according to his same words “when have you done something for one of these and have not done it for me?” (Mt. 25: 40).

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: All the works of charity that we will be able to do to benefit others, suppose from our neighbor a necessity and in us the desire to remediate him, under the impulse of the virtue of mercy. Precisely mercy, which is the act of charity, moves us to exercise benevolence, which is its exterior act, more typical and characteristics.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: Mercy is one the virtues which refers to the neighbor that is most recommended in Sacred Scripture. “The merciful does well to himself; one with a hard heart, condemns himself” (Pv 11: 17).; “I prefer mercy rather than sacrifice…” (Hos 6:6). Our Lord puts us as model to his Father: “Be merciful as your Heavenly Father is merciful” (Lk 6:36) and moreover makes of it the object of a beatitude: “blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy” (Mt 5:7).

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: What is mercy? St. Thomas Aquinas, following Saint Augustine, defines it as “a type of internal compassion before the present misery, which moves and impels us to release it if possible”. It is called mercy because it makes man’s heart compassionate before the present misery (“miserum cor”).

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: Following the merciful compassion of the human misery, it occurs that we are sorrowful of the present evils or miseries for a double motive: “either because we love our neighbor in such a way that his disgraces affect us as if they were our own, or because the present importunacy can easily become ours and submerge us in an identic calamity”. For that reason, the elderly and weak are more inclined to mercy that the strong and powerful, whose abilities does not help them in overcoming evil. This is particularly applicable to a woman, for a “woman has a comprehensible heart, which permits her to confer a delicate and concrete style to charity.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: This is how our mercy has this double foundation. In exchange, only God is compassionate of us, because he loves us as his own.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: What is the dignity of the virtue of mercy? St. Thomas answers:

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: “In itself, mercy is the highest of all virtues, for it corresponds to watch over the unfornate, and remediate their deficiencies or disgrace, what properly belongs to the superior. For this reason, mercy is most proper of God and in it shines His omnipotence in the highest level”.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: “With relation to who has it, mercy is not the greatest virtue, for it doesn’t make the one who possesses the greatest, that is to say, that he has none above him, but all under him; hence, for the one who holds one above him, it is for him greater and better to unite himself to the superior than to remedy the defect of the inferior. For this reason, for man that has God for superior, charity, with which he unites himself to Him, is better and more excellent than mercy with which he helps the deficiencies of his neighbor. But, among all the virtues that looks to the neighbor, mercy is the highest because its act is also superior, for it does not limit itself to compassion for the present miseries, but also remedies them, and this is what is proper of the superior and the better”.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: Benevolence properly is an act of the virtue of charity, but it depends on mercy when this moves us to help the neighbor in his needs, in such a way that the other works of benevolence coincide with the words of mercy, for they are its exterior act, realized under the interior impulse of mercy. Benevolence manifest itself principally in charity in relation to corporal things, and by fraternal correction in what refers to spiritual things; but also, it belongs to it all that is called works of mercy, from which one of the most important is the apostolate, directed to the neighbor practicing the good and with it reaching eternal happiness.

h: Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General
t: All that is done under the impulses of mercy for the good of the neighbor is a true work of mercy. But the tradition of the Church from the ancient times lists fourteen; seven corporal and seven spiritual. St. Thomas studied the works of mercy when speaking of Charity, which is a part of benevolence, and also divided them into seven corporals and seven spiritual in conformity with the diverse deficiencies of the neighbor.

In consequence, it will attend with diligence and in a personal manner to the poor and needy, in a special way, to those who are lacking what is indispensable for a life worthy of dignity.

h: Chapter II: The corporal works of Mercy
t: “The poor are Christ: ‘they represent the image of the Song of God’; the pilgrims are Christ: ‘receive them as the same Christ’; the children are Christ, the one who receives them ‘receives me’ (Mt. 18:5); in all men, it is Jesus hidden in the depth of his soul’. Hence said St. Augustine: ‘in Him we are christs and Christ’”.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: It is one of the most urgent and indispensable works of Mercy, because although those of the spiritual order are more important, by prudence the oportune moment to exercise it can differ, as is the case with fraternal correction; on the contrary, the hungry cannot wait.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: It is sure thing that in the world today there is hunger, and that instead of bettering the situation, it becomes worse each time. A problem that is thrown into the hands  of hopelessness and of human degradation of the multitude of our brothers in the five continents of the terrestrial globe.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: Saddness is another emotional sign of the people that live in a cronic hunger; sadness that not even the stimulating action of alcoholism can extinguish.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: The hungry, finally, under his diverse forms, drags along with himself a great load of miseries and moral degradation.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: Our religious family considers that global solution of the problem will give in base to the practice of a strict justice, completed by the most beloved charity.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: For this reason, it will be precise to establish in the world social justice, as it is understood and propagated by the Catholic Church. Our institute will try to diffuse the social doctrine of the Church through conferences, courses, systematic studies in our communities and especially houses of formation. But it is not only because of lack of knowledge that this doctrine has not been implanted in the world, but more because of egoism, and definitely because of lack of charity. Therefore, this formation on the social doctrine must be integral, instilling intellectually the principles of social justice, but at the same time forming men capable of molding it with charity.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: Charity, in effect, is the unique solution, complete and adequate, of the problem of hunger. When we assert to see in our hungering neighbor a brother who is suffering, a suffering member of Christ, the generous and splendid rescue will spontaneously blossom like a sweet exigency of Christian Charity.

h: Article 1: To give food to the hungry
t: “As to the poor, we must always have them be with us, over all giving them food. We will not be afraid that there will not be enough for us, God is never outdone in generosity.

To set out to relieve these necessities is a great work of charity and mercy.  We must not forget that in the condemning sentence of Christ, this inexorable clause is figured: “Because I was naked and you did not clothe me” (Mt 25:43); while in the contrary, the other gives a guarantee of eternal salvation: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (Mt 25: 36).

One of the most opportune ways with which our Institute will be able to exercise this great work of mercy, is to contribute to it with the greatest generosity, to the sustainment of wardrobe of charity where the circumstances require them.

It will be moreover appraisable to ferment among our lay people this works of mercy. Among other things, they can promote traditional pious works, such as dressing a poor child on the day of Christmas, in memory of the Child of Bethlehem, or dressing the whole family on the day of the Holy Family, or dressing children of indigenous families for their First Communion, etc…

And give to all the honor that is due to them, especially to our brothers in the faith (Gal 6:10) and to the pilgrims. Hence, following the announcement of any stranger, the superior and the monks will set off for the encounter with the most obsequious charity”.

t: In the world today there is presented a grave problem intimately related to the work of mercy that we are speaking about: the problem of housing. This brings disastrous consequences that this situation has to produce in the physical, intellectual, and moral order of the peoples.

t: Lastly, our Institute will be able to intervene directly through the creation of Nursing homes, homes for children, residences for youth, etc...
The key to the problem of suffering, one of whose inexorable manifestations is sickness, is only given through Divine Revelation.

God does not make suffering. Hi primitive plan for humanity excluded it positively. But with the catastophe of original sin, God handed over to man all classes of physical and moral sufferings (Gen 3: 16-19) and removed the preternatural gifts of integrity, impassibility, and immortality. As the consequence the body was left subject to suffering, to sickness, and to death “and thus death came to all, inasmuch as all sinned” (Rom 5: 12).

But sickness more than being a chastisement, is also medicine that not only heals, but also can preserve from future sins and move to good. It can follow that one who has not committed any faults is assailed in temporal things so that he may look for the spiritual which is superior. Many of the afflictions of the present life are hence permitted by God solely to humiliate us and try us.

Sickness as well is an instrument of salvation, for many men have thence encountered God. Also it is a fount of grace for all the good Samaritans that exercise this work of mercy: doctors, nurses, etc. For this reason, it is as well very important the apostolate with doctors, assistants, nurses, etc…

The sick as well as all who lovingly take care of him, obtain many graces, not only for themselves, but also for the whole Church. St. Paul says that he fulfills in his flesh what is lacking in sufferings of Christ through his body which is the Church. Therefore, no one but the sick can better complete with his meritorious suffering the work of the Redemption. “and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if only we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom 8:17).

The religious must know how to teach the sick to suffer and the value of suffering, just as Christ who became one with us to be able to save us, it is permitted us to do the same as well… “Without our suffering, it will not be an excellent social work and service, but neither will it be the work of Christ, and it will not form part of the Redemption” for the “Cross is the only way of life, the sign of the predestined, the scepter of the kingdom of holiness, … ‘ it is the fountain of all blessings, the origin of all graces’”.

This work of mercy must be practiced with a true Christian spirit, which supposes, before all, the intention to thank God, serving him in the members of Christ. It is for him that while this work is a true fountain of merits for the one who does it, it must be realized with faith, seeing in the sick the same Christ who suffers in one of the members of the Mystical Body “Come you blessed of my Father… because I was sick and you visited me” (Mt 25: 34-40). When another spirit does not move us to give completely of ourselves, it is then that the sense of this work of mercy is completed. This is not to say that other human finalities does not move us with the visit: to cure the sick, the console them, to comfort the family, etc., but the formality of all this must be to attend the sick as a suffering member of Christ.

Following charity, the principal motor, we must fundamentally preoccupy ourselves of the spiritual health of the sick, animating him and lifting up in a holy manner his sickness, to see in it the expression of the merciful will of God, and preparing him for the worthy reception of the Holy Sacraments. Sickness makes it possible for many sick people to approach for the first time the sacraments, it is for that that our solicitude will be very important, working with his family and especially when this oppose itself to the Sacraments of Confession and the Anointing of the Sick by fear of the fear that this will produce in the patient. Due to the psychological alteration in which  the sick find themselves, it will be more convenient to arm ourselves with patience and abnegation in order to fulfill its exigencies. Same with prudence and delicacy in order to avoid disliking him or afflicting him or rousing in the soul sentiments of rancor, impatience and other similar things, creating a climate of peace which is founded on the knowledge that God does not allow evil but with a gaze at the greater good.

Our Institute will show particular solicitude in the exercise of this work of mercy, trying with all means that they be no sick without spiritual attention nor who come to die without receiving the Holy Sacraments.

In our houses of formation, this idea must be inculcated. The religious will put great care in the attention of the sick, above all in the ones that are in grave situation, so that all the activities of the religious must be oriented to the salvation of the souls and will be a grave responsibility before God if because of her negligence or fault of zeal, one of these souls die without due spiritual attention, which includes, according to  CIC; the apostolic blessing with plenary indulgence in the article of the dead which will be procured to the sick.
We must put all the means for the attention of the sick members of the Institute, given that they are “key pieces” of our religious family.

As well the Lay people who in some manner are instilled to our religious Institute will need to be formed in this respect. Especially those who deal directly with the sick as for doctors and nurses; organizing in the measure possible, courses, conferences, congress of training, etc., in order to serve better the sick, helping so that others may participate in his service.

It is important to have present the obligations that a catholic doctor has. He must in his part take account of this, yet at the cost of sacrifices and extraordinary studies, to bring back the health of the sick; to freely attend to the poor sick; to never attempt to go against the health, nor the life of the soul in order to save the body, even it be the difficult parts, trying to save the life of the mother and the child never without attempting to go directly against the life of one of the two, nor never provoking abortion to save the mother, baptizing any aborted fetus in the form prescribed by the Church, even if it is few days, never giving immoral advises in the pretext of corporal health and advising with time the family and the priest for the administration of the Sacraments.

It is of capital importance in our days, now being for the high testimony of charity that are offered, as for the gravity and the risk that are enclosed for society many sickness or situations such as AIDS, homosexuality, drug addiction, etc. that our Institute studies this problem in order to later try to solve it in a concrete manner.

One will be able to occupy herself of all the aforementioned by way of chaplaincies, lay groups, and included the erection of centers of first help, dispensaries, hospitals or houses of special internship, were the situation obliges it.

Another way to visit the sick will be to bring the pilgrim image of any devotion of our Lady, now that “Mary Most Holy continues being the loving Consolation of much physical and moral pains, that afflict and torment humanity. She knows our suffering and our pains because she as well suffered, since Bethlehem to Calvary: ‘ and a sword will pierce your heart’”, and as well incorporating the sick in any confraternity in which he can offer his suffering for the salvation of souls, etc.

The spirit who informed this great work of mercy in the centuries in which it had immediate application (some Religious Orders were founded, principally that of the Trinitarians, founded by St. John of Mata and approved by Inocent III in 1198, and the Mercedarians, founded by Saint Peter Nolasco and Saint Raymond of penafort and approved by Gregory IX in 1235) can be expanded today in various forms, principally visiting prisoners to bring them our help and our advise and redeeming the moral and material slavery of so many disgraceful victims of the same.
a).  Visit to the prisoners

Our Lord reminds us of that phrase which will sound with the judgement: “I was in prison and you did not visit me” (Mt 25:43). Saint Paul says:  “Remember the prisoners, as if you yourself were a prisoner with them, and of those who suffer bad treatement, as if it was in your body” (Heb 13:3).

Our Institute will have to put particular interest in the apostolate of Jail, following the weel of the Incarnate Word who came to free the captives and oppressed, for all that was anteriorly mentioned and because the correct meaning of prisons has been lost in our days, now that they are converted in spiritual prisons. In this way, great importance will be given to the periodical visit and catechesis to the prisoners. We have the example of St. Joseph Cafasso, who awoke religious vocations from the women’ jails, as the life written by the Cardinal Carlos Salotti relates to us. In this way, one will look to provide them with good literature and if possible, to help his family spiritually as well as materially.
b). The redemption of moral and material slavery
Moreover, other forms of slavery can be: work; men trapped into economical ambitions; drugs; alcoholism, etc.

These diverse forms of moral and material captivity can be suppressed or alleviated by Christian charity, for that reason, our Institute in the midst of its possibilities will look to alleviate these situations, showing the true meaning of life and the place things must have, teaching men how to have fun, to rejoice in the true Christian joy.

The cadaver of a Christian is a sacred relic. During his life he was the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19), and one day, at the command of the word of God, it will gloriously resurrect from among the dead, to be eternally happy in mansions glory (1 Ts 4: 13 – 18).
Nevertheless, the cadaver of a man inspires of itself horror, and consequently is a work of mercy toward the deceased, to remove him from the sight of men and to give him a christian burial.

It is here the recompense that one obtains from God for her charity, communicated by the archangel Raphael to the same Tobias: “when you, Tobit, and Sarah prayed, it was I who presented and read the record of your prayer before the Glory of the Lord; and I did the same thing when you used to bury the dead. When you did not hesitate to get up and leave your dinner in order to go and bury the dead,  I was sent to put you to the test. At the same time, however, God commissioned me to heal you and your daughter-in-law Sarah. I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who enter and serve before the Glory of the Lord." (Tb 12: 12-15).

The death of a dear being signifies a great pain. It is for this reason that showing affection, charity and compassion, united to the cadaver of a dear being reaches to the depths of the soul, and his memory will never leave a thankful heart.

As well, it is a great work of mercy given that if comforts the private debtors of a dear being and makes his heart turn more probably towards God, for the testimony of charity which it signifies, and because strengthened in the faith and in hope grants him to value the ephemeral of this life, and the permanent of eternal life.
Our Institute will consider of vital importance this type of apostolate which in another way is a field each time more invaded by the sects, with the fatal consequences which follow from them.

resuming what must be our spirit in the practice of the works of mercy, let us remember the exhortation of Mother Teresa: “we are not here for the work. we are for Jesus. Before all we are religious. not social assistants, teachers, nurses, doctors. we serve Jesus in the poor…all that we do… all for Him. Our life do not have another meaning. This is the thing that many do not understand. We serve Jesus 24 hours a day and He gives us strength. We love Him in the poor and the poor with Him, but always the Lord first”.
f: Cf. Il sorriso dei poveri, Aneddoti di Madre Teresa di Calcutta, Citta Nouva Editrice, Roma, 1982, p. 17.

t: To teach the ignorant
To give counsel to the needy
To correct the wrong
To console the sad
To forgive injuries
To suffer with patience the one who afflict us
To pray to God for the living and the dead

These works are the ones who are more oriented towards our cultural end, for we are conscious that the great battle of our time is intellectual, given that it consists in eliminating error, fundamentally the sin against light, of militant atheism, of liberalism to the maximum, of the ideologies, of all idolatries, and in the last place of the ignorance of God.

We have here one of the greatest works of mercy that we can exercise for the benefit of the neighbor. The human intelligence has a thirst for truth over all for the transcendental and eternal Truth revealed by the Incarnate Word, and they are so many that have not encountered it yet, or at least have not glimpsed at it completely.

So it is understood that the principal ignorance of this work of mercy must take care of dissipating, is the one which refers to religion and the eternal destiny of man. There is no worse ignorance than what this refers to, although a great saying or nobel prize suffers it in the order of human knowledge.

Saint Paul warns us explicitly that “the wisdom of this world is nothingness before God” (1 Cor 3:19). Nevertheless, however in small steps, it is also a great work of mercy to teach the ignorant the things that they need for their human life here in the world, for grace builds on nature.

Certainly, it will be important to offer to the individual through education the means necessary for employ themselves in society. And like this our colleges will be able to be oriented to teach and read and write to the poor and illiterate, faciliting the indispensable mean as for an intellectual education proportional to his talent. This will be repeated in the high schools, and universities. But the fundamental end that we must move toward in the educational apostolalte, will be to form youths that have a “spirit of principle”, youth that distinguish but do not separate the human and the divine as is demonstrated in the Incarnate Word. Youths that want a world where lay people and religious united, fight so that truth and virtue might reign. Hence, it seems to us that all our educational establishments, primary, secondaries, and superior must  bring forth in its midst the impression of a true human and theological formation. Feeding itself in the classical culture and in the permanent values of the spirit and of faith, for it is faith the one that allows man to attain the highest object of the intellect, which is God. And in this manner to edify over the rock which is Christ, the only mean to inculturate the Gospel. Only in this way will we be able to bring souls “to the unity of the faith and the full knowledge of the Son of God, to the state of the perfect man, attaining the stature proper to the whole Christ” (Eph. 4: 13).

Another way to teach the one who does not know is to publish, propagate, and profusely distribute books, pamphlets, journals, newpapers, religious articles, computer programs, etc. “Through the oral and written word, we want to prolong the Word”. For it, we must count with our own editorials.

Also, this must realize itself through the apostolate of modern means of communication, through all types of recording, whether videos or audios, as well as radios and television programs. For all, this is precisely to dispose of all the equipment necessary.

To collaborate with all the means at our reach for the great work of the propagation of the faith among the unfaithful world. There are more than 2,000 millions of pagans in the entire world that have not yet received that message of Jesus Christ, nor consequently baptism. For that reason, it seems to us indispensable that our Institute, prioritize that foundations in mission lands. For this, we must form suitable missionaries in the ministry of the word, catechisis, popular missions, spiritual retreats, etc. And so well the best mean to help the missions consists, without any doubt, to offer them missionaries, and this as well will be able to bring us to implement an adequate pastoral to attract native vocations.

h: Article 2: To give good counsel to the one who needs it
t: Many are the souls who give the definitive orientation of their lives to the way of the good to a good advice given opportunely by a friend or a good person who separated them from an irreparable going astray. There are personal situations that cannot revolve itself with agreement for the own interest, but which need the orientation and advice of a prudent and experiemented person.

h: Article 2: To give good counsel to the one who needs it
t: But it is necessary that the advice feeds on charity, in such a way that one advised can really make use it. For this reason, one must evade from showing airs of superiority to the advised, and of the advice and occasion of shame and humiliation in front of the others.

h: Article 2: To give good counsel to the one who needs it
t: This work of mercy speaks of a special reference to paternity, because it is proper to fathers to advise. Hence our religious must be true spiritual mothers, which implies a coherence of life and faith, in order to give effective advices over all in spiritual matters.

h: Article 2: To give good counsel to the one who needs it
t: Also, great importance will be given to form lay people in this way. It is rightful that the fathers illumine their children with their advices.

Fraternal correction is one of the greatest works of mercy. By fraternal correction, it is understood “the warning done to the culpable neighbor in private and for pure charity to separate him from sin”. It will be done in private and for pure charity because it is not justice that obliges it, but love; it will procure the reprehension of evil in so far as evil will wound the one who execute it, and not insofar as it wounds the common good or the good of a third party.

It is evident that if we have the natural obligation to help the neighbor in his corporal necessities, with greater motives will we have the obligation to help him in his spiritual necessities. “if your brother sins against you, go and reproach him in secret. If he listens to you, you will have won your brother over.” (Mt 18: 15). “If you are careless to correct, you will be worse than the one who sinned”.

We must practice this work of Mercy primarily in our religious family but also with anyone who needs it and always imbued with charity, patience, humility, prudence and discretion. The practice of fraternal correction, as it is described and pointed out in the Constitutions, will need to be a true distinction of our love for our neighbor.

In this respect as well, it will receive particular importance in our time, given the great confusion of ideas and the facility of its expansion, to direct this work of mercy towards the refutation of errors, knowing that we must hate the sin and not the sinner. And this for two reasons: first, for the good of the one erring, so that he may come out of his error. Second, for the common good, to correct the damages that the diffusion of the error has produced.

Sadness is a passion that comes from the appetite, in face of a present evil. Among all the passions, it is the one who harms more the body; St. Thomas Aquinas says: “it puts itself against the life of man with regard to the essence of its movement, and not only in respect to his medium or quantity as the other passions of the soul."
f: Ibidem, 37,4.

t: Each day there is more sadness in the world because each time there is more misery and less love to alleviate it. Many souls which have lost the illusion to live lie in graves in a great sadness and moral atmosphere, produced by the terrible fight with existence, the unsatisfied vital necessities, the reverse of fortune, imcomprehensions, sickenesses and death of dear ones. In these conditions, few charitable works can bring back the peace and joy life to many of these souls. But there can be nor can there be a more radical and profound consolation than the one who springs from the truths of the faith, for it shows that no disgrace is total and definitive, except the eternal lost of God. This is the fundamental idea that must come out of the souls beaten down by sadness.
St. Thomas Aquinas, among the  five remedies that can be opposed to sadness, numerates delight, the contemplation of truth, and the compassion of friends.

Delight is certaintly the repose of the appetite in a connatural good, in turn sadness comes from what is contrary to the appetite. And so, like all rest of the body is a remedy against any fatigue which provokes it in any natural cause, equally delight is a remedy to mitigate all sadness, whichever is within its providence.

Following this idea, our religious family will be able to alleviate many souls depressed by real or apparent evils, giving testimony of the Christian joy. This will be done individually by each of its members, or by means of artistic representations, musicals, theatres of any other type, which delight in the licit good of the said souls.

With this end, the testimony of the Christian joy acquires much relief, which our communities must give, in such a way that it can be said of them what was said of the first Christian: “ See how they love each other”. Our communities must show how the love of Christ separates from the darkness of sadness.

Analogically, in the interior of the community, a culminating moment in the practice of this work is constituted by the Eutrapelial activities in which trough the generous giving of each one to the communitarian recreation, joy is consequently brought forth.

The greatest delight that we can reach in this life is the contemplation of the truth, and given that all delight diminishes pain and sadness, we must conclude that delight in the truth is one of the most efficatious remedies against sadness.

All that is done to contemplate thetranscendental truth of God will be a great remedy therefore against sadness. This will necessarily bring one to contemplate the beauty of the Supreme Being. Beauty which participated to man, is encountered reflected principally in the great artistic works of humanity. Trough this, all that we do to diffuse and know the great works of art, painting, sculpture, music, etc. will be a highly positive contribution to the expansion of the human spirit which will alleviate it from the weight of sadness from small evils.

A friend who sympathizes with the sorrows of the other is naturally a consoler. First because he alleviates and lightens the burden of the neighbor, imitating our Lord who offers us His alleviation and rest. Second, because the condolence of a friend is a sign of love, and to feel loved is always consolation and joy.

This work of mercy constitute at the same time, an indispensable work of charity for the person itself, given aht the pardon of the neighbor depends that God pardons us, remembering always that “Charity covers a multitude of sins”.

The doctrine of Christ is clear and does not require any commentary: “You have heard it been said: you shall love your neighbor and hate your enemies. but I say to you: love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you so that you may be children of your father, who is in heaven, and who makes the sun rise over the bad and good and pours rain over the just and the unjust” (Mt 5: 43-45). Christ clearly explained this doctrine in the servant who owned ten thousand talents.

From this, we can deduce that this is not only a simple advise of perfection that we can accept or refuse without compromising our future salvation, all who want to persevere in the grace of God must forgive from all their heart, accepting this divine law.

Moreover, we must imitate Christ who practiced this doctrine in a heroic and sublime way especially on the cross. “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Lk 23: 34), and later he forgives the repentant thief: “I tell you solemnly, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Lk 23: 43).
Also, we must follow the example of the saints, among many, the example of St. Jane de Chantal, who became the godmother in baptism of one of the children of the assassin of her husband.

For this forgiveness to be authentically Christian, it must be Prompt “do not let the sun set on your anger” (Eph 4:26). Spontaneous, as is indicated in (Mt 5:23) that before presenting the offering, we must first forgive our brother. Unlimited, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times” (Mt 18:22). From the heart, not only the external forgiveness “Then in anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he should pay back the whole debt. So will my heavenly Father do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from his heart.” (Mt 18: 34-35). And for love of God, this is the most important condition for our forgiveness to be Christian and meritorious.

Our family of the Institute of the Incarnate Word will need to put special attention in the fulfillment of this work of mercy, loving our enemies and praying for those who persecute us, also included is a fact experienced for us that our greatest enemies have converted to be our greatest benefactors.

On account of the communitarian dimension, it is important to point out here in the paper the chapter of faults, in which the mercy not only must bring forgiveness to injuries, but also leads to profess greater esteem to the one who accuses himself.

h: Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us
t: Saint Paul in prison wrote to the Christians in Ephesus: “I, then (…) to live in a manner worthy of the call you have received, (…) bearing with one another through love, striving to preserve the unity of the spirit through the bond of peace”. In fact, charity must bring us to surpass the differences of temperaments, opinions, and ways of being that manifest itself in community life. Since it is only by means mutual comprehension and tolerance that it is possible to conserve peace and hope among men. “What man cannot correct in himself or in others must be supported with patience until God orders it in another way.”

h: Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us
t: The ultimate sustenance of all imperfections is the hereditary pain of original sin, who in other parts offers us the possibility of suffering for God on behalf of our brothers, as they suffer on our behalf.

h: Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us
t: Let us not forget that it belongs to small souls to see small defects in great men. Hence we must not allow little imperfections of our brothers to impede us from seeing the wonders that the grace of God realizes in them.

h: Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us
t: We also know that the Providence of God in respect material things is much less than its relation with spiritual things. For this reason, the damages in material things must not retract us from fomenting the spiritual goods.

h: Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us
t: This work of mercy must be exercise with all men, but we have the opportunity to practice it more correctly with our brothers in religion, in whom generally there is no intention to harm us, but even if there were, we will still be obliged to fulfill this work of mercy. “I have become all things to all, to bring them to Jesus Christ”

h: Article 7: To pray to God for the living and the dead
t: Charity is a friendship that has as its fundamental the common participation in the eternal Beatitude. Therefore we are obliged to practice this charity helping within our capacities, that all those who are able capable of salvation may arrive at it. The only ones that are excluded are demons of hell and the condemned.

h: Article 7: To pray to God for the living and the dead
t: It is clear and evident that with relation to the immense majority of men who live on earth, and the souls in purgatory, we cannot exercise our charity more than through prayer. To pray for the living and the dead is as well an indeclinable exigency of Christian charity.

h: Article 7: To pray to God for the living and the dead
t: In general, we must ask for all those to who we can extend our charity but in a special way we must ask for the most needy: the poor, pagans, sinners, dead, sick, etc. For those closest to us: brothers in religion, parents, friends, etc. For benefactors. For those who hear us or have hurt us.

h: Article 7: To pray to God for the living and the dead
t: Our Institute will need to inculcate in each one of its members the obligation to exercise this work of mercy. And moreover will offer sufferings and prayers, especially the Holy Mass, for its deceased members, the intention of the superiors, benefactors, enemies, etc.
